Hon. CHARLES MURPHY (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 209) to amend the Canada Temperance Act. He said: The proposed amendment to the Canada Temeprance Act relates only to the province of British Columbia. Its purpose is to enable a vote to be taken in that province under the Canada Temperance Act in the same, way as that a vote is taken under that Act in any other province. For instance, in the interpretation clause of the Canada Temperance Act, the word ' county ' as respects the province of British Columbia is defined to mean an electoral district therein in accordance with the division of the province for the election of members for the House of Commons. The 228J
legislature of British Columbia has passed an Act called the Counties Definition Act by which the province is divided int'O counties for certain purposes and it is proposed that the definition of ' County ' in the provincial Act shall be substituted for the present definition of ' County ' in the Canada Temperance Act.
Then the Canada Temperance Act, as it stands at present, contains no definition of a city or city municipality and it is proposed to introduce into the Act as far as British Columbia is concerned the definition of city or city municipality, which appears in another provincial Act of British Columbia, called the Municipal Clauses Act.
Part 1 of the Canada Temperance Act sets out the proceedings for bringing part 2 of that Act into force. The commencement of these proceedings is to be by the deposit of a notice and petition in certain designated offices for public examination. So faT as the province of British Columbia is concerned, those offices are restricted to the five electoral divisions that existed at the* time the Canada Temperance Act was revised. There are at present seven electoral divisions in British Columbia represented by seven gentlemen in this House, and it is proposed to correct that anomaly by the amendment in question.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have received the very regrettable information that a coloured clergyman who has been seen in the corridors of this building for a few days past, was instructed by the sergeant-at-arms to leave the building, not to frequent the building. We have a large number of coloured people in eastern Canada, a very respectable class of people, and I would like to know if it is correct that this has been done, and if so who is responsible for it. I hope it has not been done, because it would be a great pity that such a course should be adopted when a man is conducting himself respectably and well as I have seen him. I have not the honour of his acquaintance, but I understand he is a clergyman ol very high standing in the church.

maintopic: STRANGERS IN THE CORRIDORS OF PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
I think it is unfortunate that my hon. friend has not given to the House any more particulars. The House would be loath to believe that the se,rgeant-at-aTms, whose courtesy ifs well known, would be guilty of any act of *iiscourtesv to any coloured gentleman or anybody else, and at the present time we

maintopic: STRANGERS IN THE CORRIDORS OF PARLIAMENT.
speechtext: The reverend .gentleman referred to is a well known citizen of Hamilton, and a very respectable minister of the Methodist coloured church there. He told us yesterday that he had been soliciting subscriptions for his church as he has been dome- in years past, and as a great many other people, ladies and gentlemen, have done, but that he was spoken to by the sergeant-at-arms yesterday in a way that he thought rather rude. He tells me that he at once told the sergeant-at-arms that if there was any objection to his soliciting lie would stop at once, but that he claimed the right to be_ in any of the public portions of this building just the same as any other citizen. Then he says that a policeman was called and he was very much offended at that. I spoke to him and did my best to cool his anger. I told him I thought the better way would be to take no notice of it, and that I was quite sure the sergeant-at-arms could have no intention of offending him because he was coloured. He was very indignant find expressed himself very warmly, saying that though he was coloured he would not submit to be differently treated in any manner from anv other person in the country. That is all I know about it, and that is I think all that can be ascertained about it. I would not for a moment intimate that the sergeant-at-arms had any feeling against this gentleman on account of his colour. I believe that an expression of regret from the sergeant-at-arms to the gentleman personally would be the simplest solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to make some further allusion to the matter which the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) brought to the attention of the House yesterday. I was not aware that the hon. gentleman intended to mention this matter yesterday, and in what I said yesterday about it I was relying entirely on my memory. Of course it is impossible to keep in mind all the details of 2,000 or more similar cases which pass under consideration in the course of a twelve months. Since the House adjourned, however, I have verified my recollection with regard to this matter by referring to the past, and am therefore in a position to speak definitely and accurately at the present time. The article which the hon. gentleman read to the House is taken from the current April number of a journal called the 'Canadian Municipal Journal,' published I think in Mon-
Sir WILFRID LAURIER,
treal. It is entitled ' Where was the pull,' and pursuing the idea suggested by that caption, it proceeds to charge that two prisoners to whom clemency was extended by His Excellency some time ago, were released because their counsel, Mr. T. C. Robinette of Toronto, was a personal friend of mine, and a man who enjoyed with me a considerable amount of personal influence, or ' pull.' Speaking fropi memory, as I was yesterday, I could not feel absolutely sure that there might not be some memorial or certificate of character among the papers which bore the signature of Mr. Robinette among others. I did not think it was so, but I could not be absolutely positive. I wish now to state that in the first pla^e, Mr. Robinette was not counsel for the prisoners, or either of them, as stated in this article; nor was he concerned in any way whatever in the application for clemency on behalf of these prisoners, and did not in any way intervene in the matter even by so much as signing a petition or certificate as to the character of the men. In short, the fact is that he had no single thing to do with this matter any more than the hon. member who brought this matter to the attention of the House yesterday. Yet this article, in order to found its attack, states categorically :
Mr. Robinette, K.C., defended the prisoners -though it seems strange that an eminent lawyer should stoop to such a dirty case

and he, it is understood, is a personal friend of the minister.
The prisoners were defended by two gentlemen each of whom is a personal friend of mine quite as much so as Mr. Robinette. The gentlemen are Mr. Geo. Tate Black-stock, K.C., of Toronto, and his partner, Mr. Hugh Rose. These gentlemen are the men who made application for the clemency of the Crown in regard to their clients, the prisoners. The article in question states that these men were convicted for distributing obscene literature and post cards, that evidence was given by two stenographers that they had refused to work for the prisoners, so filthy was the business. After making other statements in regard to the case, the article proceeds :
The question that is now being asked is, ' Where is the pull ? '
Now, I am sorry to say, Mr. Speaker, that this article, like a good many other newspaper articles, relies upon its imagination for its facts. There is not merely inaccuracy in the statements I have referred to, there is what cannot be properly designated otherwise than untruth, in short. It is simply an instance of a newspaper writer fabricating his own news in his own back office. It is not a fact that two stenographers at the trial of these prisoners gave evidence that they had refused to

work for the prisoners so filthy was the business. No evidence whatever was given at the trial; the facts were admitted. It was in short a question simply whether upon the admitted facts the offence charged in reality existed. The offence charged had nothing to do with post cards, it was the circulating of obscene books, as they were called, tending to corrupt morals. The prisoners were either partners, or one the proprietor and the other the manager of a business in Toronto for the selling of books.
I have forgotten the name under which the business was done; but so far as the papers show, and so far as any report on the matter which I received, shows, the business was the ordinary legitimate business of respectable book selling. But among the volumes which had been sold by these men were such books as English translations of Balzac, of Petronius and other Latin authors, of Brantome, also a French writer; and undoubtedly in these books, which are classics, and which are to be found on the shelves of our own library or of any other large library, in these books are to be found passages, just as I need not say there are to be found passages in that best of books that we all revere, which, if they were singled out or collected and published together, might properly be described by the word indecent. But the business which these men were carrying on was of the legitimate character I have described. A prosecution was instituted against them. It is not for me to express an opinion of the judiciousness of that prosecution, but a prosecution was instituted against them, not for distributing obscene post cards, for there was nothing of the kind, but for circulating books said to be obscene and tending to corrupt morals. The learned judge, upon the admitted facts of the case, made a conviction and sentenced the two prisoners. In sentencing them he said that it had come within his knowledge, or that he had been told-I have forgotton the exact way in which he worded his remarks-that one of two young women who had been engaged as a typewriter by this firm, had been compelled to abandon the position by reason of the character of the work that she was called upon to do. There was no evidence of it, but that observation was made by the learned judge when passing sentence. There was sent to me an affidavit or statutory declaration from this young woman who said that she was the only woman employee of the business, that she was the stenographer and typewriter engaged by this firm, that she had been with them for some length of time, and that there was not one word of truth in the charge that she had been compelled to abandon her position by reason of the improper character of the work that she was called upon to do. That statement then, as this
other statement of fact to which I have adverted, is entirely without foundation in fact.
Now, with regard to the application for clemency, I have only to say this: The application was made by the solicitor whom I have mentioned. I received a large number of letters with regard to the case from prominent men, business men, men of standing not only in Toronto but in other parts of the country. I do not think it would be right that these letters should be made public. There is nothing in them to conceal, but of necessity any communications of this nature are of the most confidential character. The department must obtain information with regard to the reputation of prisoners in the community by all means available and unless all communications were permitted under the seal of confidence there would be an end to the possibility of obtaining information or getting the particulars with regard to each case which are of importance in order that the application for clemency may properly be dealt with. I, for the same reason, think that it would not be right even to mention the names of the writers of such letters. I will say simply that I have had letters with regard to this case and urging clemency from more than 25 people of undoubted respectability and standing in the community, such people as managers of banks in Toronto, clergymen, a bishop of the Protestant faith, three other prominent clergymen, one a leading clergyman in the Methodist church, and business concerns of different characters in the city of Toronto, who are acquainted with the prisoners and knew the style of business that they had been carrying on. 1 am quite content to hand to my hon. friend, or to any hon. gentleman in the House, a list of the writers of these letters which 1 have made and which I have before me, but do not wish to put it on ' Hansard.' Just one word more. I have had the advantage, in connection with this matter, of a personal discussion of the case with the At torney General of the province of Ontario, who. I am proud to be able to say, is another warm personal friend of my own, and who, perhaps, on that account, would have had some ' pull ' in the matter. He expressed his opinion to me in conversation with perfect freedom. He did more than that; in his capacity of Attorney General of the province, charged with the responsibility for the administration of criminal justice, and whose representatives prosecute in the province, he wrote me a candid, frank letter in the matter, which is upon tile, expressing his own views and his own recommendation in regard to this case. I seek to put no resDonsibility upon him in the matter, I willingly assume the whole responsibility myself. I gave the advice to His Excellency that these men should be sum-
7] 87

marily. released, because, in my humble judgment, speaking as a lawyer, they were not guilty of the offence with which they were charged.

I would like to draw the attention of the government to a report appearing in the Montreal ' Gazette ' a few weeks ago which, I think, has been referred to before. The article is a follows:
It is reported that government engineers employed in locating the Hudson Bay railroad have been obliged to 6top work, having come to an impassable obstacle in the shape of an extensive muskeg, which cannot be bridged. The country may have cause for satisfaction if a physical muskeg keeps it out of the financial muskeg into which the construction of the railway threatens to plunge it.
The ' Globe ' a few days ago, had the following statement:

A bottomless bog had been encountered on the survey of the Hudson Bay railway, the Montreal ' Gazette ' said in a recent issue. The writer added that if it prevented the building of the railway it would be a public benefit. Whether this attitude towards the Hudson Bay railway represents a majority of the people of the Dominion it is impossible to say, but that it represents a number who have given the subject some attention there can be no question.
This is followed by a long article which opposes the project of building the Hudson Bav railway. I would like to ask, on behalf of the west particularly which is greatly interested in this undertaking, whether the government has any knowledge of any impassable bog having been encountered, or whether it has any intention whatever of abandoning the project of having the Hudson Bay railway constructed in the near future?
I had noticed the articles in question to which my hon. friend (Mr. MacNutt) refers, and I communicated with the chief engineer, Mr. Armstrong,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: in reference to the statment that a bottomless bog or muskeg had been found on the proposed route of the Hudson Bay railway. The chief engineer informs me that no greater obstacle has been encountered than is often encountered in works of this importance, and that the muskeg spoken of is not at all an insuperable barrier to the construction of the road. As to the other point, I may say that the government, so far from having any intention of abandoning the Hudson Bay [DOT] railway, intends to proceed with it with all possible speed, and having undertaken the construction of that line, I think the country will have confidence that this government will not stop until it completes its work.

I wish to ask some questions in reference to articles which have appeared in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' on the use of dirty dollar bills. The subject does not concern some of us as much as others. I would first quote one or two items as follows:-	I
' Free Press.'
Why use dirty Dollar Bills when clean ones mav be had from Banks.

Pyne, an analyst from Toronto, has examined a well-worn dollar bill and thereon he found no fewer than 2,067,200 microbes.
Truly it was a case of overcrowding. Nobody cares to find out how the doctor managed to make the count, but the fact remains that the dollar bill was very, very dirty.
The other day an American scientist found something over 3,000,000 microbes on a bill.
According to the Toronto 'Telegram' on the bill Dr. Pyne examined there were 243,200 microbes which he styled as ' liquifiers,'' 184,400 ' non-liquifiers,' and 1,337.600 moulds.
In this connection a banker told The ' Free Press' that the one dollar bills were the dirtiest, the two's next, and so on. The

reason, of course, is that the one dollar bills net the most handling.
After all, is'nt it time in this country that we had clean money?
You can always get clean money at the banks, but most times you have to ask for it. If people demanded clean bills when doing business with stores and shops the banks would soon make an extra effort to have better bills.
The system by which the banks obtain the one and two dollar bills from the government is a rather complex one, but for the purpose of this article it may be briefly explained. In the capitals of each province the Finance Department of the Federal Government has officials known as Receivers General. The banks are supposed to send all their old worn-out bills there and in return get back crisp new ones. The Receivers General in turn ship the old ones to Ottawa and they are destroyed in some of the secret recesses of the Finance Department.
In these days the government keeps ahead of any demands the banks may make _ for clean money. In fact the federal authorities have lots of clean money on hand doing nothing, but there are lots of dirty, filthy bills floating most industriously from hand to hand.
' It is a well-known fact that bank bills are capable of carrying almost anything. Your agitation for cleaner paper money is certainly a good one.'	,
So said Dr. Higgins, Dominion bacteriologist, to the * Free Press' regarding the campaign for clean money.
' Paper absorbs moisture,' continued Dr. Higgins, ' and moisture is laden with germs. Some men moisten their fingers with saliva to count bills. If such men be tubercular there is certainly direct infection. The danger is continually increasing.'

Kennedy said:	' Bank bills are certainly a medium for the conveying of disease germs from one person to another. Some of these old and worn-out bills simply reek with germs.'	.
' It is almost an insult to offer a man m payment of debt a bill like some of those ip circulation,' Dr. A. T. Shillington said. ' There is considerable danger from a sanitary point of view.'	.
* Soiled and dirty paper money is not. fit for use any more than any other filthy thing, remarked Dr. M. O. Klotz. 'The one dollar bills are the worst, in view of the fact that thev are the most handled.'
' People would never think of picking dirty, filthy paper up in the street and putting it in their pockets, but that is lust about what they do when they handle some of these dollar
bills.'	,
' We are handing out clean money now, one city bank manager told the * Free Press ' to-day. ' Your campaign's a good thing.'
' Are you sending all this dirty stuff to the Receiver General in Toronto?' was asked.
' No. the bills were not bad enough for that. We are iust sending them to the smaller branches.'	.
Next time you go to a hank ]ust ask tor clean money. It is healthier, cleaner, and it feels more like money.
The teller may say things, but he'll dig down and get 'em for you. The teller has the clean money, and if he has'nt, he ought to get it for you.
' The teller has orders to he on the lookout for badly mutilated or badly soiled bills,' said the accountant of the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
If the bill is torn or tattered, he puts it aside. But if it is whole, out it goes through the wicket, utterly regardless of how filthy it may be.
* Of course, everything that passes from hand to hand very much has any amount of germs on it. Another thing that must be considered is the expense; every new note costs the bank about two cents and a half.
' In spite of considerable expense the Bank of England never issues a note a second time. The new note is issued and when it comes in it is replaced, whether it has been in circulation five minutes or a year.'
The important point is that the bank teller is the worn-out bill censor, .
And so on the evidence of medical men goes. Each and every one agrees that there is danger.
' Of course, the public need some educating on this question of clean money,' he went on.
* We don't have to have dirty bills. If people only demand clean ones, they can get them. The storekeeper will then get after his banker, and the bankers will get after us, and we can keep well ahead of the game.

Mr. Speaker, before ' you leave the Chair to go into Supply, as my estimates are to be taken up in the committee, I would ask the patience of the House while I make a slight preliminary statement of the operations and the work of the Agricultural Department. Many questions have been asked by members during the session, and it will be more convenient for the members if I make a general statement in connected form free from the interruptions which necessarily take place in the Committee of Supply.
I am glad to say that, as a rule, my department has received very generous' treatment at the hands of the House of Commons. The members have taken a1 great interest in the work of the department' and shown a legitimate and laudable desire to know and to understand that work;
I have also to say that the Committee of Supply have been generous in the way in' which they have consented to vote the necessary sums of money to carry on the' work of the department. I must confess' that on this occasion I am asking parliament to grant me larger sums than have ever before been asked or spent in regard' to agriculture.
I feel that some slight explanation is necessary to justify this request on my part. I do not wish to burden my remarks with any number of figures, but I would like to draw attention to the fact of a very great increase in the expenditure in regard to agriculture in Canada, and I would just read one or two figures to show this. I ' Mr. GUTHRIE.
do not propose to-day to deal at all with any subjects which are not really of a purely agricultural character, and I will therefore allude simply to the items of that description and no other. I will show what has been effected. Here are the estimates of parliament for 1896 and 97 and for the present year 1909-10. For experimental farms in that year 1896-7, parliament voted $79,000. I asked last year and obtained from parliament $153,000 for the same purpose. For the printing and distribution of farm bulletins and pamphlets in 1896-7 parliament granted $4,000; last year we spent $8,000. For dairy in 1896-7, we spent $30,000; last year $90,000. For cold storage in 1896-7, we spent $20,000; last year $75,000. For, health of animals in 1896-7, we spent $22,000; last year $250,000. In 1896-7, we spent $7,000 for the aid of agricultural societies in the Northwest Territories. Since the provinces have been established there, that work is left to the provincial governments and consequently last year we had no vote for that purpose. But in addition to the votes we had in 1896-7 for certain objects in connection with which I have given the figures for this last year, we have had in addition during last year for fumigation stations, $5,000, which was not dealt with at all when I came into office; for the seed division, $49,000, for which there was no appropriation when I came into office in 1896-7; for live stock, $52,000, for which there was no appropriation at that time; for Canned Meats and Foods Acts administration, $110,000, for which there was. no appropriation when I came into office; for tobacco stations, $5,000, for which there was then no appropriation; for the Rome institute of agriculture, $10,000. Now, taking the total of the expenditure for purely agricultural subjects in the department for 1896-7, I find there was an appropriation of $162,000. For this year which was closed, for the same objects and for purely agricultural objects, there was an appropriation of $807,000.

A change of this kind, an increase of this kind certainly requires justification, and for that reason I want to say a few words in regard to the agricultural industry and interests in this country. I have not the figures for the census of 1896. At that time there was only a decennial census, one in 1891 and one in 1901. But lately we have been taking census work especially in connection with agriculture much more frequently, and the result is that I have these statistics of agricultural products in Canada for the year 1909. I will, however, give as a comparison a few figures from the census of 1891, the census of 1901, and the reports

of 1909. In the first place, I would say, with regard to the acreage of land in Canada which was under cultivation in 1891, that there were fifteen and a half million acres under cultivation. In 1901, there were nineteen and three-quarters million acres, and I think I am justified in saying that in 1896 there were in the neighbourhood of seventeen millions acres of land under cultivation.

fully aware, and I am quite ready to state in general terms that there is no doubt that out of the increase, a very large proportion, perhaps the largest proportion, I will say the largest proportion, is in what we commonly call the northwest. But I would point out to him, and to other members of the House, that that is the one chief reason why it is necessary to increase the expenditure on agriculture in Canada. If we were simply dealing with old provinces, if we were simply dealing with well known conditions, if we were dealing with what had gone before, and there was nothing more to do, it would not be so necessary to increase our expenditure or to increase our organization as it is when the new development of agriculture is under new conditions and in connection with new lands. Therefore, what I stated a few minutes ago as showing why it is necessary to spend more money to-day than it was when this government came into office, in 1896, is moTe than justified by the fact that the development of agriculture is chiefly in the northwest. speechtext: Dear, dear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
My hon. friends are evidently less interested in agriculture and the people connected with it than they are in their own amusement and their party work in the House. The Department of Agriculture while it has to-day a good deal to do with agriculture, at one time had not much to do with agriculture. In
1867, although it was called the Department of Agriculture, there was absolutely no agricultural work pure and simple going on in the department. The department had under its control immigration, census and statistics, patents, trade marks, designs and copyright, and quarantine, but nothing of an absolutely agricultural character. I suppose that the reason why all these things were put under the department was the simple fact, deplorable as it was, that there was nothing doing in agriculture on the part of the government and the minister, having nothing to do in the way of agriculture, was given all these other things to attend to.
I want now to please my hon. friends opposite by telling them that the Conservative government in 1885 and a Conservative member in this House on 1885 made the first move towards getting the De- _ partment of Agriculture to do something for agriculture in Canada. In 1885, Mr. Gigault, the member for Rouville, an earnest, studious man who appreciated the interests of the people whom he represented, moved for a committee to consider the agricultural industry of Can ada. The committee sat-I had the honour of being a member of it myself-and for a long. time we did a great deal of hard work in obtaining information as to what other countries were doing for agriculture. The report of that committee recommended the establishment of experimental farms and the result was. that Hon. Mr. Carling, then Minister of Agriculture in 1886, introduced a Bill to establish experimental farms. This was really the first purely agricultural work which the Department of Agriculture attempted to do since the confederation of this Dominion. All honour to the government of that day, all honour to Mr. Gigault who instituted the work, who brought forward the question and with a great deal of labour, thought and study presented a report of the greatest value to this House.
I say again all honour to the government and all honour especially to the present Sir John Carling, then Minister of Agriculture, because I know that in doing What he then did, in the institution of experimental stations in Uanada, he met with but a lukewarm assistance or support from his colleagues or from the House. He, however, carried it through successfully and he was fortunate, as well as wise in the choice of the gentleman whom die chose to carry out that work. He called to his assistance Mr. William Saunders, of London, now known all over Canada, and I might say all over the agricultural world as Professor Saunders, Director of Experimental Farms for Canada, and gave him an opportunity to

study, work out and establish an organization of experimental farms and stations in Canada which would do something for the progress of agriculture in Canada. Today the work of our experimental farms is a monument to the foresight, the skill, the energy and study of Professor Saunders. Our present organization is on exactly the same lines although somewhat amplified. Professor Saunders has done a work which is recognized and acknowledged by everybody to have been of inestimable advantage to the agriculture of the country. The system is a monument to that gentleman which ought to last and ought to be recognized by everybody in Canada.
In 1890, Hon. Mr. Carling appointed a 'dairy commissioner in the person of Professor Robertson. Professor Robertson was first attached to the staff at the farms, but 'after about four years he resigned his position at the farm, was appointed dairy and agricultural commissioner, especially for outside general agricultural work, and development in the country. This was a new departure again in the Agricultural Department and one of the greatest value to the country. Professor Robertson started in on what I may call an educative campaign all through Canada. He was able with his extraordinary faculty of clear exposition, with his extraordinary power of attracting people to him and to his teaching, to arouse the enthusiasm and interest of the people in the country towards agriculture in a way that probably was never equalled in any country and certainly never in Canada. He went on with this work from year to year and in 1896, when the government changed and this government came into office, he was doing this work.
I must go back a few years to the establishment of the veterinary branch of the department. Many years ago there was an outbreak of contagious diseases among 'animals in the United States, and in 1868, the first order in council was passed prohibiting the importation of cattle from the United States. An Act was passed in 1869 affecting the contagious diseases of animals and in 1876 quarantine stations were established at Halifax, St. John and Quebec, and Dr. McEachran, of Montreal, was appointed head of the service. The Doctor did not give up his own private practice and gave a portion only of his time to the service. This went on until 1902, when I found it was necessary that we should have the entire time and attention 'of such an officer. Dr. McEachran was not *willing to give up his private practice and therefore, retired from that executive position and Dr. Rutherford was appointed head of the veterinary staff with his resi-

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
dence and office here in Otawa, giving his *whole time and attention to that work. I may say that Dr. McEachran did not have his office in Ottawa, and the secretary of the department attended practically to 'all the routine work. I am not going *into the details of that now, because T want first to say a word or two of the 'general work of the department.
In the general development of the work which has been going on, the farmers of the country have taken a tremendous interest, and they have been stimulated to study their business much more than they U3ed to do. With the exception perhaps of a few live stock men of Ontario who have always been in the forefront of agricultural progress on the continent of America, the great mass of the farmers of Canada were evolving what I may call a very elementary agriculture into the scientific work of the cultivation of the soil and the management of stock on farms. The work of the department has been mostly of the nature of instruction, for the purpose of rousing their interest and giving them information. In this connection I would like to make a statement as to the amount of literature and bulletins that we send out from the Agricultural Department to the farmers. In 1907 we sent out 534,000 bulletins or leaflets in English, and 238,000 in French, or a total of 772,000 pieces of literature distributed to individual farmers over the country, not in bundles, not in bulk, but addressed to individual farmers. In 1908 the quantity dropped a little, to
726,000	pieces. This year, however, I am satisfied, without knowing the figures, but by reason of the fact that our originization has been improved, there has been a material increase in the quantity sent out.
Now, having thus given a general outline of the work, I want to say a few words in regard to the veterinary branch. I spoke a few moments ago of the establishment in 1876, of quarantine stations at Halifax, St. 'John and Quebec. In 1883 a station was established at Point Edward, Ont., for the 'purpose of dealing with importations from the United States. In 1884 another one *was established at Emerson in Manitoba, 'and there was an arrangement made for an inspection of animals coming in from the United States along the northwestern boundary. Five years later, in 1889, another 'quarantine station was established at Victoria, B.C. There was an outbreak in 1884 of the foot and mouth disease which was 'dealt with at the quarantine in Levis, but it never spread outside the quarantine, and it was occasioned by the importation of animals from the old country which were diseased when they landed. In 1885 we had the first case of hog cholera which no doubt came in from the United States where that disease had been very prevalent. In 1890 quarantine stations were establish-

ed at Manitou and Deloraine, in Manitoba, in 1891 and onward other stations were established in the "west. In 1902, Dr. McEach-ran resigned, and Dr. Rutherford was appointed chief veterinary inspector for the Dominion, with head office at Ottawa. Later in 1904, Dr. Rutherford's title was changed to Veterinary Director General.
I wish to say a word or two in regard to the general work of that branch. Originally the branch was only intended to work at the frontier to protect Canada from the introduction of animal diseases from abroad, As time went on the difficulty of dealing with that disease from a local standpoint and under provincial laws, has been growing, and we have found it necessary to deal with it from the Dominion point of view. The Animal Contagious Diseases Act applies to the whole. Dominion, regulations made under it apply to the whole Dominion, and by reason of the fact that there is a constant passage of animals from one province to the other, and constant danger that disease may spread beyond the confines of any particular province, it has been found absolutely necessary to deal with this disease on broad Dominion lines. The work has continued to increase, and I am glad to say most successfully in some respects. The hog cholera which came in from the United States into the southwestern part of Ontario, and which, at the time I came into the office, was very virulent, continued for some years afterwards without much abatement, but it has now been practically stamped out. Some seven or eight years ago we were paying on an average something like $30,000 a year as compensation for the slaughter of hogs. The last two or three years the expense has gone down, one year as low as $2,000. I think last year in consequence of one particular herd of great value being slaughtered, the sum went up a little; but the average for the last few years has been well under $5,000. We have not completely stamped it out and do not expect to, but we have it pretty well within control, and whenever there is an outbreak we are able to localize it and prevent its spreading. There was an old disease called the Pictou cattle disease which, for a long time, was a source of great trouble in the counties of Pictou, Guysboro and Antigonish, N.S., and notwithstanding our efforts, it spread a little into Prince Edward Island. Years ago, in the early part of my administration, and before then, we were spending on that disease a few thousand dollars every year in paying compensation for slaughtered animals. The disease did not increase to any great extent, but it did not decrease at all. When Dr. Rutherford came into office he assured me that he was satisfied the disease was altogether due to the eating by the animals of a certain local weed
'commonly called the stink weed, or rag-'wort. Exhaustive experiments were undertaken to find out whether that was the case, and after several vears of investigation it was absolutely proved that that weed was the cause of the disease, and we refused any longer to pay compensation for the death of those animals, because it had become very evident that the existence of the disease was due to the failure of the farmers to eradicate that weed. They naturally replied to us, how can we eradicate that weed? We immediately set to work to try experiments with sheep on a farm in the neighborhood of Antigonish, and we showed clearly in the course of three seasons that the pasturing of sheep on a piece of land infested with that weed, would destroy it and absolutely clean the land of it within a few years. speechtext:
In addition to the Pictou cattle disease, which we have been able to deal with, and in regard to which we have been able to reach pretty fairly accurate conclusions, we have had a good deal to do with sheep scab, and I am glad to be able to say that by careful observation, watching, quarantine and dipping, when the disease existed, we were able a little while ago to notify the United States authorities that there was no sheep scab in Canada! That was of great value to the country, because two years ago the American authorities put on a quarantine against Canadian sheep going into the United States. That) was of great importance to our sheep breeders, because one of the -best markets for our sheep is in the United States, and the quarantine practically shut them out of that market. The sheep breeders of the country approached me and urged that we should deal with the American authorities and secure the abrogation of the quarantine. We made representations, and after a careful discussion of the question and satisfactory proof being submitted to the American authorities that no sheep scab existed in Canada, and that we had a com-ple organization which would enable us to deal promptly and effectively with any outbreak which might occur, the American authorities, some months aso, removed the quarantine to the great relief of the sheep breeders and dealers of Canada.
There is another disease which has been brought to the attention of the public just lately, which has not been altogether finally dealt with, and that is rabies or hydrophobia. The question has been up in the House recently, and I need only touch upon it as being a paTt of the work of that branch of the department. In conjunction with the local authorities, there being some question as to the respective powers and authority, we agreed simultaneously, and have been able to issue orders in regard to this disease. The local authorities, having local officers all over the country,
undertook to enforce the regulatians. I understand that the result has been the ar-restation of the spread of the disease. It was an unfortunate accident that a certain dog came across the bridge at Niagara and introduced the disease into Ontario. The spread was extraordinary, and we have been -able by our organization throughout the country to follow up, and locate practically all the animals which were likely to have been affected. I am glad to say today that by the effective work of the local authorities, the authorities of the government of Ontario in whom the hon. gentlemen are very much interested, working under the regulations issued by my department, the disease has been reduced, the dangers have been confined, and I believe that in a short time the disease will be stamped out, and we will be able to reach the position which we occupied a few years ago in which it could be said that there was no hydrophobia in Canada. In connection with our other veterinary work in 1904, we established at the Experimental Farm here a biological laboratory in which specimens of diseased animals or meats can be examined biologically by experts, and a decision come to in regard to this and other diseases. This was an absoulte necessity if we were to carry on the work so as to be sure of our ground, while costing a considerable amount this laboratory has enabled us to work on correct lines, and effectually and to 'be sure whenever we take steps of enforcement. We had a notable example a while ago which I think is very gratifying to all Canadians of the efficiency of this branch of the department. That was in the case of an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in the New England States. As the result of ,that outbreak, the American government quarantined the New England and some other states, New York and Michigan, where there were also outbreaks of the disease, and the imperial government in England forbade the entry of any animals into England that came from these states or from ports in these states. We immediately put quarantine on the boundary line, and shut out all communications, not only the passage of animals, but of hides, and of cars without thorough cleaning, and of everything that could possibly bring in the disease. The result was that notwithstanding the long contiguity of territory, over 2,000 miles with territory on one side in which the disease existed, and on the other side the Canadian flocks, and herds among which not one case of disease occurred. We were able to guard our people from the terrible loss that came to the Americans on the other side of the line in consequence of this disease and to keep open the English market to our cattle.
We have lately had the question of tuber-

culosis before us. This is an important question, and is agitating the whole people of the country. We have done a little towards aiding the spread of knowledge in regard to it, and we have tried to see what can be done to decrease bovine tuberculosis in the country. We have refrained from taking drastic steps which might not be effective, and which would entail loss and stoppage of trade. At the same time we have been investigating, and trying to find out a method by which this disease could be dealt with without undue harshness or causing undue loss to the farmers in the slaughtering of animals, or undue stoppage of trade. Just lately we have arranged with the veterinary association of the North American continent that a committee should be established to consider and investigate methods which might be employed, in the interests of all classes of the community, to stamp out this disease. It is a most important, complex, and difficult subject, but one the importance of which I consider justifies our taking great pains, devoting to it great study, and considerable money. I am glad to know that the North American Association of Veterinary Surgeons - named Dr. Rutherford the chief veterinary officer of the Dominion of Canada, as chairman of that committee, and he has taken the lead in that investigation work.
A word in regard to glanders. This disease in the old days was hardly known in Canada. There were a few sporadic cases, but some years ago it began to be dangerous. For a few years the efforts to restrain it were ineffectual, and I was obliged to ask a vote to pay compensation, and to order the slaughter of all dangerous animals. This was granted, and a large sum was placed at my disposal. I am glad to say the work has been going on very satisfactorily and successfully. We have been able to show a decided decrease in glanders which is proved by the fact that while in the first year we undertook to pay compen-'sation we paid out about $150,000, this year we paid only a little over $40,000 in compensation, and yet the organization, and system is such that we are to-day better able to reach all cases that are reported or suspected, and I am satisfied that the proportion as between about $150,000 a year and $40,000 a year in compensation, is a fair showing of the proportion of the disease in the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
One question more, and it is a pretty important one for the stock men of Canada. That is the establishment of what is known as Canadian records or herd books or stud books of Canada. The live stock men of Canada and of the United States evidently depend largely upon what I might call joint books for recording and registering pedigrees of their animals and securing their certificates of pure breeding. These books in general have been managed in the United States and in the interests of the associations of that country. The breeders in Canada of pure bred stock have been rather impatient for a long time under this, and in some instances have suffered no doubt. Some time ago, in connection with the live stock interests in Canada, representations were made asking me to establish in Canada, Canadian records for the registration of pure stock. It was a difficult and involved question. I did not feel it was proper and right for the government to undertake the management of such records, and therefore I suggested to the leading stock men that if we were to establish a committee under their management, to establish and run an office of the kind, I would give them office room and the necessary stationery, printing and so on, and aid them by a grant of money. I am glad to say that this has been running now for a number of years, I think about five or six years, and that while the work

is not done altogether in a way that is entirely satisfactory, it has been a great boon to the stock men. The committee have entire charge of it, and they have recently come to an arrangement, with the officers of my department to make certain improvements and rearrangements which I trust and believe will lead to the satisfactory carrying on of this work. The live stock men of the country are unanimous in saying that the result of its being done, I wont say under government command, but undei government patronage, if I may use that term, has been a help to them. The result has been that abroad, those records have been recognized in a way they could not have been recognized, if they had been run by private associations or individual people. There has also 'been a clear definition of such registers or pedigrees which are eligible for registration in Canada, and this has been a thing which has saved a large number of men who have bought what they supposed to be pure bred animals from abroad, introduced them into Canada, and after using them for breeding purposes for some time have found that the produce could not be registered under the recognized and well established books. When anything now comes into Canada and applies for free entry under the Customs Act, as a pure bred animal the register and pedigree are examined by this office and the owner or the purchaser is notified as to whether the animal is so registered and that it has such a pedigree as will be recognized in the Canadian book. This is a safeguard to the breeders of pure bred stock in the country which I think is of great value and which the stock breeders are recognizing as a great step in advance. It is costing more money to do it, but I think the results justify it, and I am very glad to say in this connection that the men themselves are able to run an office of this kind without interference and only with the assistance of the department.

A list of the associations or books which are to be recognized is in the Customs Department and has been sent by the department I believe to every collector of customs in the country, and any pedigree which comes in and is presented to them, but which is not endorsed or signed by the properly qualified officials 229
of this association is rejected. We have had communications and discussions with the Customs Department, and I know those instructions have been sent out from the Customs Department to their collectors all over the Dominion, and I have no doubt the collectors are carrying out their instructions. I would like to point out that in addition to this work that I have just sketched we have a live stock division, which is connected with the veterinary division, from the fact that Dr. Rutherford, who is the head of the veterinary division is also live stock commissioner. We are dealing in that division with live stock matters generally, and we are doing interesting work all over the country. We are supplying judges to the fairs, when requested by the authorities of the fairs, and the judges who have been sent have met with universal acceptance. They are not permanent officers of the department, as a general rule, but are picked out from well known stock men and without regard to anything at all except that they are recognized as judges of the character of stock they are called on to judge. In this connection I may say these men are paid their travelling expenses by us, but their entertainment at the places they are sent to, is expected to be provided by the association with which they are dealing. The live stock branch has also been editing some books, which I think are of value and which have met with great acceptance on the part of the public. Hon. gentlemen will remember that a few days ago, a book on the swine industry, a report of the commission sent to Denmark, was laid on the table. Since that day, I have had many requests from members of the House, for copies for distribution. My reply to each and every one has been that we had a long list of people to whom those publications were sent, and that if any hon. member sent a list of names it would be compared with the lists which are already in and he would be given the publication if he had not already received it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: What was the object of the commission?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I would be very glad to answer the question, but I will just spepk for the moment, of the publication. A little while ago a publication in regard to the sheep husbandly of Canada was prepared and put out by the gentleman under Dr. Rutherford, who is in charge of that branch, Mr. Spencer, which has met with a great deal of praise from the people of Canada and elsewhere. It is nicely got up and a large number of copies have been printed and distributed. One reason why it was done in regard to that particular class of



stock was that every one connected with the departmental work feels that it is deplorable that in Canada sheep husbandry seems to be declining. There are not as many- sheep in Canada to-day as there were a few years ago. One reason it is stated, is that there is no duty on wool. Another reason given is that the dogs are so bad that they cannot keep the sheep. Another reason is that a great many of our farmers, especially the new farmers, are not disposed to raise sheep and are not successful in sheep raising. We made a special effort to give information to those who might be desirous of going into the sheep raising industry, because we all believe that in Canada there is a splendid opportunity for large industry. We think it is very unfortunate, in view of certain things connected with that class of animals, that they should not be kept in greater numbers unfortunate not only as to themselves, but because of the value of flocks of sheep on the farms for the enrichment of the soil. My hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe) asked what was the object of the commission to Denmark. Representations were made to me that the swine industry was going down, that there were difficulties in regard to the production of swine, particularly in the province of. Ontario, where this industry is the largest, and that the men were not getting a fair return on their investment in swine. They pointed out that in Denmark and in Ireland and England, this industry was very successful, that the Danes were our chief competitors in the English market, and that we might be able to learn a good deal. I believed that our officers of the Agriculture Department had all the information that could be got, but I found that the farmers were not prepared to accept that statement, and I thought it would be well to send a small commission of farmers engaged in the industry in Canada, to those countries to find out how our competitors did their work, and how it was that the industry flourished in Denmark and England, while it did not seem to flourish in Canada. I felt that the swine industry is of such vast importance to the farmers and to the country, that anything we could do to stimulate it in Canada, would be money well spent. One officer of the department, Mr. Spencer, was sent as secretary, to edit the report with other men who were themselves actually engaged in the raising and fattening of swine. Mr. Ballantyne, of Ontario, Mr. Gareeau, of Quebec, and Mr. Sinclair from Prince Edward Island, representing the maritime provinces. They went there, and you saw the result of their visit. Evidently from the demands for the report, it is a report that has received acceptance, not only at the hands of the people of the Mr. FISHER.
country, but also at the hands of the members of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House took recess I had given an explanation of the work of the commission which went to Denmark and the old country to investigate the swine industry. I do not think I need enlarge on that matter further unless hon. gentlemen opposite wish me to. There is, however, one feature of the work of the live stock branch of my department which I must say a word about. I refer to the establishment of books of record -for French Canadian horses, and a reference to that matter is due especially to my hon. friends from Quebec who are particularly interested in it. There had been a record established in Quebec of what is known as the French Canadian horse, much in the same way as the record for French Canadian cattle had been established. When the national records were established in Ottawa, these as well as other local records were brought under the consideration of the department and of the National Live Stock Association. The records of the French Canadian cattle were accepted without hesitation as national in their character, but in the case of the French Canadian horse the officials of the department and those interested in the matter themselves were not satisfied with the existing conditions. Conferences took place between the Breeders' Association of the province of Quebec, and and the officers of the department and myself, and an agreement was come to by which the character of the records of the French Canadian horse already existing were thoroughly sifted. A commission was appointed of well known horse-ibreed-ers as well as some officers of the department to deal with the matter, and that commission instituted a new record for the French Canadian horse. It was found that a very large number of animals had been formerly listed which did not come up to the standard as pure-bred, and consequently the new book opened with a fewer number of horses on the registrar. This entailed some hardship upon individual owners, but in the interest of the industry at large and of the producers of these animals in the province of Quebec, it was decided to take that course no matter who suffered. I wish to say that it is greatly to the credit of those interested in the breed of French Canadian horses that they Svere satisfied to make the sacrifice in order to establish on a firm basis that breed of horses. The French Canadian

'breed of horses is pretty wen established 5n the province of Quebec, and is now Spreading into other parts of Canada and the United States. It is a valuable breed and I believe that the breeders will be enabled through the medium of this new 'record to realize in future handsome profits.
' May I say a word on the question of the cattle embargo in England. This does not come within the scope of the work of my department in Canada, but my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) has referred to it and I think I should answer him. The cattle embargo in England was established by the English people and it is purely a matter of their own concern. Representations have been made by the former Conservative government and by this government from time to time since it has come into power, as to the injustice and lack of necessity for this embargo from the point of view of protecting the health of the animals in Great Britain. So far as the existence of any cattle disease in this country is concerned I have no hesitation in saying that the embargo in Great Britain to-day and for many years past has been unnecessary. Still, the British people have the right to take all the precautions they deem necessary in the interests of their live stock and it is not for me or the people of Canada to teach them how to administer their affairs. We have to accept their regulations, just in the same way, as if, were the conditions reversed they would have to accept any regulations we might impose.

speechtext: What are the regulations?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: In brief: That all horned animals coming into England from abroad must be landed at certain specified ports where there are lairages and slaughtered there within 10 days of arrival. I may say that at the present time only animals coming from the United States and Canada are permitted thus to be landed. Argentine had that privilege, but it has been taken away and I understand the_ government of Argentine is negotiating with the British government with a view to the privilege being restored to them.

speechtext: A few years ago the Committee on Agriculture passed a resolution asking the minister to confer with the Ministers of Agriculture in the different provinces and endeavour to find a means to have this embargo removed. Would the minister give his reasons for paying no attention to that resolution from the day it was passed until the present day?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
My communication with the imperial authorities on this question and my knowledge of the opinions of various Ministers of Agriculture in England, leads me to believe that it would not be dignified or proper for the government of Canada to take any further steps until there is a change of view on the part of English statesmen. I do not think it would be consistent with the dignity or the interests of the Dominion that we should go on our knees and appeal to the imperial authorities, or undertake to censure them for a course which it is undoubtedly within their right to take. The feeling of the people of Canada on this subject has been officially expressed to them over and over again, and the replies have been such as I think make it impossible for us to deal further with that matter until such time as a different expression of opinion comes from the authorities in England. I may say further that within a year and a half there has been a most positive official statement on the part of the English board of agriculture that the embargo must remain. Under these circumstances I think it would be unwise and improper for us to take such steps.
I propose now to say something about experimental farms. The policy of the experimental farms was first adopted in 1885-6, and made a work of the Agricultural Department. I have already expressed in the highest terms of commendation what I considered to be but justice and fairness to the Minister of Agriculture of that day, and to the government and the party who established the experimental farm. I have said a few words in regard to the work, the extraordinary work, the highly important and very successful work, of the director of the farms in the original organization of. the establishment and its continuation up to the present time. I would also like to say here that Dr. Saunders has been assisted and surrounded by a body of men on the experimental farms who have devoted themselves to this work with great self-sacrifice. For many years they did their duty at salaries which were not in any way commensurate with the salaries of other officials who were doing what I do not think it is improper to say was less important work for the Dominion

of Canada. There had been very little recognition of that work for many years. Soon after I came into the office I felt that the time had come to increase their salaries and make some substantial recognition of the value of the work of those officers at the experimental farm. That has gone on to a considerable extent. I make no apology for that, I know the House has endorsed that action over and over again, and I am proud indeed to say in this House that the work done in the interest of Canadian agriculture has been fairly well recognized as of the highest character and as the greatest honour. I am glad to say that to-day the status of the men who are doing this work on behalf of the people of Canada, has been improved, and that today they occupy a position as honourable before the country as that of any other officials in the employ of the government. I think this is but due to them, and parliament has done no more than its duty in treating them in that way.
Now I want to say a word or two in regard to the expansion of the agricultural farm system. It has been the natural and legitimate consequence of the increase of the agricultural interest in this country during the last fifteen years. At the time I came into office the staff was perhaps quite equal to the demands upon it. It is true that just at that time Prof. Robertson, who had been appointed dairy commissioner at the experimental farm, had been removed from that position and placed in another position. The consequence was that there was no agriculturalist at the farm at that time. I thought it was necessary to have one, because, aside from the scientific work of the horticulturist, the chemist, the botanist and entomologist, it was very necessary to apply to the common agriculture of the country the scientific truths and discoveries which were made by those other officers. Very soon after I assumed the office, I think about 1899, I appointed Mr. Grisdale as agriculturalist at the farm. This was but a continuation of the policy that was adopted when Prof. Robertson was appointed; Prof. Robertson having been removed, there was a vacancy, and the appointment was made. I can say without hesitation that the result has been very satisfactory to the general work of the experimental farm. In the first place, the actual general work of the farm here has been somewhat changed; it has been divided up into a purely agricultural dairy farm and an experimental farm. The experimental work goes on on some parts of the farm. There are 200 acres of the farm turned into a simple dairy farm such as might be in any part of the country. That work has been going on satisfactorily. I think it was begun in 1901 or 1902, and has reflected great credit on the agriculturalist who has been managing this work. I Mr. FISHER.

Certainly a very handsome increase, and denoting a substantial improvement of the land. I would say that the results show a profit of $573 in the case of swine alone this last year. Now I feel this is an important advance, and one that is of greatest value to the farmers. This is a work that can be taken as a model by the farmers generally in most other parts of Canada, regard being had of course to difference of climate and conditions. I may add that in numberless instances where Mr. Grisdale, and others have spoken to gatherings of farmers, usually of the leading farmers of the locality, they have imparted information of the highest practical value to the agriculturalists, who have shown their appreciation of their efforts. At the same time all experimental work, pure and simple, has been going on on a larger scale. There is a considerably larger staff now than there was then. There are to-day thirty-nine men above the labouring class on the farm as compared with twenty in 1896. The whole staff is sixty-five to-day as compared with fifty in 1896, but of the higher class men, men who are doing work in the way of experiment, in the way of investigation, in the way_of spreading the knowledge that is acquired amongst the people, there is an increase of nearly double while the whole staff is only increased by about 27 per oent. The total wages were $17,000 in 1896, and $25,890 in 1910. In addition to the agriculturist, whose work I have just lightly touched upon, we have appointed a new officer in the person of Dr. Charles Saunders as cerealist. Dr. Charles Saunders has been conducting a large number of experiments, most satisfactorily, and successfully with regard to the cereal crop of the country, and has gone into the details of hybridization, and selection of seed to show the value of certain new varieties, the use of which amongst our farmers we hope will add very considerably to the production

and quality of the cereal crops grown in Canada. In that connection I have to say that Dr. Charles Saunders, as is known to the members of the Agriculture Committee, has made extensive experiments in testing the quality of wheat not only by chemical, and other processes, but also in practically grinding the grain, making the flour and baking the bread. In this way he has been able to show that certain kinds of grain and wheat are better for bread production than other varieties, and has been able to spread amongst the people of the country that knowledge so as to guide the farmers in the variety that they shall sow, information which I believe to be most useful to them, and as a result of which they will be able in the near future not only to increase the quantity of the wheat production of Canada, but also its quality, and add to our advantages as the granary of the whole world.

speechtext: He has been carrying on that work for nearly twenty years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: My hon. friend interrupts me by saying that he was carrying on that work nearly twenty years ago. In the first place Dr. Charles Saunders was not appointed to the farm until seven years ago.

speechtext: Dr. Saunders.

speechtext: Dr. Saunders was not conducting any experiments of that kind at all. Dr. Saunders was doing some hybridization in fruits, some selection of grain, but the work that is now being carried on was not begun until Dr. Charles Saunders was appointed. Dr. Saunders, I have no doubt, would have been very glad to do it, but he had not time with the multiplicity of other work that he had to do.
