maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Is the minister not aware of the fact that nearly twenty years ago bread was brought to the Agriculture Committee, and shown to the committee as the results obtained by using different kinds of wheat grown in Canada. For instance, there was Ladoga wheat, and we were told that it was not wise to cultivate that variety, because it made yellower bread than other varieties. We had the bread shown to us. The wheat had been ground in the mills, and we were told how much flour the baker got out of it. That was all brought before the committee twenty years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
Quite true to a limited extent, but the work that wTas done then
was done outside and away from the farm. The bread was baked by_ ordinary bakers and the test was made in that way. Today it is all done under the supervision of a scientific man who has facilities, bakeries and every condition which will enable him to obtain accurate knowledge as to the results. I am not depreciating what was done before, but I am pointing out that a new officer has been appointed for the special purpose of carrying on this new piece of work. In addition to that, just lately, unfortunately, our long-time and most valued officer, Dr. Fletcher, entomologist and botanist at the experimental farm, passed away. He had been for many years botanist and entomologist, he had done most valuable work, but he had been overburdened with work, and a good deal of work which might properly have been done in the interest of agriculture by the entomological and botanical division had not been overtaken and could not be overtaken by Dr. Fletcher or by any person else. So that, when a little while ago, Dr. Fletcher, to the great regret of everybody, passed away, I thought it would be my duty to get two officers, one a botanist and one an entomologist, to take his place and start the work in two divisions. The result is that we have now an extra division there. I may say that while Prof. Shutt, the chemist, in the old days, had one assistant, he has now two and another, not a scientific assistant, as well; that in those days, while Mr. John Craig had no assistant of any kind, Mr. Macoun has now his stenographer and typewriter, which relieves him of a great deal of work that Mr. Craig had to do. In Dr. Fletcher's departmqrit there was one assistant at that time to the botanist. To-day, Mr. Hewitt, the new entomologist, has two assistants, and Mr. Giissow, the new botanist, has two assistants, adding to the scientific and experimental staff of the farm in most important ways.
Then, may I say a word with regard to some expenditures that we have made at the farm itself? One of the first things that had to be done was to provide for necessary laboratory and chemical work. Years ago, after I came into office, the laboratory was burned. It then occupied a couple of rooms in the office building. Instead of refitting those rooms it was thought best to erect a new laboratory, and a considerable sum was spent in putting up and establishing a chemical laboratory, in which for many years past the work of the chemist and his staff has been carried on and which contains all the fittings and appliances necessary for the kind of work which they are doing. A little while afterwards additional buildings were put up for the sheep which were added to the farm stock in the period I have spoken of. A building for roots and implements wai

erected, and later on a horse stable was built of a very fine character, which, I think, would serve as a model for any farm in the country. Comparatively recently the stables in the big barn of the experimental farm have been entirely refitted. When they were originally built they were built without that knowledge which has been arrived at in the course of the last twenty years in our agriculture and live stock work. The kind of accommodation for cattle that we had there, which should be a model for farmers, was very severely animadverted on by farmers who came to visit the farm. I am glad to say that to-day that stable can be taken as a model. It is well ventilated, has plenty of air, no bad odours, it is convenient for the work, convenient and comfortable for the animals, is kept clean and in every way is an object of admiration. In addition, there has been a building put up to accommodate .the horticultural work. In the old days when Mr. John Craig was horticulturalist, he had only a little office, but when Mr. Macoun took charge and as the work expanded it was found necessary to provide more extensive accommodation, and we have now a very good horticultural building. We also have had to add to the office accommodation to serve the increased staff who now have good and sufficient rooms for their valuable work.
I come now to the question of the branch farms. I am sorry my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) is not here, because some time ago he questioned me with reference to this matter. I have observed, as others have, that wherever branch farms are in existence they have had an excellent influence on the agriculture in their vicinity. Indian Head is one of the best wheat producing districts in the Northwest, and over and over again the work of Mr. McKay on that farm has been highly commended. The same is largely true of Brandon. With the desire to have the same kind of improvement in other parts of the country, we thought we should add to the number of branch experimental farms and several have been established. The first was at Lacombe, in North Alberta, the second at Lethbridge, in South Alberta, and the third at Rosthern in northern Saskatchewan. and more recently another was established in Prince Edward Island, as the people there thought they could not make use of the experimental farm at Nappan in Nova Scotia. Within the last few days, I have acquired another site for a station in the north part of Saskatchewan. For some time past I have had an officerof my department examining the different districts, and I believe I have now a knowledge of the needs of the particular localities throughout the country, which enables me to say that during the coming season, I shall be able to fix upon some five or six more Mr. FISHER.
branch stations. I want to speak on one feature of this project, which I think is of the greatest importance. The old branch farms were established on the basis of large buildings and equipment, a large staff, and the maintenance of quite a quantity of live stock. I want to say one thing in connection with the agriculture of Canada, which I would like should attract the consideration of the people generally. So far as our general agriculture is concerned, we have made greater advances in dealing with our live stock and in the utilization of the products of our land than we have in the cultivation of land and the production of crops. In the best parts of Ontario,there are a large number of first-class farmers who are not only good stock men but good cultivators of the soil as well. But, if we examine the reports from the other parts of Canada any unprejudiced mind must conclude that in view of the fertile soil which spreads all over this Dominion, and the intelligence of our people, the annual crop production per acre is not what it ought to be. I believe that is due to the fact that scientific methods of cultivating the soil and the treatment of land are not thoroughly well understood by our people generally. To instruct and teach the people, object lessons are of the primest importance. If those who live in a particular district can go to an easily accessible central point and there see illustrated the result of good management of the crops and of scientific treatment of the soil, they can learn more than they can by any amount of reading and oral instruction. It is therefore highly important that the number of branch stations should be increased. Now, if each of these stations were to cost $25,000 or $35,000 the appropriations I ask from parliament would not enable me to establish any great number. It is my belief that we should establish comparatively smaller stations and deal simply with crop production, and not include stock experiments to any great extent, if at all. After all, the experiment of feeding stock indoors is very much the same in one place as in another, and the results obtained will serve the industry in all parts of the country. But, experiments in the treatment of the soil and the production of the crops must be conducted in as many different localities as possible, and they must be shown on the land in as many places as possible. I am therefore trying to establish a very considerable number of branch stations of this character where we can show the actual application on the land of the science which has been adduced from successful experimentation. This is a new principle in the establishment of these branch farms, which I trust will appeal to the House as I know it will appeal to the farming people of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Has the minister abandoned the chicken fattening stations he established all over the country and which proved such an utter failure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: These fattening stations were successful in proving what good results could be obtained in the poultry industry, and the fact remains that where, before the establishment of these stations, it was a rare thing to find poultry meat in Canada properly fattened, the reverse is the rule to-day. These chicken fattening stations having accomplished their mission, it is no longer necessary to maintain them. I am well satisfied with the results of our work in that direction. I will not go further into detail with regard to the establishment of these branch stations. When 1 mention them I notice that the hon. gentleman opposite as well as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are all very eager for the establishment of a station in their own particular neighbourhood or county. I accept that as the very highest compliment that can be paid to the experimental stations scattered throughout the country, and I will, as far as possible, try to meet the demands which are reasonable and fair and in the interest of the country at large.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: The Minister has mentioned a new station in Prince Edward Island and several in Alberta and Saskatchewan. Is it proposed to put any station in the province of New Brunswick? I think it is about the only province in the Dominion that has not an experimental farm.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I think that is., pretty nearly true. When the system was first established a branch farm was put at Nappan, which was just at the border between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, but on the Nova Scotia side. That farm was expected to serve the purposes of the three maritime provinces. It does serve the purpose of the, eastern part of New Brunswick pretty well. The Prince Edward Island people complained that they could not reach that farm very easily and the Prince Edward Island government offered a farm near Charlottetown for us to work on a nominal lease for a number of years. We were glad to accept that offer. I hope before long to be able to investigate the possible sites for a station such as I have been describing in the more westerly part of the province of New Brunswick, inasmuch a3 I think the Nappan station serves fairly well the eastern part of the province.
I want now to say a word or two with regard to one of the branches established by Prof. Robertson at the time he ceased to be agriculturalist at the experimental farm. At that time he was appointed Dairy and Agricultural Commissioner. At first
his work was largely what it had been before, the education and stimulation of the people connected with agriculture in Canada in the direction of improvement. But he found that certain work was needed in dairying, his first special subject, and he took up that work. I will not go into details, but I am sure that hon, gentlemen opposite will be glad to hear that Prof. Robertson was much impressed with the necessity of cold storage accommodation for the transportation of our perishable food products. I am quite sure that with his knowledge, his powers of persuasion, his acquaintance with all the interests of our country, he would have been able to persuade the ministers of the Conservative party, if they had remained in power to go on and do more than they had done in connection with cold storage. He was able to persuade them to make a beginning, which was unfortunate in its details, which I will not go into now. When I came into office Prof. Robertson was one of the first to urge me to take the matter up on a larger scale and to do more than had been done. It happened that I personally had a good deal to do with dairying, being a dairy farmer, and I knew the situation, I knew what Prof. Robertson had been saying publicly and privately, for I was an intimate friend of his before I became minister, and I was only too glad to meet his views and to take active steps to give them practical effect, and the well known and much discussed cold storage policy of the department was the result. But there was one matter which had to be taken up of the most prime importance in regard to all our work, although it is not very much understood in the country, that is, the inspection of the 'handling and transportation of our agricultural food products in the course of their shipment from Canada to our great export market, Great Britain. In the old days our agricultural products of whatever character, delicate and tender like butter, or less delicate and tender like fruit and cheese and meats, or the coarser products like grain and flour, were handled in the crudest and roughest ways by the transportation companies. Complaints were universal on the part of shippers and owners of the way in which their products weTe deteriorated in quality on their way to market. It was obvious that we must take immediate steps to see what could be done, and we very soon established a system of inspection or supervision in the handling of our agricultural food products in their transportation from the producing point in Canada to the consuming point in Great Britain. This had to be done gradually. We had no authority or power over the transportation companies; we had no power over the wharfs in Great Britain where our products were landed. We could

only persuade, we could only advise, we could only use such authority as a department of the government naturally would exercise.
I cannot resist telling you an incident which occurred in the very early days to illustrate this. I went to England to meet the people who handled our products-the produce dealers of Liverpool, Manchester, London, Britsol, Glasgow and other places. -in order to gain information, to find out what they thought of our products and what complaints they had to make. Amongst other things, I found at Liverpool a condition of affairs which surprised and pained me. Frequently Canadian butter would lie on the wharf at Liverpool for days in the hot sun, and our goods would' be handled otherwise by the wharfingers in such a way as to bring a poor price in the ' English market. I may say, in justice to the Englishmen, that they were not any worse than our people in Montreal or St. John who handled our products and put them on board ship; but they were just as bad. I pointed that out to a meeting in Liverpool, where the produce dealers gave me a luncheon, and expressed the hope that they would improve their management. The Englishman does not like criticism and advice of that kind, and I was pretty severely reprimanded for having dared to say such things. I was invited to the office of a certain gentleman-I do not hesitate to give his name-Mr. Jones, who was at the head of one of the largest shipping concerns in Liverpool. We got chatting in a friendly way, and he began to criticise what I had said, saying that of course it did not apply to his business-at any rate, that they were doing the best they could, the best that it was necessary for them to do, and that of course they were going to go on just as they had begun. As I was his guest, I was of course very polite and friendly, but I could not help saying that his firm, unfortunately, was subject to the same reproach as others, and in some respects was a little worse, because the reports to me had been that this firm was very bad indeed in the way it handled our goods on their arrival at Liverpool, and that their agents at Montreal were pretty bad, too. He assured me that I was all wrong, and that at any rate, he was going to go on as before. Well, I said, Mr. Jones, there is only one alternative, and that is to tell the people of Canada what the conditions are. He said: You will not dare to do that. Oh, yes, I said, I will. It is m,y clear duty, and what is more, it is my clear duty to tell the people of Canada that your ships do not handle our goods as well as some others do. He said: You won't dare to do that; it is not the proper thing for a minister to do to discriminate. I said, excuse me, I appreciate my position and that it is mv duty to tell the people of Mr. FISHER.
Canada where they can get the best service, and to see that they have an opportunity of getting the best service. I left him and came back to Montreal, and a month or six weeks afterwards Professor Robertson and I went to a meeting of produce men in Montreal, and I told them what I had told Mr. Jones, and I told them if they wanted to have their goods handled badly, they ought to send them by Mr. Jones' line. I got next day a cable asking me if a report of what I had said was true. I replied, yes it was true, and that I was prepared to repeat it if he did not change his methods, and I found next day frond his officers in Montreal that they had received instructions to comply with the requirements of the Canadian Minister of Agriculture.

speechtext: What year was that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: That was in the year 1898, I think. It may possibly have been in 1899.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Will the minister excuse me? The year in which you found butter was lying on the dock in Liverpool for 11 days after landing, was under the regime of the hon. minister?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Yes, quite so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I thought you were reflecting on your predecessors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Not a bit. My hon. friend is so possessed with the idea that one party is not doing so well as another party, that he cannot get away from it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I would just say to the minister that I learned all that from the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
Well, I am sorry the impression I created was so contrary to my desires. I think I have given this afternoon and this morning a full appreciation of a great deal that was done in the Department of Agriculture before I had anything to do with it. I think my hon. friends opposite will do me that credit. I have not given to anything I have done myself half the praise that I have bestowed on Mr. John Carling and Prof. Saunders in connection with the establishment of the experimental farm. I have explained as far as properly as I can, and I am sure my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) will acknowledge that I have given a sketch which is free from party bias and which has been a mere statement of facts in connection with my predecessor's as as well as of my own work. Mr. Speaker, that was the beginning of work which I think was of the greatest importance to the Canadian export trade in agricultural products. We produce first class stuff here of all kinds. We are improving in the production of it, and it is differently

handled from the way it used to be handled not by the government, because the government has nothing to do with it, but by the transportation companies, Our good stuff would not get the prices it is entitled to get in the English market, if it were not for our system of inspection. It is required not only in Canada. It is required on the ships of Canada, on the railways as well as on the docks and wharfs. It is required in the packing houses of Canada, it is a rigid system of inspection by which we do not undertake to force or coerce, but to educate, to appeal and to persuade the people to do what is right in the interests of the country. I believe that is better than coercion where it is available and effective, but I do not hesitate to say that where I find that people are not open to persuasion, I have not hesitated to ask parliament to give me the power to coerce, and when I have had that power given to me I have tried to exercise it fairly, justly and reasonably, so as to accomplish what is necessary in .the interests of the whole people of the country, and especially in the interests of Canadian farmers and agriculture. I wont go into the details of that work where butter' and cheese and fruit are shipped under inspection and by the refrigerator car service to the wharfs and ports of Canada. It is a system which supervises and looks after the conserving of goods in the ships at Montreal, Halifax and other ports. We' have officers on the docks in England to report everything that goes on there, that is detrimental to our trade. I am glad to say that after years of education, and persuasion, after the occasional exercise of coercion, we have got a vastly improved condition of affairs, and I have the testimony which has already been placed before the House on various occasions, but which I wont detain the House with now, showing that one of the most important things that 'have been done to facilitate the business of the agriculturalists of Canada and elsewhere, is the system of inspection by reason of which it is rare to find our goods arriving in the motherland in bad condition, whereas, 15 years ago, it was rare to find them arriving there in good condition. Now I will leave that. I want to say a word or two with regard to some of our dairy work. My hon. friends opposite are so touchy, that I do not want to talk of the cool curing of cheese, which they have always thought was a very bad thing, and all that, although our dairymen appreciate it, and take advantage of it. I wont undertake to say much, about the experiments in the aeration of milk which took place last year and the year before, and the result of which is going to revolutionize the cheese making industry. I wont say anything about
some experiments with regard to butter making in Canada which I hope will bring good information that will help our people in that regard. But I do want to say a word as to cow testing, as I think it is one of the most important things we have encouraged in this country, and one which I trust will lead to most important results. One of the most glaring facts in connection with the insufficient realization of the proper profits on our farms in Canada, is the small average production of the cow. Those of us who have studied this question know that in Denmark and Holland, 15 or 20 years ago, they were in about the same position in - this respect as we are to-day, but by a thorough system and co-operative work and testing the individual cows, by cutting out the bad one and keeping the good one and only breeding from the good ones, they are gradually and steadily increasing the average production and have reached the point that the cows of Denmark produce more than double per year per individual cow, than the cows of Canada. Now this is a very unfortunate, a very bad condition of affairs. We knew this a few years ago, and we have been trying to induce our farmers in Canada to make some kind of co-operative or individual test as the Danish and Dutch people have done so as to bring up the average production of our cow. It was up hill work. It requires on the part of the people, a good deal of manipulation and experiment, and we had to get information to show them what the result would be. We had to make experiments. We had to get individual herds and even go so far in some instances as to make some tests ourselves before we could lay before the farming community, the dairyman especially, information which would stir their imagination and make them adapt their methods to these facts.
We got those facts, we laid them before the people, and the people to-day have begun to digest them and to act on the advice founded on these facts. The result is that to-day we have in Canada a very large number of dairymen and farmers who are testing their cows. We have a large number of herds, the records of which are. known and published, and other people, by the success of those who have begun Gariy and have done the work carefully, are to-dav incited and induced to do the same work. It is one part of that reward one gets for somewhat discouraging and somewhat long passing through difficulty and doubt, that we often experience m brino-ino- about reforms in agricultural subjects' that during the last season the effects were so striking, the success so great where it was undertaken, that this year we have a great number of applications for cow testing associations. I am satisfied the system is on the high road to success, and

that in the near future the great mass of Canadian dairymen will be doing this work. There is no reason to believe that in .a few years the Canadians will not be able to say that the average cow production in Canada is what the Danes produce, 7,000 pounds a year for every cow in the country, instead of the Canadian average of 3,000 pounds a year. If we can do this, I think all the expenditure, all the labour, all the intelligence that has been bestowed on dairy work in Canada would be abundantly justified and rewarded.
Mr. Euddick has also had_ charge of the cold, storage service of the government. This has been increased of late years by the passing of the Cold Storage Act. We have now to look after not only the refrigerator cars and the cold storage on ships, but also the subsidies to cold storage warehouses established under the Act, which require additional work and expenditure.
We have also the fruit division of our work and the administration of the Fruit Marks Act. The transportation of fruit is largely connected with our cold storage) system; it was thought better to have it all under the one commissioner, and so we have not a special branch, although we have a special division in regard to fruit. I shall not go into the work of the department in connection with fruit growing. The Fruit Marks Act has been often explained in the House and is well understood. It was passed in response to a demand of exporters and people interested, who recognize that Canadian fruit had a bad reputation. They wanted to secure that Canadian fruit would be properly packed and shipped, and the Fruit Marks Act provides a law for that. We have to administer that law. I am sorry to say that although there is an improvement, there is not the improvement I would like to see, and we have to still occasionally prosecute, to still coerce to a certain extent where I would prefer to persuade if the people would be guided by the persuasion.'
A word in regard to some work instituted by Mr, McNeill, head of the fruit branch, which points in the right direction, that is the encouragement and establishment of fruit _ growers' or shippers' and packers', associations. One of the greatest difficulties our fruit growers in Canada have ex-, perienced is that their work is largely done by each individual, and that one individual has not enough fruit to fill large orders or, to make an impression on the market. By forming an association, a group of people in a Particular district can get together and employ one efficient and competent expert packer and grader, who will grade and nack their fruit so that in the aggregate the fruit which is thus bandied in co-opeT-ation amongst a number of people will brinv in a larver return and be better accepted and received on the market than

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
fruit sent forward by the individual. This work was started in the southwestern part of Ontario by Mr. McNeill some years ago, and to-day, I am glad to know, there are a number of such associations working most satisfactorily and most successfully. It is work of the department in one sense,' because we indicate the road. It is work of the people themselves, however, and it can only _.be successfully carried on by the co-operative work of the people combining, together, mutually trusting one another, associating themselves for combined work and carrying on the whole thing as'a business transaction in a business way. I am glad they are doing it successfully as it is an important work, for the improvement of the fruit trade of Canada.
Another part of the work which Professor Robertson had in charge, but which I found it better to assign to a special division when he left, is the work of the seed division. That division is under Mr. Clark the seed commissioner and carries on several kinds of work. We passed the Seed Control Act a few years ago. That resulted from the investigations of the seed commissioner, Mr. Clark, and the work of his subdivision. Mr. Clark found the condition of the average trade in agricultural seeds in Canada to be deplorable. A large portion of our people were buying seed that did not germinate and consequently they had to buy a great deal more than they needed for proper seeding and they were also buying seeds that contained the seeds of noxious weeds. These spread weeds over the country. That is easy enough under anv circumstances. This is a large country. In some parts of the country one weed is prevalent which is not found in another part. The result of carrying these seeds from part of the country to another has contributed to the introduction of seeds not native to any one part of Canada from other parts where the seed was produced. We have also introduced into this country a large number of weeds foreign to the country. These were in many instances introduced by the seed bought by men who were enterprising, who wanted to get good seed and who went away from their own neighbourhoods to get it. They did this, however, without any opportunity of knowing what they were buying, without any facility for investigation' and without any thought or knowledge of the results. We showed to the country and the people that the average seed sold in many parts of Canada was infested with weed seeds, would not germinate and would not grow. The result was a demand for some control of this business. That I think is a proper demand and a legitimate action on the part of the parliament of Canada because

although in ordinary trade matters the old maxim 'caveat emptor' prevails, in matters of this kind the buyer cannot protect himself, he has not the knowledge, the training, the facilities, or the laboratory by which he can examine the seed he is buying and know whether or not it is what it purports to be. It is true that many old and experienced farmers can take up a handful of seed and say whether or not it is good seed, hut I venture to say there is not a farmer in Canada to-day who can take up a handful of seed and can look at it and state whether it would germinate or whether there were weed seeds in it. That can only be told by laboratory examination and testing. What I have said is no reflection on the farmers of Canada. It is impossible that men by ordinary inspection can possibly tell whether the seeds they are buying will grow or not.
I am sorry to say that in many cases in Canada they have the bad as well as the indifferent. We still continue, 'besides the administration of the Seed Control Act, to spread abroad amongst the people information in regard to weeds and in regard to seeds. Let me say a word in regard to weeds. We are still watching for new weeds, we are still warning the farmers when new weeds appear. We issued a little while ago a well known book called the Weed Book, in which vivid pictures beautifully executed and coloured are displayed of all the noxious weeds known in Canada. We spread that throughout the country for the purpose of giving the people instruction and information, so that they can recognize the weeds when they find them in their fields. It is not a very easy thing for a farmer always to know what a strange plant is that he sees for the first time in his field. If it is a weed you may be sure that the picture of it he will find in that book will show him what it is, and what its nature is. That book has been asked for from all over Canada, from one ocean to the other, by everybody interested in agriculture. My only regret is that we have not been able to distribute it as freely as I would like on account of the cost. The first edition went out, the second edition went out, and although each edition consisted of
25,000	copies, I have no doubt that in a short time we will have to publish a third edition and perhaps a fourth, because the people of this country are aroused on the question of weeds in their fields, and are determined to fight them. They all say that the book is not only a credit to the book-makers of Canada, but it is an exceedingly useful publication.
We are also administering the Seed Control Act. This is a little difficult, but we have been trying to do our best. I must
say in all sincerity that the seed merchants, and especially the wholesale seed agents, have been helping us and helping us in the enforcement of the Act. Sometimes some of them fail, sometimes we have to prosecute individuals, and sometimes bad seed is sold. But, the proportion of bad seed sold to-day is infinitesmal in comparison with what was sold before the introduction of the Seed Control Act. Now the administration of this Act takes money, and I am asking for $50,000 for the ensuing year. I venture to think that if I asked five times that amount the work that is being done would justify dt.^ But with the present sum I think we will be able to accomplish the work of instruction and properly administer this &ct.
A year ago we passed an Act in regard to commercial food stuffs. I have had a good many representations made to me, especially from the province of Ontario, saying that these food stuffs contain a good many weed seeds. I think that is partially correct. I fear there is a great deal of weed seeds distributed in the food stuffs, and we have been making investigations. I am not certain yet that we have h remedy under the Commercial Food Stuffs Act, but if we have, I think it ought to be put into force. I am told that the question is largely mixed up with provincial rights, it is one of those questions that it is hard to deal with. In the laboratory last year we tested something over 6,200 samples of seeds for the purpose of determining whether they were germin-able or contained noxious weeds. _
Now, one word in regard to a subject that will enlist a good deal of sympathy, I am sure, among many members of this House as well as throughout the country, and that is the subject of tobacco. I am not myself a user of tobacco, some of my friends do use it considerably, and I suppose most of them have heard sneering remarks about Canadian tobacco. Now, without being able to speak from personal experience, I want to say a word on behalf of Canadian tobacco. This climate and this country seem to be very suitable for the growing of a good many varieties of tobacco. In'the early days the province of Quebec was chiefly concerned in that product. The habitant raised his tobacco, cured it and used it almost entirely for home consumption. He did grow pretty good crops, for the area that he cultivated. In the province of Ontario, in the counties of Kent and Essex, considerable tobacco is grown. A few years ago there was a glut in the market for Canadian tobacco, because it was not cured sufficiently well to attract the purchaser, and the growers could not place it on the market. One reason was because of a prejudice against it, I think I may say prejudice, rather

than judgment, against Canadian tobacco. Knowing the situation and believing this was a crop which could be raised advantageously in Canada, I made some investigation, and I found there was nobody in Canada, so far as I could ascertain, who *was _ able to grow and cure tobacco according to the best scientific methods. I, therefore, took it upon myself to send to Prance, where they have a very large branch under the government doing that kind of work, and where they have a lot of scientific men studying the culture of tobacco and the best methods of treating it. I was fortunate enough to secure a very competent, skillful and well informed gentleman named Charlan, who was first sent to Canada by the Department of Agriculture of France. Mr. Charlan came out here, and before long he showed himself so thoroughly competent that I asked him to stay. After a little hesitation and some communication with his home, he resigned his position in France and became a permanent member of the Civil Service of Canada. I am glad to say that he has' quite justified his appointment. I will not go into details, but I venture to say that the prejudice which existed a few years against Canadian tobacco has practically disappeared amongst all the people that have tested it. I do not deny that there are many people still who won't use it, there are people in Canada still who say that Canadian tobacco is no good, but these people have refused to test it. I know that a good many people who talk sneeringlv of Canadian tobacco are smoking Canadian tobacco every day they smoke. As a matter of fact to-day, a very large proportion of all the cigars that are smoked in Canada are made in Canada of Canadian tobacco, and some of the highest priced cigars sold in Canada are made in Canada with Canadian tobacco in them. Perhaps the dealers and manufacturers do not like to acknowledge that, because they are still under the influence of the prejudice of consumers. But as a matter of fact, we have been able to show that we can grow tobacco and put into the hands of the manufacturers, either of plug tobacco or of cigars, tobacco that will make the finest quality of plug and the finest quality of cigars that any one needs to have.

speechtext: What about the flavour?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I am only speaking on the authority of other people, because I do not know anything about the flavour of tobacco.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: You ought to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I do not think so. With all due deference to my hon. friend, while I admire him in many ways, the fact that he uses tobacco to the extent to which he Mr. FISHER.
does, is one of the blemishes on his character which I regret.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: That is very kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I say it with all kindness. But I may add that while it is a blemish on my hon. friend, it is one that we can all forgive him, and none of us will criticise him for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. minister is justified in casting any reflection on members on this side of the House for what we have said on Canadian tobacco.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: No. I did not mean to say that at all. I had reference to the people generally.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I have often spoken about Canadian tobacco. They produce a good article, they grow a fine tobacco, a tobacco that will make excellent cigars and chewing tobacco that is appreciated by the people of this country, and I am not sure that they cannot produce a good smoking tobacco. The fault I have continuously found with it was that the flavour or taste of the tobacco was not congenial to people outside of the province of Quebec, and if the government could get somebody from France or some other country who would produce a tobacco with a flavour such as that of Macdonald's tobacco of Montreal, it would add millions to the wealth of the people of this country. It was with regard to the curing that I found fault and not the growing of the tobacco.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman has a good deal of justification for what he says. I am not prepared to dispute that. I was not giving an expert opinion as to the quality of the tobacco, but what I stated in regard to the use, the production and the change in quality of Canadian tobacco, as stated to me by the manufacturers who make it up and by users, is, I think, correct. Now, I have reached, I think, the end and I suppose my hon. friends opposite will be glad of that.

speechtext:
I have reached the end and it has taken me longer than I intended or expected to go over the work of the department. I do not think I need detain the House longer at this stage. I hope that the intention that I started out with has become evident to all parties in the House. I did not start out with any intention of boasting, of getting any party advantage. or presenting any partisan argument. I felt, as I have felt for some years, that the importance of the Department of Agriculture was not recognized in the discussions in this House for the reason that it had never come up practically except in

committee, when interruptions, proper and right in committee, were made and when questions were put in such a way that it was not possible to make a fair or connected presentment of the work of the department. I am going to say frankly that I am proud of the work of my department, not because I am the minister of it, hut I am proud of the work of my officials, I am proud of the large interests which are entrusted to the department, I am proud of the way in which the people of Canada generally look to the department at Ottawa for advice, assistance and information in the business of agriculture. I do not say that this is the case only to-day. It was the case in the old days when my predecessors were in office. I am proud of what the department does in recognition of the business of agriculture in Canada, of which I am also proud as a farmer, and I am not speaking in the slightest degree as the minister of that department. If there is one thing more than another that I think is important to Canada, it is that the business of agriculture should acquire, assume and maintain that status which is due to it in this country from its vast importance from the financial point of view and by reason of its wide spread diffusion throughout. the great agricultural territory which Canada possesses. I do not want to be little or interfere -with railway or canal work or with this, that or the other industry in the country, but I do venture to say, as a representative of the farmers and as a farmer, that agriculture as a science, agriculture as an art and as a business, has attained and holds before the people of Canada a proud, a recognized position and that this is due to the fact that the farmers have given up the old rule of thumb work, the old drudgery which was performed in the early days of the settlement of the new country, necessarily and perforce, and are to-day exercising a skill, a knowledge, a science, in the best sense of the word, in regard to this business which enables them to hold a proud position in comparison with every ether class in the community. This being the case, I say again that I am proud of the work of the Department of Agriculture, which I think has contributed to the utmost extent that it could do to that position and success. If it has attained to that position to-day it has done so almost entirely and certainly largely through the efforts of the men who have been in charge of the different branches of the department's work, men who have been unsparing in their toil and energy, sparing themselves not at all in their work, who are enthusiastic, who have been specially trained and educated, who have been chosen with a sole view to those special characteristics which they possess and which fit them for the positions which they occupy.
These men, I say are entitled to the credit, the rewards which they are given in a minor degree, perhaps, and to the position which they hold in the estimation of the people of the country, because I am proud to say that the farmers now generally look to the officers of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa for their guidance in all things relating to agriculture.

speechtext: I want to ask the minister a question. I had a good many applications from farmers throughout my riding with reference to samples of seed. In many cases they ask for a sample of seed grain and a sample of seed potatoes. The rule governing, I believe at the experimental farm, is that they can only receive ona sample, either of potatoes or seed grain. Would it be possible to change that rule so that a farmer could get one sample of seed grain and one sample of seed potatoes? For instance, a farmer this season wants a sample of seed grain and a sample of seed potatoes, and in the event of his getting only a sample of seed grain he has to wait until next year before he will know the result of the sample of seed potatoes. It would save a great deal of time and he would profit very much sooner if it were possible to allow him to have one sample of each.	1

ARMSTRONG (East Lambton)! Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to some three hours talk from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), and we cannot come to any other conclusion than that he has delivered a distinctly partisan speech and, with that lack of courage that you would not expect on the part of a minister* of the Crown, he sought to hide himself behind the Speaker and demand that questions should not be asked without his per-; mission. It seems to me that he has, taken the position, either of a Czar or of a suffragette-I have not decided fully which. He might as well have placed his speech on 'Hansard.' and he would have saved three hours of the time of the House, because he has simply devoted himself to telling us about the splendid work he has done in his department. No one knows better than the minister himself that he has been forced practically into almost every advancement he has mentioned by members on this side of the House. Talk about a partisan speech! He tried to show from beginning to end of his speech to-day

that since he took control of the affairs of the Department of Agriculture, between twelve and fourteen years ago, the department has been conducted more successfully than it was previous to 1896.
The minister has told us of the increased acreage held for agricultural purposes, but against his boasting we have the fact that the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario has declared that the population of the rural districts of that province has decreased 61,000 in the last 10 years, and in the other older provinces similar -conditions prevail. The hon. gentleman also told us that he has done his (best to have the cattle embargo removed, but -the official correspondence before us shows that up to a few years ago he never raised a finger in that respect. He knows that before his party came to power its leaders told the people of Canada that if they were elected to office the embargo would he removed, but today the embargo is in the same position as it was years and years ago. Then, this Liberal government declared that when Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman became Liberal Prime Minister in England they would get the cattle embargo removed, but Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and his government have passed away and other Liberal governments have succeeded in England, and the embargo is still a fact. Some years ago, on my motion, the Agricultural Committee passed a resolution to the effect that the Dominion Minister of Agriculture together with the Ministers of Agriculture of the^ various provinces should go before the imperial authorities and submit to them the contention of Canada and urge for the removal of the embargo. That resolution of the committee was adopted unanimously by the House, but the Minister of Agriculture has taken it upon himself to flatly disobey -that mandate of parliament. What can you expect from a minister who would act in such a way? The hon. gentleman has told us a lot about what he says he has done for the cold storage system, but he knows full well that for the seven sessions I have been here and for years before, the member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) and others of this side have been trying to drum into his head the importance of perfecting our cold storage system and applying it to our transportation routes. The suggestions coming from this side of the House the minister has adopted to some extent, and to-day he tries to make the House believe that he was the originator of all that has been done to improve o-ur cold storage. He has expended $600,000 or $800,000 on cold storage, but even to-dav he cannot control the temperature which Canadian products are subjected to on the trains and

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
steamers crossing the ocean. He told us that he went to England and that the people looked upon him as the great Minister of Agriculture, and he gave us to understand that he had brought them to their knees in connection with the question of providing protection for our goods once they have landed at the ports in England. I have here some remarks which I made on June 27, 1905, in this House, and I find I quoted from the report of the Department of Agriculture for that year the following:
The bulk of the butter discharged from the steamer is removed within a reasonable time, but the balance is allowed to remain for days before delivery is taken.
He knows that our products have been allowed to remain on the wharfs in England exposed to every deleterious influence, but to-day he tries to make us believe that he has taken measures to remedy that defect. It is time we should set the hon. gentleman right. Any one who studies the subject cannot but come to the conclusion that instead of our having at the present time a broad system of cold storage that would bring the products of western agriculture to the consuming centres of England in proper condition, the antiquated sissy system which the minister has in force bears no comparison to the modern and up to date system which the Argentine republic, and New Zealand, and Australia have perfected. Let the minister himself consider this, iand he must conclude that our defective system of cold storage is quite a serious loss to the producers of Canada. Then, as to transportation facilities, the minister knows full well that I have already called his attention to the fact that in 1907 freight was carried from Liverpool to New York for 7 shillings and 6 pence per ton, from Liverpool to Halifax it costs 15 shillings per ton. The hon. gentleman knows that I have frequently called his attention -to the discrimination against the Dominion and in favour of the United States in the matter of freight rates on our produce. The minister must know that the farmers of Canada are paying practically $1,000,000 per annum -for the privilege of sending their goods through the por-t of Montreal. What has he done to investigate this question and to relieve the situation? Unless we can have our products carried to the markets of the world in the best possible condition and at the lowest possible rate, we cannot expect to have the best possible returns for the farmers of this country. What has the minister done in regard to. opening up markets? The great boast and -cry of the men leading the Liberal party previous to 1896 was:	Place us
in power, and we will open up the mark-

ets of the world to the 'Canadian farmer; we will obtain for you the great- market of 80,000,000 people to the south. Let them point to one market that they have opened up. They cannot do it, and they know it. Until a few months ago they had closed to Canada the second best market in the world, and who helped to close that market? The Minister -of Agriculture boasted of his position in that respect. Let me call attention to a statement which he made on the 21st of March, 1906, in reply to an address which was delivered by a prominent apple shipper of the city of Toronto. He said:
There is reason to believe that the Germans will in a short time seek to open negotiations, but in the meantime I -think 'we can get along without them.
Yet the Minister of Agriculture is the man who above all others should be interested in opening up the markets of the world for the Canadian farmers. Where did we find the Minister of Agriculture in regard to the treaty with France? Was he looking after the best interests of the farmers of Canada when he allowed the only item in that treaty which would have been of advantage to them to be taken away? Instead of protesting against that being removed from the schedule, he helped to vote it through. He talked about crop bulletins. Long before he thought of issuing crop bulletins, we on this side of the House urged that policy upon him. We also urged him to let the people of Canada know what amount of money they would receive from the sale of their products in the markets of the world. He does not give the farmers of Canada any definite information as to the prices of agricultural products in the different markets of the world, because he does not want to interfere with the exporters at the port of Montreal, or the other ports. About $60,000,000 worth of perishable products are going out of this country every year; but unless we revolutionize the system of transportation and cold storage for the carriage of these goods to the markets of the world, the minister knows that our farmers will continue to lose millions of dollars every year for the lack of proper transportation facilities; and yet he will not go to work, and put into force some progressive system for carrying these goods in proper condition to the markets of the world. He talked about experimental^ arms, and was good enough to say that they were started by the Conservative party previous to 1896. He says he is going to change his ways and give the people throughout the country smaller experimental farms, and a greater number of them. The members of this House have for six or eight years coaxed and begged the minister to establish more experimental farms
in different parts of the country, and at last it has dawned upon him to do so. He boasts of having improved the tobacco industry of this country. Who urged this upon him during every session of the last parliament? Time and again Mr. Clements, the former member for West Kent, brought to his attention the condition of the tobacco industry in the southwestern part of the province of Ontario. When we jind the minister rising and taking to himself credit for all these things, we cannot help feeling that he is deserving of the severest censure for not being alive and progressive in these different matters. He tells us that the swine industry is declining. He knows that it has been declining year after year, and he has never apparently, until the last year, realized the condition that industry was in; and when he does realize it, he sends a few men across the Atlantic to investigate the swine industry in Denmark and Ireland. One would naturally suppose that they would first investigate the condition of the swine industry in their own country, and when you ask the minister why they did not, he tells us that they knew enough about it without investigating it. So the swine industry, which was formerly one of the boasted industries of this country, has been declining until to-day we hardly export any products of that industry-an industry which, in the older sections of this country, can be and -ought to be developed, and there is no doubt that it would be if we had men of proper energy in charge of the Department of Agriculture. The minister tells us that the sheep industry is also declining. How many of the industries connected with this great department which the minister controls are declining year after year, when they should all be advancing with the progress of this great country of ours? He says Canada is a good country for sheep to be raised in. There is no question about that. But he says that the decline of the sheep industry may be due to the cruel dogs in this country. With regard to meat inspection, he knows the debate that took place a few days ago in this House, which went to show that the meat which goes to foreign countries is inspected, while our own people in their homes can eat whatever trash they like, and apparently the Minister of Agriculture does not care-he is not going to bring about a better condition of affairs in that regard. When our people realize that the choicest meats of our country go to foreigners and that there is no inspection of the most of the meats used for home consumption, they will resent the position taken by the Minister of Agriculture. A few years ago he told us about chicken fattening stations.
He has been spending tens of thousands

speechtext: Hear, hear.

That is the position taken by the Minister of Agriculture who knows full well that if we had mutual preference with Great Britain it would increase the value of every farm in Canada, and of every product of the farms of the Dominion of Canada, and that it would bring to the shores of the Dominion immigrants by the tens of thousands, men who are interested in agriculture, men who are ready to come and develop this country for the general benefit of the empire. But the minister takes the position on that question that he knows that the farmers of the Dominion of Canada do not want mutual preference. Then what about the navy? He is prepared to spend money on a navy which a large portion of the farmers of Canada do not want, an independent navy. I might call his attention to this fact that to obtain that independent navy he will have to spend ten or twenty times as much each year as he is spending on the agriculture of this country. I only call attention to these things to show the many blunders and mistakes he has been making. Then what about the government weigher at the port of Montreal? Three million packages of perishable products go out of the port of Montreal every year. One of his own commissioners went_ to Montreal and investigated this question and definitely stated that the people were being robbed in the position they are placed in at the present time. Did he move the minister? No, Sir. He is still clinging to this condition. Take his position on rural mail deliveries, something

that should be an advantage to the farmers of Canada. On that question he comes out boldly and frankly, says it is not in the best interests of the farmers of Canada, and that he is not willing to grant it. What kind of Minister of Agriculture is that to have in a Dominion when on an important question, which is of (practical benefit to the farmers of Canada, he rises in his seat and takes that position. He tells us that the cows of Denmark produce double what they do in Canada. Yet this man has been at the head of agriculture in this country for the last fourteen years, and what has he done? He tells us of little cow testing experiments which are going to be of great benefit. We have been hearing of these little toy propositions going to be of great benefit to the farmers of Canada for many years. But instead of taking hold of this industry in a proper, manly way, he brings forward these little suggestions. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up any more of the time of the House. It is late in the session for the Minister of Agriculture to bring down the statement that he has made to-day. Might I say that it ill becomes a minister of the Crown to the position he did this morning. It ill becomes him because he can depend upon it that if a minister of the Crown can come here year after year and, hiding behind the Speaker, give out figures which would be distributed in the hundreds of thousands all over this country without any contradiction, we are not going to have aggressive legislation in the Department of Agriculture.
Transportation facilities have improved, but instead of the minister raising his hand or doing anything worthy of the position he occupies or anything worthy of consideration, he has taken the position he has to-day, he simply tells the people he is getting along nicely, and has been developing this wonderful agricultural interest of our country through the steps he has taken. I sincerely hope that the minister another year will bring down his estimates early in the session. Year after year it is the same story, bringing down his estimates in the last days of the session, generally on a Friday when there are few in the House and generally in the evening when he knows there will not be many members present to discuss these estimates. Agriculture is a great and important industry in Canada. What would your other industries, your railways, your manufactures, or any other industry be were it not for the agricultural interests? They would amount to nothing and instead of that great industry being debated and discussed, we find the minister coming in the last hours of the session and making a three hours' speech which is a partisan speech. The minister cannot deny 230
that he has made that speech in order to send it out to the people of Canada to show the great development of this great industry under his worthy suffragette or Czar.

The minister, after he had been speaking this afternoon for about an hour and a half remarked that he wished to direct the attention of his hearers, and to attract also their thought. I would only say that if the minister seriously wished to attain that object he exhibited the moat singular way of going about it I have ever witnessed in this House by the elaborate campaign speech which he introduced as the result <Jf a question by a member from this side of the House, He remarked that members on this side were touchy. I do not know that there is any gentleman more touchy than the minister himself. He remarked that we were always fighting him although we were afraid to carry our fight to the logical end of voting against his estimates as he knew we were afraid to carry our measures that far. He added that where he did not find us fighting against him and obstructing his efforts in this House as Minister of Agriculture, he found a veiled opposition from this side. In fact he assumed altogether the air of a martyr, although he did return thanks to the gods that the country, and this House had always stood by him. I would like to refer to this extraordinary statement of the minister, because I object very strongly to the tone of these remarks, which I think must have resulted from an exceptional thinness of the minister's cuticle, and probably from a lack of the sense of proportion. I object to their tone, and to their substance. Last session we had a discussion in this House upon horticultural matters, and the subject was introduced by myself, and spoken to rather extensively by various members including the minister. Let me quote the passage in which I closed my speech:-
I sincerely trust that the minister will accede to these very moderate requests. They are made not in any political or party spirit but with the sole desire to build uf>
what I believe can now be truly designated a national industry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I appreciate the spirit which has inspired the remarks of the two hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House. I recognize their criticisms as a perfectly fair and friendly effort to secure an advantage to the very important fruit trade of this country.
Why does the minister not remember this sort of thing a little longer? I think it would be better for him, and better for the progress of his estimates if he would take a somewhat fairer line. It would be foolish on our part to say that no good had ever come from the Department of Agri-

culture. We could not take that foolish position, we recognize the good work that has been done, we recognize the very excellent work that has been performed by many officials, and very first-class officials of the Agriculture Department. We also recognize the good work done in the various provinces by provincial officials, and otherwise by the people of the country at large. The agricultural industry has achieved great progress, and if the minister, and his department have contributed to that progress in any way, they will get the just amount of praise that is due them. And he should remember that a certain amount of praise is due to those on this side of the House who have supported the minister's hands in putting on the statute-book measures for the advantage of that industry. I sometimes think that in this country we are getting too much of the spirit of brag and boasting in what we do, and I fear sometimes the minister has fallen victim to this spirit, and occasionally in giving three blasts of the trumpet irr praise of Canadian agriculture he does not forget to give an extra three for the minister. It might almost be concluded, I think, that the" demerits of the Department of Agriculture must be very grave if they demand a three hours speech to introduce the estimates. I have noticed about a baker's dozen of supporters of the hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, and a good sprinkling on this side, members going in and out, and I could almost fancy the minister might have included in his speech the quotation from the poem:
Men may come and men may go,
But I go on forever.
The government is very prone to accuse members on this side of delaying the work of the session, but I think it will strike many that we have had the most singular instance this afternoon of delaying the work of the session at a very late period. Even in defending himself from imaginary attacks the minister has indulged in a most extraordinary redundance of phraseology, and wealth of detail which I fear is characteristic of his remarks, and which have done much to delay the work of the session. He has given us, save the mark, a ' sketch,' and I may say with all respect to what he may have said to Jones in Liverpool, or to what Jones may have said to him that it would have been better at this stage of the session in the Agricultural Committee or somewhere other than the House, where there would have been no difficulty in getting the minister's remarks printed so as to reach the country. That would have avoided this three hours' speech, and would not have encouraged the debate which must be a necessary consequence of the assertions made during his Mr. BURRELL.
speech. I do not want to be a sinner myself in delaying the work, but it would have been better for the minister to have dispensed with his three hours' talk and to have gone on with the estimates, and to have risen as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the only member in this House who was thoroughly entertained by the campaign speech delivered by* the minister was himself. He even refused' at the beginning of his address to allow1 us to ask him a question. This is putting' on the thumb-screws even tighter than the Prime Minister would do. We all admit that this minister has charge of the most' important department in the whole government. We may talk about our mines or our forest departments, and we are all proud of them, but we must admit that the Agricultural Department is the most important in Canada. The land will keep on producing, and will furnish employment and give support to many millions of people in this country long after our forests and mines are exhausted. Therefore, I say that agriculture in Canada is the most important industry we have. Notwithstanding all that the hon. minister has been pleased to tell us this, afternoon about *what he has done for the people of Canada, when we come to investigate the other departments and come back again and look at what the Department of Agriculture is doing, we are compelled to. admit that the Department of Agriculture is the most undeveloped department in the whole government. Take the esimates of 1909-10, when we look at the heading we find in staring figures $1,114,000 for that department. But when we go through the1 estimates and sift out what is really spentj in the interest of agriculture, we find that1 those figures dwindle down to $657,000. I know that the minister figures in another item which brings it up a good deal higher, and that item is the health of animals. Now, Sir, knowing something about how this money is being spent on the health of animals throughout western Canada, I claim it is not being spent in the interest of the farmers. Take the estimates for last year. Last year the government were retrenching, they found there was not enough money to go round, and they had to retrench. We find the other great departments cut down about ten per cent, but when we come to the Agriculture Department, we find it cut down from twenty to thirty per cent. This leads us to one of two conclusions, either that the government considers this the most unimportant_ department. or that the Minister of Agriculture is the weakest minister in the cabinet and cannot get what is needed for the great producing classes of this country. I claim that if the governments, whether Dominion or provincial, have any function

at all that function essentially is to stand between the producer and the consumer, and to see that there is no undue toll taken from either. I would ask the minister when he has ever stood, up in his place in parliament for either the producers or the consumers against the grafters. He has never done so during the two years I have had the honour of a seat in this House. Still, we find combines starting up everywhere, beef combines, pork combines, cement combines, and every other kind of combine, from one end of Canada to the other, which are taking undue tolls from the people, yet the minister has never' raised one hand or one finger to protect them. I consider that the conditions in regard to his department are in a deplor-, able state. Would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, the exportation of everything raised or grown on the farm, except wheat, is going down year by year? I claim that this condition in that respect is not only regrettable but deplorable. Let me give you a few figures of our exportations to prove what I am saying:
