These are eight of the most important products of the farm, and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that unless these eight branches of farm production are kept up, the produc-v tion of wheat cannot possibly last in this, country. In the United States, some years ago, the average production of wheat was about twenty bushels to the .acre; to-day the average production of wheat in that country has fallen to twelve or thirteen bushels per acre. Our average in western Canada is about twenty bushels per acre at the present time, but if we do not keep these eight branches in a flourishing com dition, the production of wheat in western Canada will very shortly be down to twelve or thirteen bushels per acre. Therefore, I say that these important branches of agriculture must go hand in hand with the production of wheat, j^ast year we had Professor Robertson before the Agricultural Committee, and he told us that the farmers of Quebec, on account of their poor methods of farming, were losing about $100,000,000 a year.
If the province of Quebec lost a revenue of $100,000,000 because the farmers do not farm the land in a proper manner, what does 2.304
it mean for the whole of the other provinces of this country? If that statement is true in connection with Quebec, then the whole Dominion of Canada lost a revenue equal to $400,000,000 or $500,000,000. The minister says that the reason our farmers are not more successful is because of their slipshod methods and of their lack of interest in their work. I want to tell the minister that is not the facts. I am speaking particularly in connection with western Canada, because I am more in touch with conditions there than in eastern Canada. When, some years ago, the government and the Canadian Pacific railway joined hands and sent a train through western Canada to give demonstrations to our farmers I remember quite well the day that that train reached the town that I lived in. It was in the dead of winter, there was a blizzard, it was cold and stormy, but I know of lots .of farmers throughout my constituency who drove 12, and 20 miles to be there to get the information that these men had brought for their enlightenment. Farmers, throughout western Canada particularly, are hungry for information. They want to have demonstrated to them how they should do things and they would be only too glad to follow up the instructions that were given to them. I spoke a little while ago in connection with the exportation of products of this country falling off year after year. I have spoken to several in connection with it and the argument that I have received from each one was that it was because of the great internal expansion throughout this country. When I first heard that argument I thought perhaps there was a good deal to it, but when I looked into the records of other countries that were expanding and going ahead practically on a par with Canada, I found the condition altogether different. Instead of the productions of the Argentine republic, New Zealand and Australia going down from year to year as ours are, they are going up. They are exporting more of their farm products than ever each year. The Argentine republic is expanding just as fast as we are if not a good deal faster. In 1865, 11,667 immigrants arrived on their shores and in 1895, 125,205; and in 1907, 329,122. So you can see that they are getting just as many immigrants, if not more, than we are in Canada. They exported, in 1887, 13,185,000 bushels of wheat; and in 1907 they exported 86,360,000 bushels. Their exportation of wheat is practically on a par with ours. We find that in 1900 they exported wool to the extent of 101,113 tons. That shows that they have gone into sheep breeding, and in 1907, the exportation of wool had increased to 154,818 tons. Instead of their being the same as we are in Canada, instead of the exportation of

sheep and wool going down, year after year, the exportation of sheep and wool from the Argentine republic is going up year after year. I wish to speak particularly in connection with the cattle trade of the Argentine republic. We find that they have two systems of shipping their cattle. They ship some on the hoof, and some in a frozen state. In 1900 they exported 66,496 head of cattle; in 1903, 249,000; and in 1906, 509,112. That shows, in my opinion, that they must have some persons in the Argentine republic who are looking after the interests of the great producing population of that country. In Australia, our sister colony, they are expanding too. They are developing their country according to population as fast as we are. They exported beef in 1906, 294,392 quarters ; in 1907,	308,114 ; and
in 1909, 390,626; showing a gradual increase all the time while our exportation is going irf the opposite direction. I claim that the interest of this present government is particularly favourable to the manufacturers. I have shown how the exportation of farm products is going down from year to year, but when we look at the exportation of the manufactured article we find it going up from year to year. In 1900, $14,222,000 worth of manufactured goods were exported from Canada; in 1905, $21,191,000, and in 1909, $28,957,000, showing a gradual increase all the time. If the great expansion of our country was eating up the extra products of the farm, why should not this great expansion also eat up and take the surplus manufactured goods that we are producing in this country? I claim that this ig a very serious state of affairs.
The minister took three and a half hours to tell us what a great department he had, but he forgot to tell us why the exportation of these products has been decreasing year after year. Well, Sir, I claim the reason is that the minister is not looking after the interests of his department. The hon. gentleman tells us what he is doing for Canada, but when we compare what Canada is doing with what other countries are doing it is absolutely laughable to hear him boasting. France spends $9,200,000 each year in the interest of agriculture; Austria, $9,270,000; Hungary, $9,400,000; the United States, $10,000,000; Russia, $25,280,000; Japan, $3,750,000, and all poor Canada can afford to expend on her agriculture is a paltry $657,000 a year. France has 71 experimental farms, Germany has 80, Austria has 61, the United States 60, Russia has 101, and Canada has 6 or 7. Why, Sir, I hold that in an agricultural country like this the Agriculture Department should be one of the greatest spending departments of the government in its efforts to promote the welfare of the agriculturalists of the country and to extend Hr. W. H. SHARPE.
our trade. Now, I ask the Minister of Agriculture to give me his special attention while I refer to the question _ of experimental farms. Let me remind him that there is only one experimental farm in the whole province of Manitoba, and that is situated at Brandon, so that in order that the farmers of that province may obtain the object lessons in scientific farming which the minister has referred to, they have to travel long distances to Brandon and to lose a great deal of their valuable time. It may be said that to the majority of the farmers of Manitoba the experimental farm at Brandon is useless. I trust the minister will see_ his way to establish other such farms in Manitoba without delay. I think there shpuld be a model farm in each farming constituency in Canada. Let me for a moment direct the attention of the minister to the combines existing in western Canada. In the little town of Mowbray, in 1908, the elevators handled over 300,000 bushels of wheat, but last spring a spur railway was built across the line into north Dakota, and an elevator erected there, with the result that last year instead of handling
300,000	bushels on the Canadian side there were only 100,000 bushels handled, while the United States elevator handled 300,000 bushels. Our farmers took their grain across the line and shipped it in bond back into Canada to the lake ports, and by pursuing this course they received from 13 to 14 cents a bushel more for their grain than if they had dealt in Canada. Let me tell the Minister of Agriculture also that whereas in the province of Manitoba along the boundary line the land is worth only $20 or $25 and in some cases $30 an acre; right across on the American side on account of the better treatment which is accorded the farmers in north Dakota, the land is worth from $40 to $50 an acre. Then, with regard to the beef industry, I might remind the minister that he has been asked many times to investigate the beef industry of the United States, Australia and the Argentine republic, but he has always refused or neglected to do so. I represent a mixed farming community, and last year we shipped 512 cars of cattle to the city of Winnipeg. I know numbers of farmers in my constituency who always in the past have kept from 50 to 75 and 100 head of cattle, but these men are selling out their herds and going out of business because the combines are robbing them of-every dollar they should make. It goes without saying that the farmers must keep stock in order to keep up the standard of their land, and if the cattle industry declines so much the worse for general farming. There were 110,000 head of cattle shipped to the city of Winnipeg last year, and all the farmers could get from the beef combine in that city was an average of

$3.76 per hundred weight, while at the same time the average price of similar cattle in Chicago was $6.27 per 100 pounds. There must be something wrong with the cattle trade when such a condition exists. In 1907, the Roblin government appointed a commission to look into the conditions of the beef trade in Manitoba, and they found that on each beast a farmer raised in that country he lost $5.80, that the retail dealers made an average profit of $13.60, and the abattoir men-in other words, the great beef combine of Winnipeg-made $23.10 per head. The public abattoir in Montreal charges $1 for killing, so that we may infer there was a clear profit of $22 per head to the abattoir owners, or the beef combine in Manitoba. With 110,000 head of cattle going in, the meat combine in Winnipeg took out of the producers between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 more than they should have done. Is it any wonder that the producers are quitting? ' The combine is simply driving them out of business. The drovers from north Dakota come across to Manitoba and buy cattle and drive them across the line and pay the duty, which I think is 25 per cent. Alberta is the finest country in the world for producing beef and pork, but the combine is driving the producer out of Alberta. Mr. Paddy Bums, the beef king of Alberta, says that in five years Alberta will be importing beef and pork, because the producers there will not be raising enough to supply the demand. I would like to read to you what the Edmonton 'News' of February 19, 1910 says:
One of the most important matters before the. people of Alberta is that of chilled meat, it is absolutely essential to the prosperity of tne province, both in town and country, that the value of our flocks and herds should not only be maintained but increased, and there never was a more opportune time than now to strengthen the hands of the farmer and stock-raiser m the production of beef and mutton.
It is roughly computed that the average price of first-class beef for the last three years has been from 3 to 31 cents on foot, hardly a paying proposition to the stock-raiser. The figure average would not be at all likely to go over 3i cents per pound. This is a most unsatisfactory state of affairs when we consider our many and great natural advantages.
What seems to be mostly required is a stable and steady market for live stock the year round. This can only be obtained by cold storage and chilled meat exportation. By this latter method not only would the grower obtain a far better price for his beef cattle, but the markets would be steady and such as he_ could depend upon. It would be a fairly safe estimate to make, that good, well-fed cattle could be sustained in price at 5 cents per pound, and would seldom if ever go below that mark. The difference between selling a good 3-year-old steer of, say 1,200 pounds weight, between 3 cents and 5 cents per pound is $36 in one case, $60 in the other, a difference of $24.
Counting the cost of rearing, attention and feed, three-year-old steers, sold at 3 cents per pound, represent in most cases a deficit, while if the same animals are sold at 4J, even, or 5 cents per pound and over, they represent a healthy state of trade and are a source of profit to their owner who is encouraged to go on and bring others into the business.
This extra money earned would not only benefit the producer, but would also be found circulating in all branches of trade and would be a benefit to the whole community.
This is the condition in Alberta, and the same conditions prevail in Saskatchewan, and I am told that they are almost as bad in eastern Canada. Now, the Roblin government have offered $50,000 towards the establishment of a public abattoir in the city of Winnipeg, and while this is in the right direction, I claim that it does not go far enough. What we want in Manitoba is something to relieve the condition for the whole province, and not merely for the city of Winnipeg. While we recognize the importance of the city of Winnipeg, it is not of very much importance when it comes to the producing of beef. Therefore, what we want is something broader, something that will relieve the situation throughout the whole province of Manitoba. The government of Alberta are also talking of going into the abattoir business, and there is no doubt that in course of time the province of Saskatchewan will have to follow in the same direction, because, as I have said, it will be impossible to keep up the productiveness of the farms of western Canada if we do not keep stock on the land. I think each province should own and control the abattoirs of that province, and I think the Dominion government should put on a cold storage system throughout the whole Dominion. All the governments should work in conjunction, so that we could have our products shipped to the British market in a chilled state. In this respect we in Canada are in a very favourable position. While Australia and New Zealand, owing to their distance from the British market, must freeze their products in order to get them to that market, we on account of our nearness to the British market, can ship our products in a chilled state. In that way the chilled products of Canada will bring practically as much on the British market as the newly-slaughtered products over there, while the frozen goods of these other countries will bring a much smaller price. Therefore, we have a very great advantage over them. The hon. minister spoke of the appointment of a commission t<f go to Europe to look intojthe conditions of the hog industry there. They went to England, Scotland, Ireland, Denmark, and Holland to study the conditions in those countries. I have looked through the report of this commission, and I [DOT] have also visited the
v

Experimental Farm at Ottawa; and I may-say that if there is one department of the Experimental Farm which the hon. minister deserves credit for, it is the hog department, because it is in splendid shape, and he has got there some of as fine animals as I have ever seen. So I do not think it is the conditions in these foreign countries that we need to look into. The conditions in those countries could not be on a par with ours, and anyway my idea of this question is that what we want to know of across the water is the price and the conditions of handling, what we want to look into are the conditions under which these other countries get their products to the British market. I think that if he had gone to work and -sent that commission to the United States, the Argentine Republic and Australia, to look into the conditions under which these countries send their products into the British market, then I say he would have been doing a splendid thing for the producing population of this country. But instead of that, he goes to work and puts the cart before the horse, and sends the commission over to Europe to look into the conditions there, instead of to the countries on this side of the water and looked into their cold storage systems.

speechtext:
I have given notice of an amendment on the third reading which I think is obviously in the interest of the country. That amendment reads:
Nothing in this Act contained shall he construed to revive any powers of the St. Lawrence Power Company, being chapter III., 1 Edward VII., which may have become null and void by reason of the said company not complying with the provisions of the said Act of incorporation.
As every one knows the St. Lawrence Power Company was incorporated by a Mr. W. H. SHARPE.
special Act of 1901 which conferred certain powers on the company in connection with making dams, &c., along 57 miles of the St. Lawrence river. That included our water-powers and section 13 of the St. Lawrence Power Company's private Act defines the time after which the company will forfeit its right unless it goes on with its works, that- is three vears from the passage of the Act. As a matter of fact the St. Lawrence Power Company, incorporated under the Act of 1901 has not constructed any works whatever. Section 14 of the present Bill provides:
Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to constitute an1 approval by parliament of ainfy, future development of water-power by erecting a dam in or across the St. Lawrence river under the chapter 111 of the statutes of 1901, intituled ' An Act to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Company,' or otherwise; nor shall the company hereby incorporated be authorized to transmit power generated by the St. Lawrence Power Company other than the power generated by and in connection with the works already constructed by the said St. Lawrence Power Company.
That is making an affirmation that the company constructed certain works which as a matter of fact they did not. This idea is amplified in section 13 by the use of the word 'further'.
The Governor in Council shall not give his approval to the construction of any further canals, &e. ... by the St. Lawrence Power Company.
They have not constructed any works and consequently the word 'further' is a misnomer. The whole list of amendments incorporated in the present Bill are admittedly irregular to say the least. I do not think that in the memory of the oldest parliamentarian that it was ever known that rights of certain promoters under a previous Act have been cut down or curtailed in a subsequent private Bill. Even admitting that these amendments are regular, this parliament does not want to do anything that will revive rights that have lapsed. The amendment cannot possibly do any harm, and I do not think the gentleman in charge of the Bill desires to ratify any rights if the company have lost them by not constructing their works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
It has been correctly stated by the hon. Minister of Finance that an understanding has been arrived at between the opposing forces in connection with this Bill. Let me say at the beginning that I notice a report in the Toronto

papers this evening that I, acting for the Moral Reform Association, had negotiated a compromise. This I may say is entirely incorrect. It is only just to say that. I want for a few minutes to explain my position in accepting the compromise.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Dispense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I think it is only right that I should explain my position in that regard, because I know that I shall be criticised for having accepted a compromise, and the question may be asked as to why, if I accept a compromise now, I was not willing to do sp when the matter was before the House. Let me say that I, with many of the parties who with me supported the Bill do not, by accepting a compromise, concede that it is a proper or right thing to allow professional betting in any place, either on or off a race-track, or at any time. However, I was unwilling to accept any compromise until we were defeated by a vote in the House, and it was found impossible to get that for which we asked. Then it occurred to me that there was just one of two things to do-either to renew the fight, with the hope of getting something more at another time, or else to accept some sort of compYomise. If the fight were renewed, I did not know what might or what might not have been obtained; but in accepting a compromise I knew that we were certain of securing^ a good deal of that for which we asked. I was talking with one of the leading lawyers of the province of Ontario, a man who does not belong to the Moral Reform Association, but who was very much interested in the passage of this Bill. After the vote of last Thursday night this gentleman said to a friend of mine that he hoped that I and those associated with me would not accept any compromise. However, in talking with him afterwards, the gentleman,-who is a very eminent practitioner of great ability, as well as common sense, said that I would be accepting a grave responsibility in refusing a compromise that would bring about a law that was so much better than what we have at present. I thought that in that statement he was perhaps right. Then I realized, too, that there was a danger of the public coming to the conclusion that we were wanting rather to win a fight than to obtain good legislation, and if any large number of the public had that idea, which was not a correct one, it would, nevertheless, prejudice a large number of people against the measure, and make it more difficult to obtain legislation again. I want to point out that the legislation we shall have, if his compromise be carried through, is a great step in advance. It will abolish hand-book making entirely; it will abolish the keeping of pool-rooms; it will abolish the advertising of tips and racing Mr. MILLER.
information, and the transmission by telegraph or otherwise of racing news; it will limit book-making on the race-track to a seven day racemreet at the longest and not exceeding two meets at any one association track in the course of a year. That will make a very great difference. It will reduce the spring meet of the Woodbine from thirteen days to seven days. It will make impossible the meet of thirty or forty days held at Vancouver, the 60-day meet at Victoria, and the long meets held at other race-tracks. We realize that a great many men both in the House, and out of the House who opposed the Bill as I first introduced it were nevertheless quite earnest, and honest in their desire to have clean sports.
Many of these men, with greater experience than mine, have stated to me that they believed that for the first six or seven days of a race-meeting men went there, because of their love for the horse and for forse-racing, but that after that it became rather an affair of gambling and these men desired to see the length of the meets shortened. The committee will also see that there is a provision that makes _ it impossible to establish tracks belonging to any association incorporation hereinafter unless the track be located within a Canadian town or city having a population of not less than 15,000 people. That will, I think, .be a great restriction. A question that may be asked is: Why am I willing to accede to a compromise to-night, when I refused to accept it on Thursday night? It was not because of my determination to have my own way in the matter. I did not like the compromise offered at that time, and if that compromise were offered now, I would not accept it. There is a difference in the reduction of days. The compromise offered on Thursday night provided for a reduction to eight days and that offered to-night is for seven days. That is a reduction of one-eighth of the time. But another and very material difference, and one I strongly objected to on Thursday last was in the amendment introduced then, that allowed and exempted in express language, ' bets between individuals.' Now, I had been advised by the most eminent legal authority in this House, that the words ' bets between individuals' would exempt betting with the book-maker at all times, and at all places, because in the last analysis, the bookmaker is after all .an individual. If that advice which I got from that eminent authority was correct, and if bets between individuals in that language would have exempted the book-maker, then the amendment offered to me, perhaps not by any intention of the person who conceived the amendment, would have made the amend-

ment and the law quite valueless, so that the amendment I offer to-night is a much better compromise in my opinion, than the compromise offered last Thursday. I know I will be criticised for having accepted any compromise. I was criticised before for being too narrow and too extreme. Criticism and fault-finding is the natural diet of a politician and I do not mind it any more than other politicians do. Now, just this in conclusion. I have said that those who promoted this Bill who were in favour of the passing of it, do not concede that it is right to allow persons to bet or gamble as a business at any place or time, and I would like to emphasise this. I notice an article in one of today's papers that there would be another agitation next session to wipe out the book-maker altogether. I do not think there is any foundation for making that statement. If we pass this law in this parliament, I think it is fair that there should be a reasonable time to see how the legislation passed works out in practice, and new legislation will be asked for when public opinion demands it. The coming of that time depends very largely on how the racing associations conduct their tracks in the interval. I have nothing further to say then, except to thank those who, in the. House and out of the House, helped me with my Bill and to say this that I have no feelings against those who opposed the Bill, and who, possibly, were as conscientious in opposing it as I was in promoting it. I move, seconded by Mr. Mc-Coll, that clause 2 of the said Bill be reconsidered.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to be controversial at all in this matter, I am and always have been strongly in favour

of the abolition of the worst vices that appertain to race-track gambling; but I would point out that Winnipeg and the people of the west desire to hold a World's fair in Winnipeg sometime in the near future. Surely it is not the intention of this parliament to legislate in such a way that if Winnipeg does hold a World's fair, we can only have seven, days' racing at that fair. I would like some provision inserted in this Bill that will get over that difficulty. I am only suggesting it to the good sense of the House, and not with any desire to raise any controversy in the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: The World's Fair is a special event, and perhaps we could let that matter stand, and make it a subject of legislation if necessary when the World's Fair is finally decided on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I think that is quite right, if it were possible to give Winnipeg a guarantee to that effect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I would like to ask the promoter of this Bill one question. Will this clause, as I find it in a copy of the Bill, prevent newspapers published in Canada or elsewhere from publishing bets or the odds on sporting events?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I do not think it will. That clause is not a new one, it was before the House foT a long time, and no newspaper publisher, or newspaper dealer has made any protest. I should think their interest is not being affected, or they would have protested.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not here, but the Solicitor General is here, and I would like to have his opinion on that question. For instance, would that clause prevent the ' Globe ' newspaper from publishing the odds, we will say, on the Jeffries-Johnson fight? Also, suppose a newsdealer sells a copy of the London ' Times ', which constantly contains sporting information, and odds on horse-races and on cricket matches, would the seller of the London ' Times ' be subject to prosecution under the Code? It is important that that should be made clear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: The language here is intended for use in connection with bookmaking, and surely it could not be held to cover any such case as the hon. gentleman mentions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I think this is important, because in case of a prosecution under this Act, the intent of the House will always be considered by the courts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: It cannot be considered at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I do not think it is part of my duty to guide the House of Commons with any legal opinions I may entertain on any provision of this Bill. My hon. friend may consult the Minister of Justice if he chooses.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Then perhaps the promoter of the Bill will let me know whether he has presented that view of the case to the Minister of Justice, and whether the Minister of Justice has informed him that it would not affect newspaper publishers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I may say that the question has never seriously arisen, although many lawyers have examined the Bill from beginning to end on every possible point. I think the Bill has received the approval of the Minister of Justice from beginning to end.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: This section provides for two meets in the year of seven days each. I think there are cases where the association only holds one meet a year. It seems to me that the Bill should make provision for cases of that kind, that it would be a better thing to make provision for, say, a 10 day meet, where the association has only one meet a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I may say in reply to the hon. gentleman that there has been no willingness and no anxiety on my part in effecting a compromise to accommodate the Bill to every possible contingency or racing or gambling interest. I utterly refused to do that. The solicitors appearing for the racing association contended for an eight day meet throughout, and I said that if the number of days were not reduced to seven there would be no compromise at all. Now, we cannot legislate in one way for the eastern part of Canada and in another way for the western part, in our Criminal Code. The argument that was made for perpetuating race-track bookmaking at all was that racing was necessary to improve the breed of horses, and that book-making was necessary to keep up the races. Now, a gentleman from the city of Vancouver who is representing horsemen there, asked me to consent to the very thing the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) has just suggested, and his reason was this: He said, We have no race-horses in British Columbia, our horses all come from Texas and California, and they will not come for a seven day meet. I said in reply that if horse-racing is necessary for breeding good horses, and if book-making is necessary for racing, I do not think it is any part of the duty of the legislators of Canada -to give special terms to racing men in Vancouver to improve horses that are bred and owned in the states of Texas and California.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I think there are some places in Canada where the Bill will work a little hardship. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan), According to the Bill, any association that holds two meets during the year can have races for 14 days within the year. Surely it would not be too much for an association that is supposed by its by-laws to hold only one meet, to have that meet last 10 days. Take the town in which I live, it is a long way from the general settlement of Ontario on the east and from Manitoba on the west. They have races there, and horses come from both the east and the west, not American horses hut Canadian horses, and I do not believe they would come for a seven days meet. The proposition, not to increase, but to reduce by four days the racing on that track, is not asking the hon. member to yield anything. How can it work any hardship? I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I made the suggestion because I think it would bring this compromise more in line with the original Bill which I supported. I can. see no necessity myself for two meets in the year. I think it is our duty to encourage a reduction of the number of meets and encourage it in that way. Whv do you insist on having two meets in the year? For my part I would be quite content if there were only one. But I think the least we can do is to make some provision which will he an inducement to the association to limit the number of meets to one a year. Probably it is not the number of days that each meet continues that brings the evils altogether, it is the number of meets as well. I think that the association which chooses to have only one meet in the year is doing much less to aggravate the evils of betting and race-track gambling than the association which has two meets. I think it is right that we should hold out some inducements to these associations which limit the number of their meets to one a year. I am prepared. I will prepare an amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman will not press his amendment for the reason that his amendment will not necessarily reduce the number of meets. The hon. member wants to make it optional as to whether a racing association will have two meets of seven days in the year or whether it will choose to have one meet of ten days. Wherever it will be possible to hold two meets they will have them, but if it is impossible to hold the two meets they will hold one meet of ten days. I am told that the undesirable, obnoxious crowd that the hon. gentleman himself spoke of as frequenting the race-track are Mr. MILLER.
much less likely to attend and follow a short meeting than they are a long meeting, and after six or seven days the racing becomes utterly bad, while it may be comparatively respectable for the first six or seven days. For these reasons, I am utterly opposed to the long meeting, and I hope my hon. friend will not press his amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I must disagree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller).

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: What do you race there?

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: We race some very good horses, not all owned by ourselves, but horses coming from a considerable distance. I do not wish to be understood as saying that we have no good horses, because we have. I hope the hon. gentleman will not take the ground that this Bill is, like the laws of the Medes and- Persians, unalterable, and that no change can be made in it under any circumstances. Here is a proposition that is in line with my hon. friend's argument from start to finish. It reduces and does not increase. It diminishes the number of meetings and diminishes the number of days. I do not agree with the idea that associations which hold their meetings for ten days are controlled by less reputable men or conduct their races less carefully, or that the class of people that attend a ten days' race-meeting is not equal in intelligence and otherwise to those whom you would meet, perhaps, at other places. The circumstances and the locality might make a difference. I am told that in the west a great many of the associations prefer one meeting in the year of ten days rather than two meetings. That is the case, I know, at the head of the lakes, and I do not like the idea thrown out that because of the extra three days the attendance there is disreputable in any respect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: They can Tace as long as they like, but they can only sell pools for seven days.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I do not think that is so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Carried, carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: I do object to the disagreeable accessories of race-meetings to such an extent that I want to see only one race-meeting in the year instead of two where that can be brought about, and I think it is perfectly in line' with the original amendment as brought in that we should do everything we can by way of encouragement and restriction to limit the number of meetings in a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext: Carried, carried.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you left the Chair at six o'clock, I was speaking of the combines and mergers which harass the people of the west, and as another filustration of how we are held up by mergers and combines,1' I will instance the cement combine. Cement is coming into general use throughout the country, and last year the town of Manitou, in which I reside, and which hasi

a population of about 1,000, put down ce-* ment walks costing $13,000. Had that town-bought the cement since the merger, it would have cost the people between $1,200. and $1,400 more than it did. If the Minister of Agriculture is looking after the interests of the people, it is his duty to take measures to prevent such combinations in this country. The hon. gentleman took three and a half hours to explain to us what he had done for the people of Canada, but when we look at his record during the past fourteen years as Minister of Agriculture, we are compelled to come to the conclusion that he has done very little indeed1 to improve the condition of the people. The fact is that he has simply followed the beaten path trod by the Conservative government before 1896, and whenever he departed from that path he has found, and we to our sorrow have found, that he has invariably come to grief. His cool curing of cheese experiment is an example. He constructed four cool curing stations respectively at Brockville, Cowansville, St. Hya-cinthe and Woodstock in which to demonstrate to factory men the increased money there was in the cheese business from properly curing the cheese. From the outset the experiment was not on a practical basis. On these four stations the minister spent $45,000 for construction, and he ran them for five years at a cost of $137,300. Against that outlay he had a revenue of $82,029.22, leaving a loss on operating account of $45,270. It is easy enough to understand that the cool curing of cheese is a good thing, but what the cheese producer wants to know is something about the financial results. The minister has never revealed this, and when one looks at the Auditor General's Report for the years in which these curing stations were in operation, it is easy to understand his silence. Right at the start, he began purchasing-from the factory men cheese to the value of $47,514.94, and after curing it in his model stations, he sold it for $47,385 or $129 less than he paid for it originally. In this losk there is not one cent included for the cost of handling, the cost of curing, the cost of insurance, or the interest on the investment, and any one knows that it will cost a good many thousand dollars to handle a business of $47,000. It will, therefore, be-seen that this attempt of the minister to butt into the cheese business in order to1 show the factory men how to increase their business, was quite an expensive affair foi the country. It may be urged that the operation of the curing stations was more or less experimental, but there was nothing experimental about the transaction in the cheese itself, which after having been bought and paid for and cured was sold at a loss. That is a mighty poor business pro-Mr. W. H. SHARPE.
position. The stations, however, were not an experiment. They were intended as a demonstration. They undoubtedly did some good. But how much more would they have done had they been conducted along business lines and afforded factory men financial as well as technical proof of the value of cool curing.
That is only one of the many times the hon. minister has made blunders in connection with his department. At the time he started in to show the farmers' wives throughout this country how to fatten chickens, he bought a dollar's worth of feed and fed it to a dollar's worth of chickens, sold the product for a dollar, and tried to figure out a profit. But he is great on the poultry department. Some time ago during this session I took a trip to the Experimental farm, and I found conditions there in what I considered very bad shape. After I came back I asked a few questions in regard to the poultry department, and I found that they had 320 head of poultry there, and that it took five men to look after them. One of those men received $1,500 a year, another $1,300, another $640, another $620, and another $500, making a total of $4,560 to look after 320 hens. The revenue fronr that department during ten months of this year amounted to $350.87, and the feed would have to be bought out of this. I want to say to the hon. minister that while these conditions are here at Ottawa at the present time, if he would take time enough to visit the Agricultural College at Guelph he would find one man there, employed at $35 per month, looking after over 1,000 head of poultry. I may say that our poultry department on the Experimental farm here was started 22 years ago, and it has been on the same three acres during those 22 years.
Taking the report of the Agricultural College at Guelph, we find that the best results are not obtained by keeping fowl on the same ground all the time. For the information of the House I will read what that Teport says on that point.
Our experience is that in order to grow the best chickens at the least cost and as quickly as possible, one must be careful to put them on new or untainted ground. We find year after year that where we raised chickens on new ground, they grow faster and make larger birds.
Still with this evidence before him, the minister continues to keep the fowl and tries to carry on experiments on this little three acres of land at the Experimental Farm. I might also say that the buildings which they have there are all long out of date. We are liable to look lightly on the poultry department; but I want to tell you that while we in Canada have not started in to experiment at all in poultryraising in connection with the experimen-

tal farms throughout the country, yet the revenue which we received from poultry last year amounted to over $25,000,000. In the "United States, where they have experimented to a certain extent, the revenue from poultry amounted to over $600,000,-
000.	This is only a sample of the conditions prevailing at the Experimental Farm at Ottawa. The hon. minister this afternoon spent a great deal of time on the Health of Animals Department. The most deplorable thing, iij connection with that department is that when we ask the hon. minister a question, very often we cannot depend on the answer we receive. For instance, last year, in Committee of Supply, I asked the hon. minister why he kept five veterinary surgeons in the city of Winnipeg and paid them over $10,000 a year. He answered that the five veterinary surgeons in Winnipeg did all the veterinary work throughout the province of Manitoba. But I had a list, which I have before me to-night, showing that they had paid out to other veterinary surgeons outside of Winnipeg, and within the bounds of Manitoba, over $6,000. I consider that it is a very serious state of affairs when we cannot get an answer that we can depend on from one of the ministers. The hon. minister had told us what great things he was doing, and how cheaply he was getting them done. But during the year 1905, which was the last year that the Roblin government had control of the health of animals for the province of Manitoba-the next year they turned it over to the Dominion government-it cost the province to look after the health of animals $3,655, while last year this government paid for the same service over $16,000, besides paying something like $15,000 for the slaughter of animals. Then, there is the quarantine inspection. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that in 1908 we had a general election in the Dominion of Canada. They had to get up a party fund in some way for some of their friends, and we found them getting up a small-pox scare throughout the province of Manitoba. They appointed ten frontier quarantine inspectors in my constituency, and in other constituencies in southern Manitoba, and they paid them $508.06 each of the people's money. Since then I have inquired of other doctors in southern Manitoba, and without one exception, they have all told me that they never heard of one case of small-pox during that whole year in southern Manitoba.

Some of them, only one, and one wrote to the department and said, tell me where you heard there was some small-pox so that I can get a case, or words to that effect. When I asked the minister for the return in connection with this matter of thd appointment of these inspectors, he absolutely refused to furnish it and said it was not the custom of the House to bring them down. These men are good party workers and I want to say right here, that the quarantine inspectors and the custom house officers at Gretna were the best organizers that the reform party had in the whole of my constituency. They took an active part in every way possible, in every election in that part of the country. Now, we have 34 of those quarantine inspectors throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan. These men draw $65,258 of the people's money, and if they are anything like the quarantine inspectors we had throughout the province of Manitoba, it is no wonder there are not many members on this side of the House from'those two provinces. The minister does all this under the name of agriculture. This money, I claim is being spent largely as an organizing scheme for the reform party, and before I take my seat, I want to tell the hon. minister that as far as I am concerned, and as far as I have heard from other members on this side, he will not find any criticism at all of any legitimate expenditure that he has a mind to bring forward. I would willingly support the hon. minister, if he spent ten times what he is spending to-day in the interests of the agricultural people throughout this country, because we must remember that the man who made this country what it is to-day, is the man behind the plough, and I would appeal to the hon. minister to put forth an extra effort and try to give him a fair deal, in this great country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I do not propose to occupy the attention of the House at any length, but there are a few statements made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, to which I wish to reply.



Agriculture in the Dominion of Canada occupies a position of which we are all proud, irrespective of party affiliations and notwithstanding what may be said for political effect or from a partisan standpoint. The work that has been done by our Minister of Agriculture during the last 12 years stands out clearly as evidencing progress and development on lines that make for agricultural betterment, in every sense of the word. I am sure it is not necessary for me or for any member of this House to occupy the time in substantiating what the Minister of Agriculture has placed before us this afternoon. The statement that he has made, I am sure will meet with the approval of the people of this country, when they have an opportunity to read what he has presented to us. The hon. member who has just taken his seat, has endeavoured to make a point against the department by claiming that our agricultural exports have not increased during the last two years and he quoted three or four of our products, namely, cattle and cheese and butter and one or two others. He took as his basis, the years 1903 and 1904, as compared with the years 1908-9. We all know that the exports of those products have decreased somewhat, not very materially, in fact I do not know but that the exports of our dairy produce are a little more than they were last year, perhaps not quite as much as they were in 1903-4. But there is a good reason for that. Those years 1903-4 were exceptional years for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The pasturage was exceptionally good and our exports were correspondingly large, especially of cheese and butter. Those products have, I maintain, not decreased materially, although as I say, they have been a trifle less probably within the last .three or four years, than they were during 1903 or 1904.

The hon. member referred to the increase of our exports of manufactured goods as being something to be proud of, and certainly the increase has been large; but taking our exports as a whole or taking our agricultural products as a whole and compare them with all our other products, I find the percentage of increase has been as large as or larger than in the case of our other exports. We have had an increase in our exports of about 120 per cent in the twelve years. During that period our population has only increased about 30 per cent, so you will see that the increase per^capita has been very material. If you take into consideration the increase of population during that period, you will find that it was something over 1,500,000, and the increase in consumption owing to that increase in population amounted to at least $75,000,000 yearly, and in that fact we have perhaps the strongest possible reason why our exports of dairy and meat products have not increased as we would desire. We all know that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are the principal provinces for the production of dairy products. With the increased demand by reason of the trend of our population to the towns and cities, by reason of the increased purchasing power of our population caused by better times, all our dairy products are finding an increased home market. Considering also the fact that the population of these provinces has not increased in the same proportion as that of the rest of Canada, it is not reasonable to expect there would be the same increase in these particular products. The western provinces have become consumers to a very large extent of our dairy products. When we consider the whole of our agricultural products', which I contend is the only proper I basis, we are able to see at a glance that I we are making very rapid progress on the line of agricultural development.

speechtext:
Hill recently made the statement that in his opinion it would be only a few years when the United States would be importers of all kinds of farm products and inside of ten years he predicted they would be importers of wheat. Thus I contend that the argument the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) was endeavouring to make that our agricultural exports were not increasing as rapidly as they should, has really no foundation in fact. The progress we have been making on agricultural lines has been such as to attract the attention of people in foreign countries to the condition of agriculture in Canada. Only two years ago, in 1908, a commission of Scottish farmers visited Canada to gather information and ideas in regard to Canadian agriculture, and the compliments paid by that commission to the Dominion of Canada on agricultural lines are something of which we have reason to be especially proud. It was only last year that the live stock commissioner of Denmark, Mr. Peter Morteborg, visited Canada. I had the pleasure of meeting that gentleman, he called on me, and I am sure he was particularly impressed with the advanced position we were taking in agricultural pursuits.
Reference was made to the cool-curing rooms established by this government for handling and curing cheese, and figures were presented in the endeavour to show that the investment was not a paying one. I happen to have some personal knowledge and experience of the work done by the station established in Woodstock, being closely associated with one of the largest factories in that neighbourhood. We found that by having the cheese cured under the system there established we were saving from a pound to a pound and a half on each cheese, which means from 16 to 18 cents per cheese saved under the system of curing that was there inaugurated. Not only was it proven that there was a saving in 231J
weight by curing under those conditions, but we also found that we had a better product in the cheese, making it more valuable. Further experiments which were carried on proved that fact absolutely to the satisfaction of the patrons of the factory I refer to, and of other factories whose cheese was put into that curing room as an experiment. Instead of showing a loss of a few thousand dollars, as the hon. gentleman endeavoured to show to-night, it has effected a saving of thousands, and tens of thousands of dollars, indeed I think I am safe in saying of hundreds of thousands of dollars, to the cheese industry of the Dominion of Canada. So much was the value increased that throughout the western part of the province of Ontario our cheese factories have established a system of cool curing by storing ice for use during the summer months. I am sure that the work that is being carried on by the Minister of Agriculturre, whether you consider the live stock branch, the health of animals branch, the seeds branch,, the experimental farms, the dairy department, or any other department you wish to investigate, that work will commend itself to the good judgment and the honest judgment of the people of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
I desire to make a few remarks on the subject introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. It has been well said and often repeated during this dicussion that the Agricultural interest is of the first importance to this country, and there can be no disputing that fact. In discussing this matter I wish to be fair to the Minister of Agriculture. I would not for a moment take the position that no good has been done by his department; I wish to give him, and his department full credit for whatever benefits they have conferred upon the country. But I could not admit for a moment that all has been done that should have been done, because I think the facts will prove the contrary. As I said, I wish to discuss the question in a fair and impartial manner, because it is the good of the country that I desire above all things, rather than that of' party. As agriculture is the foundation of all the other industries, I think it is deserving of the most attention at our hands. Now, when I entered this House the idea was uppermost in my mind that the agricultural interests were the most important we have to consider, and I thought the Committee on Agriculture would perhaps be one of the most important committees of this House, and that it would have questions of the very highest importance to deal with. At the close of last session we found that nothing had been done by that committee except to sit and listen to lectures from professors from the experimental farms.

As a humble member of the committee I thought that was only preliminary to the introduction of more serious work by the committee. But this session also I have found that the committee paid less attention to the subject than it did last session. It was weeks after the House met before the committee were called together for organization, and there has been no meeting of that committee since the month of February. The chairman of that committee is the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Schell). It seems to me that committee has been negligent in looking after the interests of the farming population of this country. In making this criticism I do it with the honest purpose of directing the attention of the minister to the subject, and I hope he will receive the suggestions I make in the same spirit in which I offer them. That committee is called the Committee on Agriculture and Immigration, and there are many pressing questions before the country to which it ought at once to turn its attention. Now, there is one very serious problem among others to which I wish to refer; I called the attention of the chairman of the committee to it at our closing meeting held a few weeks ago, because I thought ithat something would be done about it in the House during this session. The question I refer to is that of production and consumption, particularly as they relate to the products of the farm. That problem has become a very serious one in the older provinces where we find the population of the towns and cities increasing, in some cases at a very rapid rate, while the population in the rural districts is decreasing. As a result of the decrease of population in the rural districts, production must naturally decrease likewise. Of course it does not always follow that a decrease in population means a decrease in production, because one man can do more work in some lines on a farm now by means of modern agricultural appliances than two or three men could do years ago. But it is a fact that in the province of Ontario the rural population is decreasing, and I am told that the same decrease is taking place in Nova Scotia, New' Brunsw'ick and Quebec and the the result is a very large decrease in the amount of food stuffs produced.
Now, the superintendent of the fruiti division, at the meeting of the Agricultural Committee last session, drew our attention' to this problem which he said was facing us, and he proposed a solution of it. The solution he proposed was that the government should use the means at its disposal to encourage people to go back to the land. He cited an instance before the committee of a section of country where he was residing, I believe in the county of Middlesex,' Mr. THORNTON.
when he was a boy, in which there were fifteen families each on a fifty-acre farm. He told us that these fifteen farms, with a total area of 750 acres, wTere now in the possession of one man, and that instead of (fifteen families living on these farms, they are now combined into the one farm with two families living on it. He said that the rental per acre of that land for grazing purposes was only $2, whereas, if it were divided into small farms and planted with apples, it would be capable of producing $200 per acre. Mr. McNeill's solution of the question is that the land, instead ofi being made into larger farms should be divided into smaller farms, that more attention should be paid to the production of fruit, especially apples, and that the land should be made to produce that of which it is capable. There was a case brought to my attention just a few days ago. The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) is personally acquainted with the circumstances that I am about to relate. An acquaintance of his has a fruit farm of small dimensions in British Columbia, and that he was producing from five acres of strawberries $1,400 per acre. This was the amount of gross receipts in 1909. He is not getting any extravagant prices for his strawberries. They averaged him not more than ten cents per box, but he is making a fortune raising five acres of strawberries per year. The point I want to make is that this problem of production and consumption must be solved by the authorities of this country, and that means the Minister of Agriculture and his department, because that is the only department that can handle it. The problem must be solved,, and it must be solved in that way. It is a broad question, but it is worthy of the attention of the minister and of the department, and I would say without any feeling of animosity or any desire to stir up party controversy whatever, that this question should receive the most serious attention of the Minister of Agriculture. He should-take hold of it in a broad way. I believe there is a solution of the difficulty, but it requires to be shown that the land is capable of producing far in excess of what it is producing to-day. There should be more tillers of the soil. When we touch the question of making the land more productive, we are face to face with the labour problem. One of the difficulties that faces the farmer to-day in older Ontario is the scarcity and dearness of labour. I believe that a good class of experienced farm labourers could be had from the older countries. I saw a letter only yesterday from a member of the Ontario legislature who has been for several weeks in England, in the counties of Sussex and Kent, and he says that there are many hundreds, and,

I presume from what he says thousands of experienced farm labourers in these two counties who are willing and anxious to come to Ontario and work on these older farms. If that is so, the labour problem can be solved. The chairman of the Committee on Agriculture has made some statements with regard to the export of agricultural products', and especially of dairy and hog products that are not borne out by the facts or by statistics. There is no question at all, but that the export of fine dairy products, such as butter, cheese, eggs, bacons and hams, is decreasing at quite a rapid rate. The export of hams and bacon is decreasing at the rate of $2,000,000 a year. There is no question at all but that the farmers are not taking hold of the hog industry as they should. The Minister of Agriculture will know, as well as every farmer who has experience, that one of the chief reasons for the decrease in hog production is the fact that the farmers have at least been caught three times with large stocks on their hands when the packers thought they could take advantage of them, and they were compelled, at a tremendous sacrifice, to sell their hogs away below cost price. It is not a difficult thing to fool the farmers a few times, but they cannot be fooled too often, and there is no question but that one of the reasons of the light production of hogs to-day is that if the farmers loaded up with hogs they do not know what the consequences might be within a year and a half, because it would take that time for the farmers to get hogs enough ahead to be worth while. Perhaps the main question with the farmer, in so far as production is concerned, is the question of labour. So, I think thftt the minister should take hold of this question in a serious way. A great improvement might be made, here in the older province of Ontario at least, if the people could be led to see that there is money to be made out of farming on small farms in a way that they1 do not appreciate to-day, and until they are convinced of that they will never get back on tbe land. One of the problems is to educate the farmer along these lines. These are important questions. I started out with the question of the scope and work of the Committee on Agriculture of this House, and I think that the committee should take hold of this question. _ The Minister of Agriculture should lead in it, and I know that a majority of the members of the committee are anxious that some effective work should be done by the committee along these lines. I think they are perfectly willing to do it in a manner altogether free from party spirit. Unless something is done to better the condition of things in the older provinces there is a serious problem ahead of the people living
in these provinces. I trust the minister will give this matter his most serious con-', sideration.

I will always concur with pleasure in the granting, of sums of money for the purpose of promoting agricultural reforms. These are badly required in the district of Quebec, for the population of the magnificent parishes on the banks of the St. Lawrence is yearly dwindling.
The minister might secure the progress of agriculture by establishing an experimental farm in the eastern portion of the province of Quebec. I will not, however, enter this evening into the reasons prompting us to insist upon an experimental farm in the Quebec region. They are well known to the head of the department.
We are in a position to appreciate the beneficial results of the fruit station established at the village Des Aulnaies by Auguste Dupuis. Such a station in our region has already become a source of very marked progress.
The Minister of Agriculture of the Quebec government has established an agricultural society in the county which I have the honour to represent. Farmers may derive great benefit therefrom and the work would be greatly helped by the establishment in connection therewith of a bee culture station. We are now making that request, in support of which you will allow me to read a petition sent by one of my electors to the hon. the Minister of Agriculture:

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.

speechtext:
Village des Aulnaies, April, 1910.
To the Honourable Sydney Fisher,
Minister of Agrieutlure,
Ottawa,
Sir,-I have the honour of calling your particular attention to the importance of bee-culture in the province of Quebec.
That branch of agriculture which you have long appreciated and encouraged has progressed since the farmers have adopted the newer methods and the modern mobile hive.
All farmers who have followed the practical methods and advice of lectures on bee culture have realized excellent profits and are naturally more interested than ever in the art. The number of hives has materially increased in all the different, counties of the province.
This increase would be more than doubled every year, Sir, if an experimental bee culture station were established under the auspices of the federal government in our portion of this province.
These experimental bee culture stations would attend to the numerous requests for hives which are yearly increasing it they would he in a position to dispose of the hives

on somewhat better terms tban private dealers.
You are aware, sir, that I am the only specialist in bee culture. I find that the business pays. I have sold hundreds of hives since 1875 at $10 a hive, and I have studied and practised the art of artificial swarming.
As a rule farmers find that $10 is too much to pay for a hive in the spring, the more prosperous alone can afford one or two at that price; the greater number do not buy and the development of this important industry is therefore greatly retarded.
The establishment of a bee culture experimental station would therefore be very useful to farmers who are anxious to go into that branch of agriculture, by enabling them to obtain hives on better terms.
Moreover, and this, sir, is an important consideration, farmers in the eastern portion of the province would enjoy the great advantage of being able to obtain information and lessons in bee culture without being obliged to incur the loss in time and money entailed by a journey to the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa.
The location of a bee culture experimental station would be easy bo find as I have the honour of placing at the disposal of the minister my own apiary and laboratory, which, after the spring sales, will contain one hundred modern hives, of the Jones type, considered the best for cold countries. I have seen them in use in Switzerland, in 1889. My apiary is at the village Des Aulnaies, in the county of I/Islet, on the banks of the St. Lawrence, an ideal spot surrounded by meadows bearing during the spring every species °f plant favourable to the making of honey and quite close to extensive orchards, containing not only fruit trees but also ornamental trees such as acacia, linden tree, chestnut tree, willow, poplar, aspen and alder. All these trees bear the pollen and nectar indispensable to successful bee culture, more especially with respect to the feeding of larva; in the spring.
You are also aware, sir, that this establishment is in close proximity to the fruit farm and experimental station of Des Aulanies, managed by my brother Auguste Dupuis, to which farmers come from all parts of the province to study the culture of fruit trees. The success of this establishment is in a measure due to the presence of the bees who are the very best cross breeders of fruit blossoms.
The establishment of a bee culture experimental station in such a spot could not fail to succeed and numerous visitors would derive benefit from the object lessons to be had there both in horticulture and apiculture.
Another important consideration is the absence in the eastern portion of the province of that disease of the hive called 'foul brood'; it is unknown from the county of Yamaska on the south shore and from the county of St. Maurice to the north. The Agricultural Association of the county of L'Islet has a membership extending from the counties above mentioned to the peninsular of Gaspe. JPirectors and members of the association use every effort to prevent this plague of the hive from spreading here; lectures are delivered and the importation of hives and of queen bees from infected districts is guarded against. You will readily understand, sir, the importance of such an ex-

maintopic: SUPPLY-ADMINISTRATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.
speechtext:
perimental bee culture station; it might save the district from a great danger by the breeding of queen bees. The disease having been originally introduced into the province by the importation of queens from abroad.
I am in a position to state that such importations, made with excellent intentions of improving the breed of bees, has been attended in many cases with disastrous results to the apiarists whose hives I have inspected since three years.
In conclusion, sir, should you decide to establish an experimental bee culture station in this portion of our province, I should be glad to be appointed to conduct it if you consider that my services, personal experimentation and observation and my studies in Europe of the best methods of breeding render me competent to do so.
And your petitioner shall ever pray.

speechtext:
This is a late hour to go into Committee of Supply to consider the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

The minister has come down to-day in the same manner that he has done every session that I have been a member of this House. He waits for an opportunity to try to steal through this House the estimates of the most important department of this government, at a period of the session and at an hour of the night when there is scarcely a member in the House. I would ask the minister to look behind him and see how many members there are to vote the money to carry on the affairs of this department. It is not fair to the agriculturalists of this country. What was the snectacle we had this afternoon? The minister knew that if he proceeded in the regular way a great many members interested in this department would be here to ask questions, ascertain facts, and make suggestions, in order that the farmers of this country might be benefited. But the minister, feeling that it was too early in the day to go with his estimates, adopted other tactics. Before the Speaker left the Chair, he brought up the administration of his department, I suppose as a grievance. Well, I want to tell the Minister of Agriculture that the farmers of this country have a great grievance against his department. He gives them data almost as old as the Laurentian hills. When I first came to this House I heard the same speech that the Minister of Agriculture has given us to-day. I said to one of the old parliamentarians: 'This Minister of Agriculture is a crackerjack, well up in his department.' He answered: 'Wait till you are here a year or two; you will find he presents the same speech to this House every session, and he expects it to go to the country to convince the farmers of Canada that he is administering the department to the best of advantage.' He came here today to make a great play to the gallery. Before he began he looked around. I looked around at the same time, and what did I find? I found that he had some of his officials here to listen to his oration. I think it is not just to the agriculturalists of this country that he should come at eleven o'clock at night, at a time when there is scarcely a member in the House, and ask us to make provision for carrying on the affairs of his department. I have a great many questions that I want to ask the minister, and I purpose asking them. At the same time, I do not feel that it is fair to the members of this House who have been here very late every night this week to ask them to remain any longer.
