On section 3-time and place of examination-

Under the old Act the qualifying and preliminary examinations were held only once a year. Under the Act of 1908 competitive examinations are held twice a year. For certain positions in the outside service, however, qualifying and preliminary examinations have still to be held, and this provides that they shall be held twice a year at the same time as the competitive examinations, and not to be confined any longer to once a year. This has been asked for by the Civil Service Commission and by the public.

What is ' the portion of the outside service defined by paragraph (b) of section 4 of the said Act? '
Mr. FISHER, Paragraph (b) of section 4 is as follows:
The second or outside departmental division which will comprise officers, clerks and employees of those classes mentioned in schedule B, and the other officers, clerks, and employees included in the Civil Service who are employed otherwise than on the departmental staff at Ottawa.
There have been certain parts of the outside service which in the old days were not included in the departmental staffs, according to the ruling of the Department of Justice. By the Act of 1908 all those who were in the city of Ottawa were brought into the inside service. That Act also provided in section 3 that the outside service shall consist of the rest of the public service. Therefore, according to the

decision of the Department of Justice, paragraph (b) of the original Act is no longer effective or needed.
Are there any special examinations held in addition to these regular examinations?

At any time, when a department asks the Civil Service _ Commission for an officer of special qualifications, not a routine officer, the commission may issue an advertisement of the need of such an officer, specifying the qualifications required, and announcing a competitive examination for the office. Then that examin-nation is held.
On section 4-transfer from outside to inside service
Am I not correct in understanding that this clause gives the ministers of the Crown the opportunity of bringing in from the outside service-by the back door instead of by the front door?

If my hon. friend will refer to section 50 of the old Civil Service Act, he will find that it says:
An exchange of positions between two officers serving in two different departments, or in different divisions of the same department, and the filling of a vacancy in the department by a transfer from another division of the same department or from another department, may be authorized by the Governor in Council to be made without examination of either officer.
Then subsection 3 says:
No person shall be transferred from the outside to the inside division whose age at the date of his first appointment exceeded 35 years.
When the amending Act of 1908 was passed that clause was left unrepealed. The Justice Department has given its opinion that under that clause anybody may be transferred from the outside service to the inside service. Some occasions arose of propositions for such transfers. The Treasury Board discussed these, and very sparingly indeed allowed them to be not only justifiable, but in the public interest that this should be done; and when we came to consider the question, and discussed it, we drew up the amendment proposed in section 4 of this Bill. We restrict such transfers to officers who have served for at least three years in the outside service, so that the head of a department might have an opportunity to know the qualifications of such an officer before undertaking to transfer him to the inside service.
Furthermore, that it should be done on the report of the deputy, and as you will see from section 4 it should not be made to the third division of the inside service, Hon. gentlemen will remember that the
third divison of the inside service is defined as a division where routine and other elementary work is done. It was not considered t-o be at all likely or practically to be possible that a person in the outside service should have the particular qualifications for the kind of work, although it might usually be thought that he should display qualifications for the higher order of work partly from his experience and knowledge and his service, partly, perhaps, by the fact that he had shown extraordinary capacity and personal qualifications. We therefore decided that in the first place no officer should be transferred until he had been three years in the outside service; secondly, that no officer should be transferred to the lower inside service, where purely routine qualifications are necessary, and then in the following section we provide machinery whereby the transfer shall be still more safeguarded. It is an amendment to restrict transfer from the outside to the inside service although it does not absolutely do away with such transfers. That is one of the objects of this Act dealing with many others which came under our observation.
Are we to understand that the men who come in from the outside service have to undergo the same examination as the men who are coming in by the front door as it were?
No.

It is not necessary then for the men who have been in the outside service for three years to undergo any similar examination to those who are going into the inside service, but who have not already been in the outside service.

At present, before this Act becomes law, a man may be in the outside service for a week, and be transferred to the inside service without examination. This provision restricts it; he must have been at least three years in the outside service and must have been able to show to his superior officers qualifications that are not only equivalent to an examination, but in many respects better than an examination; in the second place he shall have to go into the higher division where these qualifications and experience are necessary to qualify him for it. In the third place, as will be seen by examination of the next clause, he has to come in by report of the deputy minister that his qualifications and his services in the outside service are such as, if available in the inside service, would entitle him to the position to which he is to be transferred.
Who makes that examination?

There is no examination. It is the report of the deputy minister on

the qualifications of the man his experience and his knowledge of the business of the department.

I cannot help feeling that these clauses are deserving of the severest criticisms, and I am surprised to know that the old Act allowed members of the outside service to come into the inside service without undergoing the same examination as others who were coming in as servants of the people. I would be surprised indeed, to think that the minister would allow men to go from the outside service to the inside service without proper examination, and I think the minister would be wise to have that looked into.
Have they ever been examined when they entered the outside service?

In some cases. Certain branches of the outside service used to require what was called a qualifying examination, and they do still but not all of them. In the post office department, in certain branches of the Custom Department, and in certain branches of the Inland Revenue Department they do. My own department also requires examinations for veterinaries who are entering the outside service.

That has been a very easy way of getting into the outside service and from that into the inside service, and it looks that way yet. As I understand it, those in the inside service, now have to pass a pretty severe examination which I believe is all right. But I cannot understand why one should be taken from the outside service, even although he has had some experience, and on the advice and at the command of the deputy minister should enter the inside service, or why he should be in any different position from those who enter the inside -service by way of examination.

Under the old law there was no restriction at all. I may give an instance of the kind of thing. There was an officer in the outside service, I think in the Finance Department, in one of the Receiver General's offices, a gentleman who had shown a very considerable capacity and qualification for his work. There was an officer required in the inside service in the office of that department- in Ottawa. It was obvious that this gentleman with his experience in the outside service was eminently qualified and fitted for the position. Such an officer was brought here to Ottawa and put into the inside service. He had been some years on the outside service, I do not know whether he had been three years or not, but if this amendment passes, he would require to have been three years in the outside service before

he could be brought in. He would require to be brought into a part of the service where his experience and knowledge in the outside service would fit him for the position. I may say quite frankly that an experience of three years at least in the outside service, under the observation of his superior officers, and with the deputy minister possessing a knowledge of what he has done and what he is able to do, is looked upon and accepted as being as good as a competitive examination. Under the old law, they -could be appointed in one service on one day and be appointed to the other service on the other. No such appointment has been made since the passing of the Act last year, and we do not wish to make any such, but we have placed here restrictions and safeguards, which in our judgment seem to be sufficient. I may say that since the Act of 1908 there have been only a very few, I think less than half a dozen, who have been so transferred in the two years.

I thought we had a Civil Service Act that was really more serviceable than it is. As it is the back door is wide open and the front door is practically closed, or at least the men who come in by the front door have to undergo an examination, while the men who enter by the back door are political appointees of this government. After they have been three years in the outside service, then the deputy heads of the department- can overrule the commissioners and put them into other departments at their will. You cannot call that civil -service reform, surely.

Has that point received the sanction and approval of the Civil Service Commission Board of Examiners. In other words, are the board perfectly satisfied that their duties should be taken-over by the deputy minister and that, instead of the board giving the examinations, the deputy minister is to be the examiner under this Act?

I can only say in regard to that that the board and myself and my deputy minister discussed this whole question, and eventually this clause was evolved. I believe that the commission consider it a sufficient safeguard.
Was it at the suggestion of the commission themselves?

The commission did not make any definite suggestion. They discussed it from various points of view, as I had in dealing with them. I went over the whole of the amendments with the commission and the commission have said to me, that the amendments as proposed here were on the whole satisfactory.

Could an officer of the outside service, under this clause, he transferred to a different branch of the inside service, or must he be transferred in the same department? For instance, the minister spoke of officers in the Receiver General's office being transferred to the Finance Department here. That would be a transfer within the same department. But could a person, in the outside of, say, the Post Office Department be transferred to the Public Works Department ip. Ottawa under this clause?

I think that under the clause that might be, though that was not the intention. I should be quite willing to consider whether words could not be introduced which would provide that an officer, if transferred from the outside service to the inside, should be transferred to similar duties. I would not like to have it confined absolutely to the same department. For instance, a man might be an excellent engineer in the Public Works Department, and it might- be desirable to transfer him to a position on the engineering staff of the railway department. The words of section 5 are restrictive, but they may not cover the point referred to by my hon. friend. Section 5 provides that:
No transfer shall be made, under the authority of this section, to the inside service except upon report of the deputy head that the duties performed in the outside service by the officer to be transferred are such as, if performed in the inside service, would entitle him to the position to which he is to be transferred, and that he is qualified for the duties of such position.

I think the minister (Mr. Fisher) is right in saying that it might be better not to confine transfers to the same department, as there might be a change of department with similar duties. As to what the minister said a little while ago, that experience took the place of examination and guaranteed faithful and efficient service as well as examination could, that could not be carried out unless the work to which the -officer was transferred were a similar class of work.
I appreciate that.

Another point: This section 4 provides:

and no transfer shall be made to the third division of the inside service.
Does that mean no transfer of any kind?
It means no transfer from the outside service.
I do not think that is clear.

It ought to be; that was the intention. The whole clause refers to transfers from the outside service to the
inside. When it says: 'No transfer shall be made to the third division of the inside service', that does not mean a transfer from another place in the inside service.
It might not.

If my hon. friend would refer to section 50 of the present Act he will see that it provides:
An exchange of positions between two officers serving in different departments or in different positions of the same department, and the filling of a vacancy in one department by a transfer from one division in the same department, or from another department, may be authorized by the Governor in Council to be made without examination of either officer.
That all deals with the inside service- at least, we thought it did. The Department of Justice declares that it affects the outside service as well, and that under that a man may be transferred from the outisde service to the inside service. The amendments here proposed are in the nature of restrictions in regard to that transaction. This section 4 is to amend section 50 by 'adding thereto' the words enacted. And the same is true of section 5. I will consult with regard to the point raised, but the intention was as I have indicated.
It was because it is an addition to section 50 that it ought to be made clearer and more specific.
Would the introduction of the 'word 'such'-'such' transfer-be sufficient?
I would be glad do insert that.

It sems to me that the best feature of this Civil Service Commission was that it was to take this work out of the hands of politicans. But this seems to be a case of power given not to the commission but to the minister and his deputy.
Not the minister.

When you say the deputy minister, of course you mean the minister-no question about that; they are one and the same so far as this is con- * cemed. Certainly we do not want any repetition in relation to the Civil Service of what occurred in Ottawa during the election. We thought that the instituting of this Civil Service Commission would remedy such things as the Prime Minister and the member for Ottawa going out and -I do not want to use too strong a word-influencing the civil servants of this city. The appointment of the commission was a step in the right direction, but I am afraid this is a step in the other direction. The matter should be taken out of the hands

of the minister and the deputy and the, commission should be given full control.

I think that the restrictions provided in this section are such as 'to take the matter entirely out of the hands of the minister and to leave even the deputy minister a very restricted choice. He must declare in a formal report that an officer who is employed in the outside service has performed duties which, if performed in the inside service, would entitle 'him to the position, and must also declare that the officer is efficient and properly qualified. It is only on that report that the minister acts. I do not think there is anybody in the service or among the public who mistrusts the deputy ministers.
How are they appointed?
By order in council.
On whose recommendation?

The ministers choose their own deputies-that is a well known faot, and it is the rule that has applied ever since the organization of the departments. At the same time, I might go out of office to-morrow and the deputy minister of my department remain. I think in a majority of the departments to-day the deputies were not chosen by the ministers now in office.
Why not leave it to the commissioners instead of to the deputy ministers? Why should this power be given outside the commission?

I think the answer is very obvious. In the case of a transfer, the deputy minister must have been supervising the work of the officer for at least three years. Therefore, he knows all about him, and the commission do not know.
Why cannot he explain that to the commission?

They would simply report on his advice. What would be the object of that? The deputy minister is a man who has been in touch with the officer, and it is in consequence of having been in touch with him that he believes him to be the proper man to be transferred to the place in the inside service. His report would have to be a drastic Teport to be acted upon. It is against the public interest that obstruction should be put in the way of bringing in a good and efficient officer in the outside service to discharge similar duties in the inside service.
Is it the intention that the report of the deputy minister should be in writing?
Oh, yes.
Is it not so provided in this Bill?
Mr. FISHER I move that the words ' in writing ' be added after the word ' report.'
Amendment agreed to.
Has this Bill been submitted to the Civil Service Commissioners?

Yes, they have considered the amendments satisfactory.
On section 5,

If a man appointed to the outside service has anything in him he ought to make good in two years, and why should not two years in the outside service entitle him to enter the inside service as well as three years.

We wish to safeguard the inside service so that nobody would be appointed to the outside service simply with a view of getting into the inside service afterwards without passing a competitive examination. Since the Act _ of 1908 the government have refused to bring men in in that way. I think I am correct in saying that nobody has been transferred from the outside to the inside service who has been appointed to the outside service since the passage of the Act of 1908.
Then it has not been abused?
We have been safeguarding it with the greatest care, because our own principle of Civil Service reform is embodied in the Act of 1908 and we wish to live up to it.
If there has been no abuse in the past, what is the danger?

We wish to make it statutory so as to remove temptation from ourselves as well as from those who may come after us. I do not think that three years' probation in the outside service is any too long, and the man who knows he will have to serve three years in the outside service is not likely to enter with the ulterior object of getting into the inside service.
Is membership in the outside service that much inferior to the inside service?

Not necessarily, but we have adopted the principle that the inside service should be entered only by way of competitive examination, and we wish to safeguard any exceptions to that. At the present time a member of the outside service could be brought into the inside service on a few day's notice.
And none, have been so brought in.
None have been brought in who have been appointed to the outside service since the Act of 1908.

In case this government should pass to its reward there may be a number of gentlemen in the outside service capable of filling positions in the inside service, and they would be debarred for a period of three years.
Yes.

The weak point of it is that it gives power to the deputy minister which should be vested in the Civil Service Board, and that is not in the interest of the public service or of the country. A deputy minister may have a favourite in the department who may be appointed without examination, although others might be equally efficient or more efficient. If experience qualifies a man for promotion, experience ought to qualify him to pass his examination. Even a minister may not have a deaf ear to the request of his deputy for the promotion of favourites. When parliament is making an effort to take the service out of politics, it is in the public interest that the Civil Service Board and not the deputy ministers should have the power of promotion.
The deputy ministers are not partisan.
They are appointed by the ministers.

The deputy ministers have a very high standing in the service and in the opinion of the community. During the discussion of the Act of 1908 there was a universal tribute paid to the deputy ministers by both sides of this House. I myself spoke very highly of them. A great many of them have been appointed by our predecessors, and in one or two cases gentlemen who have risen from the lower ranks of the service and who were originally appointed by our predecessors were appointed deputy ministers by us, and, although these gentlemen may have their political predelictions, they were excellent officers and showed themselves non-partisan. There is no .doubt tiha^ those who hold the honourable position of deputy minister are imbued with the idea of getting the best officers they can for their respective departments, and if they select a man from the outside service you may be sure it is because he has exceptional qualifications. Nobody, not even the commissioners, can so well know the qualifications of a man as can the deputy. It is for that reason we have left it in their hands. It was suggested by one hon. gentle*man opposite that the commissioners should find out from the deputy ministers about the qualifications of any officers, but that would not avail, because the commissioners could only record what the deputies told them.

This amendment will, in my opinion, cause a restriction which is not in the best interests of the service. We know that the great railroad corpora-tons are constantly finding young men in different branches who have developed certain qualifications which specially fit them to take promotion in other special branches of the railway service. It must be that in a service so extensive as the Dominion Civil Service, especially outside service, men will drift into particular branches of the service who develop qualifications which make it desirable that they should be promoted to other offices than those which they fill. If you insert the clause in this Bill as proposed, that they must be transferred to perform duties of like character to those which they have been performing, you limit the men in the service to a particular branch and you tie them down to machine method which is most objectionable, in that it takes from them all individuality and initiative.

There is certainly a great deal of force in what the hon. gentleman says, but there are two ways in which the restriction can be overcome. A man specially gifted for one branch of the inside service, may enter it by competitive examination, even though he is in the outside service; and in the second place, clause 21 of the Act of 1908 says, that if a deputy head reports that the knowledge and ability necessary for a position are wholly or in part professional or otherwise peculiar, a person may be appointed to the service without competitive examination, and without refernce to the age limit.
Could he get in without the approval of the Civil Service Commission?

He would have to get a certificate from them, but he could be appointed in that way. We are trying to reach the point where we wish to place some safeguards around the inside service and to make_ it exceptional that a man shall be transferred from the outside service to the inside service.

One consolation is that the minister sees the early defeat of his government inasmuch as he has not abused the Act himself, he is paving the way so as to prevent his successors from filling the offices in the inside service from the outside service.
I have not a telescope strong enough to see the day that my hon. friend hopes for.
If there was a man specially qualified in the outside service, he would be able to enter the inside service?
Yes, just the same as an outsider altogether.

I have before me a petition from the outside civil servants of British Columbia, which was sent to the government through the right hon. the First Minister. That petition contains this clause:
We therefore beg that under the new order of things which we trust will soon be established, any person now in the service who may be recommended for promotion to a higher class or division shall be required to pass no examination other than an examination on the duties of the office for which he has been recommended.
That bears on the point I have brought to the attention of the minister, and I believe that the outside service make a very reasonable suggestion in that respect. There may be a thoroughly practical man for a position such as we are at present discussing, who would not care to enter a preliminary examination on certain mathematical and classical lines, such as he might be required to pass to get into the service. That occurs every day in law and medicine. Many good men are prohibited from taking up those studies simply because of the fact that in their earlier days they did not pass the necessary examinations. It seems that you are putting the same restriction and difficulty in their way here. The minister has said that really under the amendment if they are prepared to leave the service, go into a competitive examination and start over again, they may be able to qualify for such a position.
I do not think it would be necessary to resign their positions in the service to enter competitive examination. Men in the service may enter the competitive examination for other positions.

They may do that but they have to enter a competitive examination based probably upon a particular qualification. If they have to pass an examination on the duties of the office it might be all right, but if they have to pass the regular examination before entering into the service it will debar these men.
On section 6, temporary transfer from outside to inside service.

This is due to the fact that occasionally we wish to bring some officer from the outside to Ottawa to supplement the staff in the office here. I have an instance in my own department where, in the veterinary branch, there was some Mr. FISHER.
work which was only temporary. There was an officer in the outside service *whom we wished to bring here for the purpose of doing that work instead of hiring some one else. This enables that to be done for temporary work, but the individual does not get any status in the inside service.
On section 7, temporary clerks for decennial census.

This is for the purpose of enabling us to appoint the census clerks to compile the returns of the census. That work has generally gone over four or five years, but we hope that in the next census it will be done within three years, and I have therefore limited it to three years. It is necessary that we should have about 150 people employed temporarily. Under the present law temporary employment would only be for six months, and there would be no means of doing the census work in that time. We make this special arrangement for census employees, we shall only employ them for three years, but we subject them to the rules and regulations of a competitive examination before they are taken on for that work. They are still temporary, and it gives them no status in the service after the work is finished.

Has the minister taken any steps to lay down the lines upon which the census has to be taken? What plan has he come to for taking the names of all those who are living in the New England states, and who have gone from the maritime provinces and Quebec?
We have no such object in view.
Have there been any of these special competitive examinations held up to the present time?
You refer to those which were spoken of by the hon. member for Kootenay?
Yes.
Yes.
When was the last one held?	.

I could not say. There are several referred to in the commissioner's report of last year, and I think there have been some recently,, but there is now an advertisement for a general one which takes place in May, and there are one or two special examinations for special positions. I could not give the information, but I can find it out from the Civil Service Commission, and let my hon. friend have it.

How is it determined as to who shall compete in these examinations?

I can understand that if any person has written on a previous examination and failed, and the government are in need of an employee, they may send him word, and give him an opportunity of trying this special examination. But, how ia it determined in the case of persons who have not written, who shall be sent for to undergo this special examination? I am informed that such examinations have been held in the past, that a person who has not been in the service has been sent for by the commission, has been subjected to examination, has passed the examination, and has secured a position.

I do not know what case my hon. friend refers to, but I think there must have been something particular about it if it has occurred. The special examination such as I had in mind was an examination for a particular office which required special qualifications. These examinations are advertised all over Canada just the same as the general examination, and they are competitive just the same as the general examinations are. Anybody and everybody may see this advertisement, and write for the examinatioin. I do not know of any such case as that which my hon. friend describes, and I cannot quite understand under the law how such a case could have occurred. The examinations are always advertised and anybody wlm complies with all the conditions is eligible.
Are these competitors to be chosen in accordance with the excellence of the marks they get?
Yes, in the order of merit.
Is this with regard to the officials that will be employed to take the census?

No, those are employed outside of it. This section 7 refers to employees who are to compile the information collected by the enumerators, all over the country. It will come here in the form of schedules, and these men will compile it.
Have the census enumerators to pass any examination?
No.
Not even a political examination, of any kind as to their party allegiance? '

No.
On section 8-schedule B amended-

This is the change which the Minister of Customs desired to make. Schedule B of the old Act placed the salaries payable to Collectors of Customs at from $300 to $4,000. The Minister of Cus-232J
toms desired to make the scale from $300 to $4,600.
On section 9-salaries of Inland Revenue officials-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This simply increases the minimum salary of collectors of Inland Revenue and probationary excisemen from $500 to $600.
Does the maximum remain as it was?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No. Under almost every head the maximum is increased by from $300 to $400-inspectors, from $2,500 to $3,000; collectors, from $2,400 to $2,800; special class excisemen, that is, the chief officers in charge of distilleries, from $1,800 to $2,200. The increases will of course be given at the rate of about $50 a year until the maximum is reached. This just, gives us power to pay our outside service a little higher salaries than they 'are getting.
What will it amount to in the first year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Very little indeed; so little that after making the calculation we did not think it necessary to take any additional vote. All salaries under the proposed minimum will, I presume, be immediately increased to $600, and then they go up annually by a percentage increase until they reach the maximum of their respective classes, the percentage of increase in the lower classes being greater than that in the higher. The amount of money involved in these changes will be very little, as the increases only take place annually.
On section 11-salaries of assistant postmasters-
Is there any examination for these officers?

Yes; they are obliged to pass a qualifying examination.
On section 13,

I would like to insert section 8 along with the other sections mentioned here. I see it deals also with salaries.
On section 14,
The object of doing that is to take out 38, which was included in the old Act. We are substituting a new 38 at the end of this Act.
May I ask the hon. minister if these increases were all recommended by the Civil Service Commission?

These increases are in the different departments of the outside service. I do not think the Civil Service Coin-

mission dealt with that matter. That is a question of general policy.
Are we to understand that the Civil Service Commission were not consulted with respect to these increases?
These increases were discussed on a resolution in the House at some length, and were passed by the House, and this Bill is based on that resolution.

What about the resolution itself before it came in the House for discussion? Was it submitted to the Civil Service Commission? Salaries and appointments are very closely connected, and it seems to me that this is a matter that might receive some consideration at the hands of the government. As there is an effort to get these appointments out of politics, I think increases of salary have a good deal to do with the matter, and when resolutions for salary increases are submitted to the House, the Civil Service Commission should be consulted. What objection would the minister see to that?

I think that is a matter of general policy, for which the government has to be responsible. There has been a request, and I think my hon. friend has endorsed it on various occasions, from the outside service to be considered in the way of increases of salary, and my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Inland Revenue and the Postmaster General, after consideration, have decided that they can meet that request to the extent] of these additions. The resolution was laid before the House, discussed by the House, and decided upon by the House, and now this Act is carrying it into force.
On section 15,

In the Act of 1908 the word ' year ' was used without any definition; sometimes it was determined to be a' calendar year and sometimes a fiscal year. As all the salaries of the civil service take effect from the beginning of the fiscal year, it was thought advisable to define it clearly. In the second part, it provides that when a clerk had passed his examination for the second division, he could not be appointed to the third division. Now it happened that the second division was filled and a person having passed that examination wanted to be appointed to the third division. We thought it rather invidious to say that they could not do so, so we have thought it should be said that they may be appointed if they so desire.

I notice that the increases are for the higher Glasses. I do not Mr. FISHER.
notice any attempt to increase the salaries of the postmen.
Is my hon. friend going back to the question of increasing the salaries?
I want to refer to the general principle of increasing salaries. I notice there has been no attempt to increase the salaries of the poorer officials.
That is not correct.
Well, I do not notice anything here about it.
If my hon. friend will take the schedules which are amended by these schedules, he will find that the increased salaries are through the whole list from top to bottom.
Do they include the postal carriers, the men who deliver letters in the street?

My hon. friend is aware that last year I increased the salaries of the letter-carriers from a maximum of $2 to $2.75. I have met the letter-carriers association since, and they said they were most pleased and thanked me profusely for the substantial increase I gave them. I met two or three of them in the streets after the Bill was passed, and they said, we can marry now; we have a salary sufficient to enable us to marry.
What increases did you promise for next year?

Without making any promise, and speaking for myself, for tho question has yet to come before the government, but I think I have the full support of the Minister of Agriculture, I propose next year to bring under the Civil Service Act, into the inside service, the clerks in the larger city offices and the railway mail clerks. That will mean a readjustment of their salaries. They will have a chance of getting better salaries.
These are the classes I am referring to.

Last year, I not only increased the salaries of the letter-earners, but aJso the salaries of the lower classes, stampers, sorters and labourers. Now, for the middle classes, I shall have to study! the merits of each class and adjust their salaries accordingly.

I do not suppose there is any class of servants that is more entitled to good pay than the mail clerks. These men are running great risks all the time, and they deserve good salaries, and ought to be treated well by the government. I am very glad to see that the min-

ister contemplates making that provision for them.
On section 20:	salaries of temporary
clerks.
Will this be an increase to the temporary employees?

It might be. Under the old Act, every temporary clerk had to go in the third division. But sometimes we wanted a man of superior quality who had to be paid according to the salary of the second division.
On section 21-no additional payment to permanent officers for any service-proviso as to annual salaries from several departments to officers in outside service.

It is intended to he the law, but the Justice Department has advised us that section 38 is not iron-clad, and this is intended to make it so. It was drawn by the Department of Justice with that intention.
