Bill (No. 197) to amend the Post Office Act.-Mr. Lemieux-read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

By the Bill to amend the Civil Service Act passed this morning the superintendents of the railway mail service are taken out of the Post Office Act, and are brought under the Civil Service Act. The present Bill is necessary in order to bring about that change.

Before the Bill is reported there is a very simple amendment which I want to propose. Some years ago the Postmaster General reduced the postage on drop letters in cities where there is a city delivery from two cents to one cent. Prior to that change the drop letters had been two cents in the cities and one cent in the rural districts. I contended then that if the Postmaster General was giving a reduction in cities, and as the revenues of the country were buoyant there was no reason why the rural sections should not receive a corresponding reduction. I do not think it is necessary for me to go further than to read the promise of the Postmaster General given in this House in 1908 when I moved the amendment
along the line I have indicated. The Postmaster General then said:
I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to be good enough to withdraw his amendment and to leave the rural section of the country to my tender mercy. Let us first try the one cent drop letter, and if as a result the revenue increases, as I feel quite certain it will, then I shall give my hon. friend's amendment very serious consideration. Will the hon. gentleman trust me for one year or perhaps two?
I at once acceded to his request, and I said:
I would gladly take the suggestion of the Postmaster General if I were sure he would be Postmaster General next year.
Well, he has continued to be Postmaster General, and I feel I can come before him now with a good deal of confidence. Then, after I read my amendment the Postmaster General said:
Will my hon. friend leave this as a notice of motion until next year? I fear it is I who am the Conservative to-night and that my hon. friend is the Radical, for we must not all at once revolutionize the whole postal system. Let us wait for a year or two to see what the result of the present reduction will be and if the increase of the past few -ears continues it is my intention to give further postal reductions. Of course, as to that I would have to consult my colleagues.
In answer to that I said:
After having heard the very strong assurance which the Postmaster General has given us, I think that my purpose will possibly be more likely to be accomplished by not pressing my amendment than by pressing it. I have no desire to embarrass the Postmaster General in this matter. I might perhaps gain a little political capital by pressing it; but my desire is to get the reduction in postage, which is of more importance than any petty party advantage I might gain. Therefore after the Postmaster General's statement, I am quite willing to allow the matter to stand over.
Then comes an important statement made by the Postmaster General:
I can assure my hon. friend that my promise to take the matter into very serious consideration is not a Vain promise, and m.y hon. friend may remind me of it at any time. I am only too pleased in postal matters to give the best possible facilities to the people; and if any further reduction can be given, which is reasonable and acceptable to the government and the House, I shall certainly bow before public opinion.
In accordance with the suggestion of the Postmaster General given two years ago I now remind him of his promise; a promise which I scarcely see how he can get over at this time, I having waited almost two years for its fulfilment. It needs no argument to show that the country districts are entitled to a similar reduction in

postage to that given in the cities. There is no letter-carrier delivery in the rural section, and consequently the government is not put to that expense as in cities, and that was my strong plea why the rural sections should get the benefit of the reduction as did the cities. A great many of the merchants in the smaller towns send out circulars to their customers and these circulars being dropped into the post office they are delivered from the same office without expense to the government. The reduction would be a great benefit to the business community as it would also be to doctors, and other professional men' who send their accounts through the post office. I, therefore, move:
That section 48 of the Post Office Act as amended by section 1 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1908, be amended by adding thereto the words:
' except that in cases where there is no
delivery by letter-carriers the rate shall be half a cent per ounce, which shall also be prepaid by postage stamps/
I do not desire to force this amendment on the government; of course I know I cannot do that; I simply appeal to the Postmaster General to do something that I think is fair, and reasonable to the rural sections, and now that he has had the matter under his serious consideration for two years I hope that he will be able to meet the request which at that time he endorsed. I have no doubt that in his usual spirit of fair play to the rural sec~ tions as well as to the cities he will accept my amendment in the interests of the country.

Before answering my hon. friend I wish to submit that the amendment is irrelevant to the question before the House. If the hon. gentleman refers to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, page 403 and subsequent pages he will find that:
An amendment which is not relevant to the question at issue shall not be taken into consideration.
Sir Erskine May lays it down as ' an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed-except in the case of amendments moved to the question for the Speaker's leaving the chair for the Committee of Supply or Ways and Means.' A motion having been made to declare Michael *Davitt incapable of being elected or returned as a member, it was proposed to amend the same by substituting an address to the Crown for a free pardon; but the Speaker promptly interposed and pointed out that such an amendment was inadmissible as it had no relation to the question before the House, but should form the subject of a distinct motion, after notice given in the usual manner.

I do not wish to evade the question at all, but I think it is not in order and if.my hon. friend can find his way clear to bring it up regularly, I would be only too pleased to answer him, but at the present time I say it is not relevant, and I ask for the decision of the chairman on the point.
There is a note at the bottom of page 444 which says that it is quite relevant.

The Bill before the House is a Bill to amend the Post Office Act.
Mr: LEMIEUX. To repeal a section.
Practically to amend the Post Office Act.
Of course.

I am simply proposing a second amendment to the Post Office Act. I think, Mr. Chairman, that if you rule my amendment out of order you will be obliged to rule the minister's amendment out of order also, because they are exactly of the same character. I am not moving an amendment to his Bill, I am moving an amendment to the Post Office Act, which is the subject before the House at the present time. I had no doubt in my own mind that the amendment I have proposed was quite in order. I never thought anything else and I hope you will so regard it, Mr. Chairman.

There is nothing in the Bill No 197 that indicates to me exactly what section 1 refers to but the title of the Bill is ' An Act to amend the Post Office Act.' I do not think I would be justified in excluding the amendment offered by the hon. member for Hal-ton (Mr. Henderson.)

Well, Mr. Chairman, under these circumstances, I must say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) that I would not feel justified in accepting his amendment, not that I have no sympathy with the rural section of the community, but I think that since the postal rate has been reduced on drop letters, the department has been giving the rural sections of the country an evidence of its good will and of its desire to improve the postal service. The other day I answered a question in the House as to the cost of rural mail delivery which is solely for the benefit of the rural section of the country. The cost of rural delivery is certainly large and will become larger and larger every year. This is benefiting the rural section of the country whose interests my hon. friend has specially at heart. As regards the rate, I do not think that the postal rate in Canada as compared to other countries is high. On the contrary I have here a memo showing

that the rate in Canada is lower than in many other leading postal countries. Take, for instance, England; the lowest rate on a letter is one penny or two cents; in Germany one and three-quarters cents; in France, ten centimes, or two cents; in the United States, the same as in Canada- that is two cents for an ordinary letter passing from one post office to another and one cent for drop letters. The rates on correspondence in Canada are, taken as a whole, lower than those of any other country. In all respects postage rates in Canada are as low as in any other country, and newspaper rates are lower than in any other country. Newspapers go from one part of the Dominion to the remotest post office, that is to say from Halifax to Dawson, for one-quarter of a cent per pound, if sent from publisher to subscriber. There is besides a special concession to rural districts since weekly newspapers, which are published chiefly in villages and towns, are delivered, within a circular area eighty miles in diameter, free of postage altogether. During the last two years the department has been pursuing steadily the idea of lowering postage rates and extending the mail services. All that entails some considerable-I would not say loss-but charge upon our revenue and the benefit accrues mostly to the rural sections of the country. When the present government came into power it found the postage rates on letters within the Dominion three cents per ounce, and the rate within the British empire five cents per half ounce. To-day, inland rates are two cents per ounce, which is a reduction of more than 33J per cent on postage paid by Canadian citizens for letters circulating within the Dominion. The rate within the British empire, owing to the initiative of Sir Wm. Mulock, has also been reduced, and you can now send a letter from Canada to New Zealand for a penny. This has been quite a boon for all concerned. Coupled with these reductions in rates has been a steady expansion in the service. Between 1896 and 1909, the number of post offices has increased from 9,103 to 12,479, an increase of more than 37 per cent. The number of post offices through which money can be transmitted by postal order has increased from 1,310 to 10,317, or nearly eight times as many as in 1896. The vast extent of the increase in the mail service is shown by the mileage of annual travel. There is an increase under that head of nearly fifty per cent. This increase in accommodation has, in spite of economy and the business methods of the department, augmented the expenditure from $4,706,887.84, in 1896, to $9,000,000, in round figures, in 1909. This is an increase of nearly $4,500,000, the expenditure being not far from double what it was [DOT] in 1896. Fortunately, the department has been able
to reap the usual compensations ot extended facilities and good management, and has thus been able to convert a deficit into a surplus, and with that surplus we intend to still further extend the postal facilities in the country. I want to show by provinces what is being spent every year out of the revenue drawn from each province by the Post Office Department. I wish to show the great expansion in the service in every province. In Ontario we spent 80 per cent of the revenue drawn from that province. While, in 1896, the total number of post offices west of Lake Superior, except British Columbia, was less than 800, since 1896 we have opened nearly 3,000 post offices. All that involves a large expenditure for salaries of postmasters, establishment of postal routes and rural mail delivery. We must 'be careful not to decrease the revenue of the department to the extent of my hon. friend wishes. After all one cent a letter is a very low rate, and the postal rate in Canada is the lowest in the world.

The former rate on drop letters was two cents in cities, and one cent in the country where letters were not delivered by letter carriers. The minister in his wisdom, and I think it was wise, reduced the rate in cities to one cent. But if there was any merit in the argument advanced before that it cost twice as much to handle a letter in the cities as in the country, I cannot see how the proposal of the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) can be rejected. For many years the Post Office Department charged two cents for drop letters in the city just as for a letter sent to any place. The country post offices had a rate of one cent for a drop letter. The suggestion is that since the rate in cities has been brought down to one cent the country post offices should get a half cent rate. No great expense is involved, and I do not think the country would suffer.

But my recollection is 'that the old drop letter rate in cities was one cent which was raised to two cents, and every one living in cities at that time thought this was rather a backward than a forward step and objected to it very strenuously. Then the rate was reduced to the old rate. I presume the post office has not lost any money by the reduction in the city rate.

I am quite sure we have not lost through the reduction in the drop letter rate in cities, on the contrary, we have done a very good business. This is because there is such a dense population and such industrial activity in 'cities. If we could reduce the rate in the Tural districts there would be a loss of revenue.

We are doing a great deal now to improve the postal service in the rural sections, and really, I do not think my hon. friend should insist. The one cent rate is no discrimination, it is the same rate although, of course, in the rural sections they have not delivery by letter-carriers. Then, we are slowly but surely establishing the rural mail delivery and each rural mail box costs money. I take the hon. member for Halton as a witness to the advantage of rural mail delivery. I passed through his constituency last year and I had there evidence of the very satisfactory servic.e given that county under the rural mail delivery system. Passing through Milton and through Halton generally I found boxes all along Hie road and the^ farmers getting their letters not at their doors but not very far from their doors. I thought it was a great improvement on the old system.

I cannot agree that there is no discrimination. I wish to repeat and emphasize a statement of his own. Whilst in the cities these drop letters are delivered at the people's doors for one cent each, in the rural sections the government saves all the expense of delivering by letter-carriers, and yet gets as much postage as in the city.
There are more people in the cities.

We cannot help that. I would not like the minister to be carried away with the idea that the rural mail delivery pervades the whole of my county. I know that he took a trip from Milton to an outlying post office called Mount Nemo, a distance of 12 or 15 miles. That is one mail route. There is another on a circuit of about 19 miles, but I am not sure that the whole distance is supplied with boxes. That is all the rural mail delivery we have in the county.
I was told that it was near that place that my hon. friend was born; so I thought it was the whole county.

It was not on Mount Nemo, but on another mount not very far from that. At present I live in the northern part of the county, and the people of that neighbourhood have no advantage of the rural mail delivery. I do not think that the argument that has been presented regarding the extension of the rural mail delivery has very much weight so far as my county is concerned, because beyond 25 or 30 miles at-the outside the people have not the advantage, though it cost them something as well as the government. I am sorry the minister cannot see his way to granting this small concession, which I thought he would be1 able to do, Mr. LEMIEUX.
from the admissions he made two years ago, when he asked me to remind him of the promise he then gave. 1 must say I feel disappointed, and I hope he is not going to turn this down for all time. I do not propose to divide the House on this question, because if the minister is going to oppose it I know that I cannot get it.
I think the country is entitled to what I ask, it is a reasonable proposition, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to grant it.

Is the minister in a position to say how the revenue is affeet-ed in towns of upwards of 1,000 inhabitants by the reduction from two cents to one cent? I understand that there is a good surplus in the revenues from these post offices. I understand also that there is a large surplus in the Post Office Department. I believe there should not be any.
I believe that all the money gained in revenue in the Post Office Department should be expended in giving the people a good mail service. If the reduction from two cents to one cent in the cities has given good results, may we not conclude that a reduction from one cent to half a cent in towns would have the same result?

The revenue in the towns is quite satisfactory, but we need all that revenue for the opening of new post offices, especially in the western sections of this country. In 1896 between Lake Superior and the Rocky mountains we had 786 post offices, whereas in 1910 there are in Manitoba, 699; in Alberta, 695; in Saskatchewan, 982, and in the Yukon, 20, an increase in those three western provinces of 1,610. We have to provide in each case for the salary of the postmaster and an allowance for fuel and light, and we have increased the salary first from $10 to $25 and afterwards to $35. We have to establish mail routes between these new offices, advertise for tenders, and so forth, All this costs an enormous amount of money, and we require all our revenue for these purposes.
It is only natural that the number of post offices should increase very much, but has not the revenue increased in a greater proportion?

The revenue has increased, certainly, but we require it all to keep pace wtih the expansion of the country. Eight or ten years ago we had jrost offices from six to seven miles apari. To-day we do not refuse to open a post office at two miles distance from -another provided there is a fair number of patrons. All this creates additional expenditure, and we mast be prepared to meet that increased demand made upon us. Now, let me give the figures. In

Ontario in 1896, there were 3,185 offices. There has been an increase of 563 since last year. Of course Ontario is a well settled province, where new offices are not so much needed. In Quebec there were in 1896, 1,640 offices. There are now 2,341 offices. In Nova Scotia there were 1,649 offices in 1896; to-day there are 1,953. In New Brunswick in 1896 there were 1,181; to-day there are 1,409. In Prince Edward Island there were 380 in 1896; to-day there are 467. In British Columbia there were 274 in 1896; to-day there are 571. In Manitoba there were 786 in 1896; to-day there are 699, but that included the two Northwest Territories. In Alberta in 1909 there were 600 offices, and in one year we increased the number by 95, there being to-day 695. In Saskatchewan in 1909 there were 861; to-day there are 982. So that since 1896, the number of post offices have increased from 9,103 to 12,885. Now, as regards the gross annual revenue and expenditure in the different provinces of the Dominion, for 1908-9, the last year for which figures are available. They were as follows approximately:
Ontario-revenue, $4,441,463; expenditure, $3,564,000; percentage of expenditure to revenue, 83 per cent.
Quebec-revenue, $1,905,942; expenditure $1,754,242; percentage of expenditure to revenue, 92 per cent.
Manitoba-revenue, $951,905; expenditure, $3,564,00.3; percentage of expenditure to revenue, 88 per cent.
British Columbia-revenue, $655,787; expenditure, $636,339; 97 per cent of this revenue was. spent in that province.
Now as to Nova Scotia, I need not give the whole figures. I will give the percentage. There we spent 124 per cent of its revenue. Of course it is a small province.
What is the reason of so many post offices in Nova Scotia?

In Nova Scotia the settlements axe sparsely situated. There is practically only one or two railways operating in Nova Scotia, and we have to provide the inhabitants of the different portions of the province with proper postal facilities. In Alberta, 93 per cent of the revenue was spent; in New Brunswick 129 per cent, and in Prince Edward Island 153 per cent. Of course, it is not always the best argument to use the law of averages, but at all events I have given the figures here. In a small province like Prince Edward Island, the people have only one railway, and the fishermen are living on the bays and on the shore where the railway has no access, and we must provide for those people. When they came into confederation they came under certain terms and we must provide for them.

Will the minister read the averages, beginning with British Columbia again?
Mr. -LEMIEUX. I will begin with Ontario: Ontario, 80 per cent expenditure to revenue; Quebec, 92 per cent; Manitoba, 88 per cent; British Columbia, 97 per cent; Nova Scotia, 124 per cent; Saskatchewan, 94 per cent; Alberta, 93 per cent; New Brunswick, 129 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 153 per cent. The figures given represent very nearly the revenue transactions, but the expenditure cannot be calculated quite so closely. Such items as the conveyance of mails by railways, for instance, which form a very considerable proportion of the total expenditure, can only be figured out on the basis of the track mileage in each province, without respect to the weight of mail that has to be carried over the different sections of railways. There is also the mileage of railway mail clerks, whose runs are partly within one province and partly within another. But this does not prevent me from giving approximately and fairly, I think, the total expenditure and total revenue and the percentage of expenditure to revenue.
Has the minister the number of post offices that were opened in New Brunswick in the latter part of 1908-9?

In New Brunswick in 1909 there were 1,397 post offices; in 1910, 1,409, an increase of twelve in the year. In Prince Edward Island there is an increase of two offices over last year. I wil. give the increases since last year in the number of post offices. In Ontario, the increase over last year was 54; Quebec, 72; Nova Scotia, 15; New Brunswick, 12; Prince Edward Island, 2; British Columbia, 24; Manitoba, 12; Alberta, 95; Saskatchewan, 121. In the old provinces, of course, in Ontario and Quebec, the increase is les3, but in the new provinces, we have to provide for the arrival of immigrants.
To what extent has rural mail delivery been extended in Manitoba?

I will give by provinces the exact number of rural mail routes authorized. In Prince Edward Island, 36 were authorized; in Nova Scotia, 6; in New Brunswick, 16; Quebec, 8; Montreal District, 2; Ottawa, 8; Kingston, 25; Toronto, 42; London, 123; Winnipeg, 29; Moosejaw, 8; Saskatoon, 3; Edmonton, 13; Calgary, 6; Vancouver, 7; Victoria, 7. The total being 339.
What were the totals for British Columbia?

Vancouver 7; Victoria 7-total 14. The increase in the cost of

mail service arising out of the establishment of rural delivery in British Columbia is Vancouver, $4,111; Victoria, $1,497. In Winnipeg, the total increase in cost arising out of the establishment of rural mail is $6,332.52. We are only beginning, but we are beginning on a safe basis, not on the extravagant basis adopted in the United States, As I said the other day, in the United States, though they have a huge revenue, this year, they have a deficit of over $17,000,000, and, according to the assistant Postmaster General of the United States, that deficit is made up of the lavish expenditure on rural mail delivery. We must take our time, and be rather conservative as regards that, for otherwise the Post Office Department might become involved in a very large deficit.

The argument of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) against the proposition of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) is the great expenditure that the post office has to face in the number of new post offices it is necessary to open in the Northwest. Now, the figures that the hon. Postmaster General has just given to the House are illuminating on this point. They show distinctly that, whilst there has been an enormous expansion in the west, yet in every case the revenue has more than kept up with the expenditure. We find that, in the great province of Ontario the expenditure is only 80 per cent of the revenue. The surplus, there, of course, owing to the enormous amount of the revenue, would represent a very large sum of money. But when we consider the western provinces, what do we find? In Manitoba, the expenditure is only 88 per ctm, of the revenue -a good surplus there. Then we come to Saskatchewan, a province which is growing more rapidly, possibly, than any other portion of Canada. We find that even there the expenditure is only 94 per cent of the revenue. In Alberta, the showing is even more favourable-an expenditure of only 93 per cent. So, the Postmaster General's argument does not really hold at all. There is no reason why the request of the hon. member for Halton should not be conceded. Especially so when we remember that every concession in the way of cheaper postal service means a greater revenue and greater profit. That has been an acknowledged maxim in the postal service ever since the success of penny posts in the old country. There is one especially strong reason why low local rates should be granted in this matter. The question brings up the big issue between the local retail merchant and the mail order house in the city. Everybody who knows anything about the post offices throughout the country knows that these post offices are Mr. LEMIEUX.
flooded daily with circulars, parcels, letters and 'come-on' documents from the mail order houses in the great centres inviting the people to send in orders by mail, and have them filled at the expense of the retail dealers in the country. The retail dealers would like to take advantage of the postal service, and do likewise. But, in the first place, he has not the enormous resources of the big city concerns, and also his expenditure for printing and otherwise is relatively larger, for, his printing would have to be done locally, and in comparatively small quantities. Even with the lower local postal rate, I venture to say, it would cost one of the great houses in Toronto no more to circularize the ^people in Milton, for instance, than it would cost a local dealer to reach the people of the town in the same way. It would be a decided advantage, however, if this cheap rate were introduced so that the local dealer could send circulars to his customers calling attention to the things he has to sell on something like the same terms as those enjoyed by the great retail houses in the cities. For that reason, I am strongly in favour of this proposition, and hope the Postmaster General will not oppose it, because it would greatly benefit local business, and tend to build up industries in the towns against the enormous, crushing weight of the mail order houses in the large centres.

The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) inquired why there were .so many post offices in the province of Nova Scotia. I would like to state to that hon. member and to the House what, in my opinion, is the explanation. The reason, I believe, is largely geographical. If you will look at the map, you will see that the whole coast of Nova Scotia is indented with harbours and bays. One of these, perhaps, runs twelve or fourteen miles into the country, It is settled on both sides, and there is no bridge or ferry. Consequently, you musft have post offices on both sides. Again,1 Nova Scotia has many rivers which are settled along both banks, and the mail must run down both banks, because -we are not accommodated with bridges for crossing at every point. The geographical situation in Nova Scotia, therefore, calls for a larger number of post offices than are needed in a province like Manitoba, or even Ontario, which are more regularly divided, and where the people may be more conveniently served by the post offices. As to the revenue, I may mention that, in a province situated as Nova Scotia is, at the very extreme of the Dominion, it is hardly fair to credit it with only the revenue that it pays into the post office. Take, for example, one of the business houses, referred to by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie)-a large mail

order house. The customer in Nova Scotia sends an order, let us suppose, to Eaton or some other concern in Toronto or Montreal. The goods are sent by mail, and the postage is paid by the large firm in the first place, but ultimately by the customer in Nova Scotia. I venture to say that there is a very large amount of money credited to Ontario and Quebec in this way that, in reality, ought to be credited to Nova Scotia. I was glad to hear the minister sa^r that he intended to reduce the distances between post offices. My own opinion is that this is the proper solution of mail accommodation in my province. Owing to the facts that have been stated, and the distance from the railway in many places, it is impracticable to have rural mail delivery in, some sections and more post offices is the only remedy. It used to be said by the department that post offices would not be pldced within four miles of one another, and I was pleased to hear the minister say that he was reducing the distance to two miles. That will lead to a great improvement in Nova Scotia. It is better to increase the number of post offices than to spend money in attempting to give the people rural*mail delivery, which is not suitable to that country.

The minister has spoken of the great improvements he is making in the mail routes of the west and has mentioned the routes running out from Winnipeg. I have been asking the minister for the last seven years to establish a postoffice in a district where at certain seasons of the year the people have had to go eight miles for their mail, and at any time have had to go about 3 miles. The minister said the other day that he had met the convenience of those particular people, but I received a letter this morning which would indicate that their convenience has not been met. According to this letter certain changes have been made, and the post office at St. Charles river has been returned to St. Charles village and a new office has been opened in Sturgeon creek, but both offices are three miles from the place I spoke of, and the river intervenes. My correspondent says that mail matter, including letters, is left at his store every day for distribution to people living near, while others coming in have to go three miles for their mail. As a matter of fact, the proper place for this post office would have been in this very store. I have tried to explain the situation in that locality to the minister and have produced a map showing how thickly settled it is. The population are almost all engaged in market gardening, and if there is any place near Winnipeg deserving of rural mail delivery it is this district. The trouble has
been that there is a little political quarrel between the old candidate and some of the settlers in that locality and the minister does not seem willing to accede to the wishes of the people, but seems to prefer to keep up the agitation. While the store-keeper may not be a particular friend of the government, I do not know that he is a strong opponent, in fact I understand he has been very independent, and the people have petitioned to have the post office established in his store. I understand that the people have to pay $3 a box for rural mail delivery.
I brought with me the other day the whole file on this case. The case concerns my hon. friend only and not the House.
I have taken it up several times.

I told my hon. friend I had given instructions to Mr. McLeod, the inspector at Winnipeg, to solve the whole question. There has been a quarrel between the two sides of the river; I received a report and have acted according to that report. The inspector has equalized the distances between the post offices and established a new one, so as to give satisfaction to the people. I am sure that Mr. McLeod has taken all the facts into consideration. However, I shall take the case up with my hon. friend in a few minutes.

The minister's statement would lead the House to believe that we had splendid mail accommodations in our country, the post offices close together and convenient for the settlers. The figures as here presented would give that impression. I admit that the post offices have increased threefold since 1896, but the revenue has increased in a far greater proportion, and the population to-day is probably six times what it was in 1896. The hon. member (Mr. Staples) complains of having post offices eight miles apart. In my country it is quite usual to have post offices fifteen miles apart, people travelling seven or eight miles for their mail. We have also post offices getting one mail a week, where they have had the mail route in the same place for ten years or more, and a large number of people are being served in that way. I think the Postmaster General might well consider the establishment of tri-weekly services in these localities. The minister should improve these services before he accumulates a surplus in his department. There is still a surplus of 7 per cent of revenue over expenditure in our province. We are generally met with the reply that the rev-

enue will not permit a more rapid extension of the service than is being made. I would like the minister to accede to the request of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and give a half-cent drop rate in towns in rural localities. The position of the small merchants in towns has been well explained. With their wide opportunities for advertising the big departmental stores in the large cities are extending their business to the disadvantages of country merchants. I hope that the Postmaster General will not try to show how large a surplus he can secure until he gives better accommodation to the rural districts, particularly in the province that I represent.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the Postmaster General may well congratulate himself upon the showing that- he makes, and it is recognized that for the administration of the Post Office Department since 1896 to the present Post master General and his predecessors is entitled a great deal of credit. Yet, the Postmaster General's Department is far from being an institution that we cannot criticise. The statistics that have been given, whilst, on their face, they are apt to justify another conclusion, are somewhat misleading. It would appear that the postal service in the rural districts, say in the province of Nova Scotia, are better than they are in the western provinces. I venture to say that, as far as rural conditions are concerned in the province of Nova Scotia, they do not receive as good accommodation relatively considered as they do in the west. As far as the charge of extravagance or generosity on the part of the Postmaster General or his department is concerned, that is a charge which certainly cannot be made. I have had a little experience with the Post Office Department, which has not 'been of the most pleasant kind in endeavouring to obtain better accommodation^ for the people whom I represent, particularly the rural population. Let me illustrate. When I went to get a Hi-weekly mail established I was obliged to surrender two offices in order to meet the increased cost of the tri-weekly service. The salaries of the two postmasters were somewhat greater than the cost of the increased accommodation. The department had to get the better of the bargain. I asked for the increased accommodation and they refused because the revenue would not justify the expenditure. Thev put it upon a straight business basis just as I would find if I were dealing with one of the Jews in Montreal. The proposition was put up to me in this form. I suggested the surrender of these two offices.
Who suggested that?
Not the Postmaster General.
Was it not suggested by yourself?

Yes, I suggested it for the reason that I found that this was the only way in which I could get a triweekly service. I wanted to benefit the greater number. These two offices had been established years ago. They were then perhaps necessary. Whilst they would afford a convenience there was not then the necessity for continuing them and they could be dispensed with without any great degree of inconvenience. Finding that I could not get this increased tri-weekly service, I suggested that these two offices be dispensed with, and I must thank the department for having carried out my wishes in this regard. I merely mention this to point out that the department cannot be accused of extravagance, nor yet can it be accused of extreme generosity. I might mention another instance of a similar character that comes to my mind in this connection. I got this tri-weekly service established and on the route there was a section between two offices about three and a half miles from either office and I suggested that an office should be established in that section. Inquiry was made and it tvas fojundi that the revenue would not equal the expendi-sure, and my request was politelv declined. Business principles were applied and the department felt that they were not justified in establishing the post office. What happened? I asked, later on, that a bag be put up, and I informed the department that one of the people living in the vicinity would take the mail and distribute it amongst his neighbours. Thanks to their generositv they granted that request, a bag was put up and the mail has been delivered in that section by a citizen who is performing the duties of a postmaster without having any salary. There is hot much generosity there. I am not finding any fault with the department about that. I have not urged that he be given a salarv. but I am pointing out the experience I have had as far as the generosity of the Post Office Department is concerned and I could multiply the instances. I may say that the people of the rural communities are not dealt with as generously as they should be. If you ask for a post office in a rural community one of the first questions that is put to you is: How many dollars can we get out of it, and how much "will we have to pay? If the expenditure exceeds the revenue the request is politely declined. I submit that you must do what is kiecessary to make rural communities more comfortable and to make life in farming districts more bearable if you wish

to retain your rural population. The boys and the girls go away because they have not the conveniences at home. It is not too -much to expect that we should have a tri-weekly service where there has been a weekly service. We receive this answer, when we ask for increased accommodation: Oh, your fathers got along with the present service, or this service has been in existence for the last 10, 15, 20 or 25 years and you cannot show any great change in the community since then. This is very true, but io, 15, 20 or 25 years ago you would not find a piano, or organ in some of the houses, or a top buggy, or silveT mounted harness, or the houses furnished as they are to-day. The conditions have changed and the people have changed with them. You might say that there is no need of these comforts or conveniences. But the people are the best judges of that, and if they have these comforts and conveniences which are not absolute necessities surely it is not too much to expect that they should have the convenience of getting their mail two or three times a week, if they are now getting it only once a week. Newspapers are so much cheaper to-day than they were years ago that nearly everybody gets a daily paper. Large dailies, such as the Montreal 'Star' and other papers, are so cheap that they go into nearly all houses. Farmers for that is one reason want a tri-weekly or a daily service where they were quite content years ago with a weekly service. In making these remarks I do not wish to be understood as criticising the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department is entitled to the credit of the people of this country. It is a department that is recognized by every one as being run on thorough business lines, but I am afraid that in some cases they are running it on too straight and strict business lines and that the officers of the department should be a little more generous when it comes to considering the farming community. In the province of Nova Scotia we have no large cities or towns, and therefore, the showing is not as great as far as the revenue is concerned as in the provinces where they have the big centres, such as Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg. The Montreal revenue swells the revenue for Quebec, and the revenue for Toronto makes the revenue for Ontario appear very large, but if you eliminate these large towns and cities and take only the country districts you will find that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island will make just as good a showing, so far as the rural districts go and the revenues received there concerned, as that of those other provinces.

I hope the debate, which has been wandering away
from the point, will be relevant to this motion of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson).

I do not know that what I have to say will be particularly relevant, but it will not be particularly long. Some very interesting questions have been raised by hon. members of the House in speaking of the matter which is now before the Chair. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). I do not think that the department can be accused of any great extravagance or generosity in its treatment of some of the postal arrangements throughout the scattered portions of the country. I am thoroughly in sympathy with the view of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down that the rural communities ought to be treated with the utmost generosity. It is the cry in Canada that we want rural population, and if we want to develop that class of our population we must certainly give the fullest consideration in the matter of mail facilities to those scattered communities which are laying the foundations of their future homes, and who are cut off entirely from their old connections and associations. I believe there are many places in the country where the department will be justified in establishjng_ post offices, even at a loss, for the sake of giving these people the facilities that they are now doing without. The geographical difficulties referred to by th,e hon. member for Guysboro as obtaining in Nova Scotia, are to be found in a much more aggravated degree in my own province of British Columbia. My own riding is probably 50 per cent larger than the whole of the maritime provinces put together, and in some instances the people are 400 miles from a railway, and are struggling to build up new districts. In such cases the Postmaster General should certainly not look for revenue. The hon. gentleman has admitted that he has a margin of three per cent between revenue and expenditure in that province, and I do think that where people are going immense distances to get their letters he should at least expend all the revenue obtained in the province to supply increased postal facilities. I trust the minister will take this matter into hi3 consideration.
