subtopic: VANCOUVER BRANCH JOURNEYMEN STONECUTTERS OF NORTH AMERICA.

speechtext:
Resolutions.
Whereas, protection is said to be in the interests of workingmen, enabling their employers to furnish them with steadier employment and higher pay than are to be had in other countries, without increasing proportionately the cost of the necessaries of life; in effect increasing their income in at least greater ratio'than their outlay, and whereas;
The Canadian customs tariff, by oversight or otherwise, leaves the occupation of stonecutting entirely outside of the scheme, and has an effect directly opposite to that supposed to be intended. Duties of 30 to 35 per cent are (outside of the British preference) levied on the importation of almost every article we eat, wear or shelter ourselves with, while the one and only thing we sell, our labour in producing stone, is protected to the extent of 20 per cent only. Instead, therefore, of being beneficiaries of the system, stonecutters are being very unjustly discriminated against, and whereas;
Cut stone is being imported here from the United States in increasing quantities while numbers of local stonecutters are walking the streets idle, we are confronted, not with a theory, but a very serious condition which requires an immediate and drastic remedy.
Therefore be it resolved, that this branch of the Stonecutters' Union appeal to the Dominion government for redress in this matter, advancing no opinion as to the relative merits of free trade or protection, but claiming a right to equal treatment with our fellow citizens. If the policy of the government is in the direction of free trade we request the reduction of duties on all the necesaries of life to 20 per cent. If, on the other hand, the policy is protection, we request an increase of the duty on cut stone to the average amount collected on such necessaries. We ask for no favours, we desire none. All we want is simple justice and equal rights with other people. We wish for no more, we will not be content with less. We do not grab timber limits, water-powers, or other natural resources (they forgot to in-Mr. BRADBURY.
elude the Indian lands, Mr. Speaker), and then agitate for further privileges and concessions. We give a fair day's work for a fair day's pay, value for value. We demand no privilege, we should be put under no handicap. And further be it resolved:
That a copy of this resolution be forwarded by the secretary to the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier with the respectful request that he give it his serious consideration.
A. DUFF, President.
J. MARSHALL, Secretary.
I presume, Mr. Speaker, that the government is in possession of this resolution as it is some time since I received a copy.1 In my own county, I think nearly all the quarries that are at the present time working in Manitoba, are situated. All the building stone that supplies Manitoba, and the Northwest Territorities come out of the Garson or the Gunn quarries in the county of Selkirk, and I think I may say these limestone quarries are second to none in this Dominion. You can get stone there from one foot to 20 feet; they have extensive plants, they have saws and lathes, and are capable of finishing stone in first-class style. I submit that an industry of that kind should be thoroughly well protected. The Garson quarry is only one of the. quarries situated in Selkirk county, and there are 400 or 500 men engaged in it. It is a notorious fact in the city of Winnipeg, which is building so rapidly, a large quantity of the stone which they are using in these magni-ficient structures is at present imported, while a great many of the stonecutters, the workingmen who are the bone and sinew of our country are not receiving the remuneration they should receive for their skill as mechanics. I would therefore ask the government to take into serious consideration the protection of the stone industry, not only against the finished article, but against the partially manufactured stone.
Bv this I mean sawn stone. Under the improved system of manufacturing stone, the stone for window sills, stringers, etc., is sawn to any dimension required and is put in place without the stonecutter putting a hammer or chisel to it. So I would ask the government, when considering this question, to consider not only the finished article, but the partly manufactured article. I think I am justified in asking this in view of the fact that so much imported stone is coming into Canada. Right here in Ottawa, in the magnificent new station building in sight of the parliament buildings, all the stone, I understand, is sandstone imported in the finished state from Ohio. We have a similar example in the citv of Winnipeg, where some years ago the government built the post office, which we designate there as the annex to the Winnipeg 'Free Press' office. It is a magnificent building, but strange to say, this government, which ought to encourage

the use of Canadian stone, passed by the Manitoba stone, which is admitted to be equal in appearance and in quality to any other stone that is being used in Winnipeg to-day, and imported every foot of stone that went into that building. I say this is an outrage. The government of this country should, wherever possible, use in our public buildings the material we are producing in our own country and encourage home industry. It is an oversight which I hope the government will not be guilty of again. Some of the finest structures in the city of Winnipeg to-day -the Canadian Pacific railway station, the Canadian Northern station, and in fact most of the great buildings-are manufactured at the Garson quarry, one of the finest quarries in the Dominion of Canada; and how the government of Canada, in face of the fact that this quarry was turning out such magnificent material, could go out of the country to get stone for a public building, I cannot very well understand. I trust we shall never have a case of that kind again in the western country, and there is certainly no need of doing so in the east, because the limestone of the Ottawa valley is not equalled in any part of this continent, If men are bound to have imported stone in their buildings, let it come in the raw state, and let our stonecutters, who, as this resolution says, are paying high duties on everything they eat and wear, have equal protection and equal rights with the rest of our citizens. I do not intend to detain the House any longer, but I trust that if there are any negotiations with the United States before the House is called together again, the government will take care of this matter as well as the protection of our gardeners, which I referred to a few days ago. Both of these questions are important to us in the west.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
* Experimental farms, $110,000.
Will the hon. minister explain the increase?
It is due chiefly to the fact that we are running three new farms- one at Lethbridge, one at Lacombe and one at Rossland, as well as a fourth on Prince Edward Island.

The minister gave us a very eloquent address the other day on the work of the Department of Agriculture, and mentioned a number of experiments that are being carried on at the experimental farm, but there are some which he did not tell us anything about. I had the pleasure a little time ago of visiting the farm, and I saw there what I presume were experiments such as I have never heard of or seen before. At the experimental farm in Ontario we have been taught to take care of our implements. At the experimental farm here I saw ploughs and other implements that were put undercover just as they had been taken out of the ground, with a great deal of clay on them. I thought perhaps this was an experiment to see whether it was better to leave the clay on or to have them properly cleaned and oiled before they were put away for the winter. Some machinery was properly housed 'under cover, while considerably more was out under an open shed, with from three to six inches of ice on the wheels. I supposed that was another experiment to see whether it would be better to have the machinery outside frozen in the ice or under cover where it would be dry. A considerable quantity of machinery was there, and one side was open and the water had frozen in the spokes of the wheels. Now, I do not know what the object of the minister was in keeping the place like that. Perhaps he will explain what his intention is with respect to those experiments.

I sympathize with my hon. friend. We have an implement shed or building in which the great majority of the farm implements are placed, but 1 certainly do not consider that any implement should be put in to that house in the fall of the year without being properly cleaned. I am surprised to hear that any implements were so placed. I will cer-f tainly inquire about it and instruct the officers that that should not occur, because' I think it would be wrong. So far as the shed in which there was water and ice is concerned, I can only suppose he alludes to a shed that was started last fall and which is not yet completed, and it is possible that some of the wagons and other' things in the shed might be in the condition he has described. I have not been able to visit that shed during the winter, and therefore I cannot say whether the condition is such as my hon. friend de7 scribes. The shed ought to be ready soon, and the implements in the shed ought to stand in a dry place. I think that it is well established that this is a good place for implements.

I can assure the hon. minister that that was the condition of affairs when I was there. I confess I was considerably disappointed when I found machinery, wagons, horse rakes and so on in that condition. That is not my idea of what an experimental farm should be. I can remember the model farm, as we used to call it in the old days, in Ontario, and although it did not bear the same reputation that the Dominion Experimental Farm enjoys, I think it is one of the greatest institutions of the kind in America. Lis-

tening to the hon. minister's address the other day, one would have thought that he had never visited other experimental farms in Canada. He practically took to himself the credit of having monopolized the establishment of such farms.
Oh, no.

There are a great many things that have been brought about by our experimental farm here, and by the very efficient experiments and tests that have been made. I do not wish to criticise a great deal of the work that is being done there, but I do wish to say that in my opinion, there is not more than half of the work being done that should be done. The agricultural industry in Canada is the greatest industry there is, and Teally it gets less attention and has less spent upon it by the government than almost any other industry in the country. An experimental farm conducted by the Dominion government, ought to be beyond reproach in every way. I would ask any farmer, or any lawyer, in this House to go out to that farm, and he will find that there are many farms in the province of Ontario that are more neatly kept. There are a great many eyesores at the experimental farm that could be removed at very little cost. One of these eyesores is the hog-pen. During the last days of the session, a year ago, another member and I visited the experimental farm, and we found the hog-pen in a deplorable condition. I was sorry, at the time, that the minister had got his estimates through and that I did not have an opportunity of drawing his attention to it. In the lower part of the pen, there were some hogs, and the manure had been piled up in to such an extent that I did not consider that half of that sty was fit to have a hog in it. That was in the latter days of April. Later, I had the opportunity of visiting the farm with a number of farmers, some 400 strong, from my riding, and West Peterborough, and West Durham, and to my utter astonishment, the manure which I had seen piled up in April, was still there, though in a smaller quantity. Now, these are things that should not exist on a model farm, if my conception of a model larm is right. I would urge the minister, if he is going to conduct experiments in the interests of the bacon industry, to at once destroy what they call the pig-pen at the experimental farm and have one put up that would be up-to-date, so that the. farmers coming from all parts of the Dominion would see a model pig-pen, model cow byres, and everything else as it should he at an experimental farm. But I certainly do protest against the class of pens used for housing the hogs.
11. SEXSMITH.

I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Sexsmith) has mentioned these things. As to the particular pen of which he speaks, that was an experiment and everything about it was done advisedly and intentionally. It is known that many people in the country are short of straw for their hogs and have tried to get other kinds of bedding. We have had many applications for information as to the use of black muck. If it were satisfactory and increased the manure from the hogs, it would be a good thing for many farmers. We carried out the experiment in this case. It is true, the results are not considerd to be satisfactory. But the hon. gentleman sees that we are trying experiments with regard to the management of hogs. As to the hog pen generally, the upper part was built many years ago. According to the then ideas of the best hog raisers in the country, it was a model. I admit that things have changed since those days, and now it is not a model. But, for two or three years back, we have been testing the best way of keeping hogs. Among other things used is the large pen below, to which the hon. gentleman referred, and which has proved a good practical pen for the running of brood sows in the winter time. It is not a very gorgeous affair, but it is very practical. When the time does come for us to put up a permanent building in that new style, we shall embody in it the elementary principles of this one, but with better construction. That also was intended for a test. Of course, we did not want to spend much money in a test that might not work out satisfactorily. The hon. member may have noticed a small pig-pen near there, a little building which was put up a year and a half ago on what we thought an improved model. We wanted to see whether it would work out before we put up the large pen. It was largely a question of ventilation, and of keeping the walls dry. That is one of the most difficult problems in hog pens- to keep the walls dry, to give ventilation and yet not make the pen too cold. That building has been a success, and we hope to put up a large building for all our hogs on the same lines of construction. But, I do not think it would have been wise to go ahead on a large scale before trying this experiment. I accept the hon. member's criticisms in the spirit in which they were intended. I think we should have all the better hog pen because of the tests we have made and because of what we have learned from those tests.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) took up three hours of the time of the House on Friday, explaining the wonderful progress made in regard to the experimental farms of this Dominion. No doubt some progress has been

made, but it has taken the minister, who claims to know more about agriculture than almost any man in the Dominion, a long time to learn. Instead of being a source of information to the provinces, which have not the large revenue for these purposes that the Dominion has, he has been content, so far as I can see, to lag along behind. The minister speaks of the hog pen. It has been constructed only within a recent date. When I first came to this House, one of the first places I visited was the experimental farm. I must say I found the condition of the buildings very inferior. And I, with other members, did not fail to call the attention of the minister to the condition of affairs. That was about seven years ago. The minister has at last wakened up to some of the suggestions then made. The minister boasts of his great progress, but, apparently, he is afraid to take the lead to any great extent. He admits that agriculture is the greatest industry of the country, but he is always slow in moving unless he is prodded from this side. He speaks of his splendid officials. I believe he has good officials; any that I know are certainly good men. If he would listen to the suggestions of his officials, in my opinion, greater progress would be made in these experimental farms. The hon. minister has been acquiring new experimental farms, of which he told us the other night. He has acquired two in the west, and now intends to acquire another in Saskatchewan. But when he decided to establish an experimental farm in Alberta. I understand, he acquired merely a quarter section of land. I had the pleasure of being at that experimental farm at Lacombe, and found, much to my surprise, that the minister had secured only 160 acres, though he might then have secured more at a reasonable price. When he comes to extend the boundaries of that farm, he will find that he will have to pay a pretty high price, for the people know the position in which they have got him. It was not necessary that he should get into that position. In superintending the affairs of agriculture for this country, the minister is not as active as he should be, and does not appear to have the originality which should characterize one in his position. A great many of the experiments he has undertaken have turned out not greatly to his credit-I do not wish to go into the details of his experiments with chickens and other things. In considering what is necessary for the instructions of the agriculturists of Canada, he should study these matters more seriously. Instead of taking trips abroad, he might visit the experimental farms. We can go away for three or four months, it may be, but I believe he hasi not been able to visit these western farms more than once since they were established. His first duty is 233
to his department, and he should pay more attention to it. He should work out bigger schemes for the education of the farmers than have been characteristic of his administration.

I am sorry I do not go
fast enough to suit the hon. member (Mr. Staples). I think I am going as fast as the means placed at my disposal and the decisions arrived at -by experts permit. He cast reflections on my taking trips and not visiting the experimental farms. I can only say that, so far as I can remember, I have not taken a journey of any kind whatever for fourteen years-since I became minister-except on official business.
Not even a wedding trip.

Not yet-been too busy. I have been hoping for a holiday when I might go for a trip, but I have been debarred from it hitherto. But I did visit every one of the experimental farms in the Dominion except the one at Nappan, and I hope to do so soon again. I can assure him I am doing the best I can and I am sorry if I cannot satisfy him.
The minister says he was experimenting with dried muck. I did not see any dry muck.
No; you saw it after it got wet.

The farmers of East and West Peterborough have been in the habit of visiting the experimental farm at Guelph for some years. Some eight or ten years ago they came to Ottawa. I had not the pleasure of being here with them then, but they did not return here until last year. On arriving here they were conducted around the farm and saw everything that was to be seen, but a great many were greatly disappointed. They had been visiting the experimental farm at Guelph, which has not the Dominion treasury behind it, but a very much more meagre resource, and coming to Ottawa to visit the Dominion Experimental Farm they expected to see something on a much greater scale, but they said:	This does
not compare with the farm at Guelph. I was sorry the conditions were such that this great number of farmers should find the Dominion Experimental Farm not anything up to their expectation. A number of these little things I speak of were eyesores then, and they are still there. It would cost nothing to have them removed.
What kind of things.
The rubbish pile around the buildings, old boards.

When building operations are going on there must necessarily be some piles of lumber and debris. The



office buildings have been under construction now for over a year, and during that time lumber, scantlings, etc., are of course piled around the building. The shed the hon. gentleman spoke of is not finished, and no doubt there was some lumber piled around there. There is a regular rubbish heap behind the implement shed, and the tobacco curing station, where it is well out of sight and where we do, for practical purposes, put any odd pieces of lumber, scantling beams, etc., until they become useful for our operations. We might destroy them and get new stuff, but that would be very short-sighted and extravagant.

I am aware there is some rubbish where new buildings are being erected, but what I call rubbish was a rubbish heap. There may have been some valuable stuff, but there was some that would never have any value. However, those are only trifling matters. How many foremen are there over the live stock department?

There is one farm foreman for the farm, and a herdsman who has charge of the animals in the barn. The man who feeds the horses and is responsible for their care might be called foreman of the horse stable, but he does other work as well.

Has the herdsman
complete control over the cattle?.
Not complete control; he has control under Mr. Grisdale, the ;agri-culturist.

Is Mr. Grisdale a
competent stock man?
Yes, thoroughly.
I suppose the herdsman would not be in a position to discard a cull animal without authority?
No.
Do you think that is the better plan, to have a herdsman and one or two over him?
He is only under Mr. Grisdale, the agriculturist, who is a scientific stockman.
How long is it since you had the first herd of Ayrshires?

I could not say. I think there have been some there ever since the farm was established, but there was a slight reorganization of the stock work about nine years ago, when the Ayrshire herd as a dairy herd was established.

I am not an expert in any of these breeds, bat when I see a cow milked and the milk weighed, I know how Mr. FISHER.
much it weighs and I have a fair idea of what an ordinary cow should milk. I happened to be there when they were milking. I only saw one or two weighed, and by looking over the herd they were in fine condition and all that, but as near as I could learn there was not what we would call a first-class dairy cow in the Ayrshire herd. A three-year-old heifer milked eleven pounds.

I am surprised that my hon. friend says that, because good experts in the Ayrshire breed would say there are some first-class Ayrshire cows. I have asked the average of the full-grown cows and it is about 8,000 pounds of good milk in the season. From the report we see that some go as high as 400 pounds of butter a year, which is a good yield. I wish I could have a herd that would average that.
I think that is a small yield when compared with many others.
Does my hon. friend say that 400 pounds of butter a year is a poor yield?
Very moderate.
I do not agree with my hon. friend.
I would not wish to say there are not some very fine looking Ayrshires.
It is not a question of looks, but of performance.

I happened to see the one heifer weighed, a fine looking animal, but the milk only weighed eleven pounds.
' Mr. FISHER. How long had she been milking?
Only a short time.
Was it her first calf?
Her first calf. 21,000 pounds is getting to be a regular yield for dairy cows.
There is not an Ayrshire cow in Canada giving 21,000 pounds.

I am not speaking of Ayrshires, bat of dairy cows. The minister the other day spoke of the conditions in Denmark, and the great change that had taken place there. If I remember the statistics, the average production of each cow was formerly about 2,200 pounds. In about seven years they had, with the assistance of the government, raised the average production up to 7,000 pounds all over Denmark. I do not suppose it is relevant to the question to ask the minister how that was brought about.

Well, I can tell my hon. friend. It has been done by systematic instruction, education and co-operation through the cow-testing associations, a work which we have been striving to introduce into Canada now for four or five years back, and which we have made some progress in instituting in Canada. At the present time the prospects for the increase of that kind of work are very good.
The government has made experiments with regard t-o the dairy cow, but is the minister not well aware that the government there undertook to raise the standard of the dairy cow?
How?

By importing and sending out among the farmers a great many sires of the Holstein type. They came to the conclusion that a certain cow was the best, and then they did everything to introduce that cow in the country. A great many sires were purchased by the government and put around through Denmark.

We have been making tests for years as to the production of cows of different breeds, but we have left it largely to private enterprise to provide the best quality of sires for distribution throughout the country. I think my hon. friend would find that there would be a very strong protest if the government were to enter into that business. I do not think that is the best way to accomplish the object, and in Canada to-day there is an abundance of good dairy sires. However, we have been trying to educate and stimulate the farmers, so that they would purchase these sires and use them, and for this purpose we have been seeing on the experimental farms what the average^ production of each breed has been. We'have at the farm four herds of different dairy breeds. I have been asked to add a herd of Holsteins, and I hope to be able to do that. But, at the present time, there are Ayrshires, Canadian cattle, Guernseys and Shorthorns, and we have tested them as to the quality of milk and butter, the amount of food consumed, and the cost of production All that information is given out for the benefit of the people. I have never thought it the duty of the farm, nor of myself, to undertake to discriminate between breeds, and I do not think that the people want us to. One breed may serve one man's purpose better than another, and we leave it to the judgment of each individual farmer to decide as to what breed he shall use.
The minister received quite a scolding the other day, and I think he must admit that he brought it on himself very largely

I do not admit it.
233J
Mr, SCHAFFNER. There is a good deal of money spent on these experimental farms, but I do not say there is too much. I believe there should be more. I am a little doubtful that the farmers receive the results that they should from the amount of money expended. We must make experiments, but it is very little use to make these experiments, and to spend money on them unless the knowledge that is gained reaches the people. These experimental farms have been in operation for some time, but I am afraid that the results are not reaching the people for whom they are intended. Personally, I believe that the best selection of land has not always been made in locating these experimental farms. The minister may say that he did not establish all these farms, that a number of them were established under the Tory regime. I am quite willing to admit that the Tories did not always do everything right.
_ Mr. FISHER. It does not matter; this is not a party question.

No, it is not a party question. The experimental farm at Brandon is in a very unsuitable place. It is the only experimental farm in Manitoba, and for a great many years it was the principal experimental farm in the west. I believe that experimental farms should be established in the western country on land as much like the rest of the land in the country as it is possible to get.
Hear, hear.

I am prepared to say that in the province of Manitoba there is not ten per cent of land similar to that on which the experimental farm at ,Bran-don has been placed. It is down on the banks of the river, well protected, and on heavy soil when, if they had gone back a mile on the hill, they would have found land for experimental purposes similar to 80 or 90 per cent of the land to be found in the country. I went through the reports of the different experimental farms the other day, and I found two or three of the main experiments that should be made not touched at all. I found out that different kinds of experiments are being carried on with respect to grades of wheat and different kinds of grain and seeds, but nowhere did I find experiments as to shallow or deep ploughing, the best time to plough, and especially as to the operation of packing the soil. I did not find packing the soil mentioned in the whole of the experimental farm reports. The farmers are visiting each other's farms and conversing at their meetings trying to find out whether it is profitable to undertake this form of cultivation. The machine they use for packing is very expensive and this is information which

should be placed in their possession. Yet, we have had no experiments as to tlie proper time to pack the ground, whether it should be packed in the fall after ploughing, whether it should be packed in spring after ploughing, or whether it is best to pack at all, or whether they should only make use of the harrow. I believe that the minister has in his mind now, something that I think will be of very great advantage. That is the establishment of small experimental stations.
I stated it the other day.

I was not here, although I believe the minister did state it. That is something the farmers are going to get very great advantage from. Southern Manitoba is one of the very important farming districts of the west, and there could be no better place to establish one of these stations than in the constituency of Souris. There should be some means taken, whether it should be done by the local government, by the railways, or how, I do not know, to get the farmers to visit these experimental farms. I do not think that enough has been done to disseminate the knowledge gained there. It seems a most difficult thing to get farmers to read the reports that are sent out. I am sure the minister will recognize that fact. It is the same in everything else. What you see gives a far greater and more lasting impression than anything you read, and we should establish these experimental stations. not too large, or too expensive, as thickly as possible, and we should try to adopt some further means of getting the knowledge gained at these farms disseminated amongst the people. I am a great believer in experimental farms, but I think that up to the present time the experiments have hardly been as practical as they might be.

I take the friendly advice of my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) in the spirit in which it is given. I may say that I have already announced in the House that I have embarked on the establishment of smaller experimental stations just as he recommended. At Lacombe, a quarter of a section has been bought, and it is not my intention to add to that.
A quarter of a section is not quite large enough. I do not think any farmer in the west would consider 160 acres of land sufficient to make these experiments.

The comparisons can be made in fields of three or four or five acres just the same as if they were made in fields of twenty acres each, and the farmer who comes to visit these stations can more easily study the results in the small fields than if he had to walk over the Mr. SCHAFFNER.
prairie. He can compare the experiments much easier and with much greater convenience if the fields are small. The hon. member from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) said that the price of the land purchased was high, but I find wherever in the west I have to get land suitable for experimental stations that the price is very high. These experimental stations have to be near a railway station so as to be easily accessible to visitors, and the land has to be suitable. Their value would be greatly curtailed if they were situated in some out of the way corner, and to get land with all the necessary requirements I have to pay a high price for it. I think the money would be better spent in buying a small area in a suitable and accessible place than in buying a larger quantity of land in an out of the way place where the land might be obtained at a less price.
What does the minister call a high price for land there?
$50 an acre.
Oh my, no.

I think $50 an acre is a good price for land, but I must admit that I have had $200 an acre asked me. At $50 an acre a quarter-section costs $8,000 and if I have to establish experimental stations all over the country it would come to quite a nice sum of money. My hon. friend will remember that sometimes we are criticised for extravagance. I am trying to do things effectively and still not spend too much money.
You expect to pay the market price?
Yes.
$50 an acre is about as good as you can do in Manitoba for good land?

Apparently, and sometimes I cannot get land for that situated near a railway station. Now, I think my hon. friend is mistaken in saying that he cannot find in the experimental farm reports the results of experiments in deep and shallow ploughing. We have been carrying on experiments of that kind for years, and if he carefully examine the reports he will find frequent references to it. Then, as to the experiments in packing the soil I may say that we have had a packer at work on the Brandon farm for three years.
I can find nothing in the report as to what is the best time for packing.

In the report on the Lacombe farm there is a reference to that very thing. I may say that we do not like to present a report on the very first trial

of a thing; we prefer to try it out sufficiently to be able to give a reasoned report on it. Frequently work has been, done on the experimental farms for a series of years before any definite report is made as to results. One of the most important things in connection with the experimental farm system is that we should not lead the farmers astray, and it is a wise precaution to be sure rather than to give ill-judged and hasty reports which afterwards may have to be modified. I am very proud of the fact that Dr. Saunders has always been very careful indeed to see that the recommendations he makes are founded on experience sufficiently long to justify them.

I take issue with the minister when he says that 160 acres is sufficient for an experimental farm. Then again, as to the cost of the land, if the minister would not spread the fact all over the country that he is to establish an experimental farm at a certain place, before the purchase is made, he would be more likely to get the land at a cheaper price. It was advertised all over the country that the experimental farm was to be established at Lacombe, and when he proceeded to purchase the land naturally everybody in the district wanted a high price. However, the farm need not have been established at Lacombe as there are other points with equal facilities for an experimental farm. Now, I am not criticising the price paid
Since we bought that farm the land adjoining has been sold at a considerably higher price, and if the farm were to be sold to-day I have no doubt we could get almost double what we paid for it.

There is probably no question about that. I persist however, in my view that 160 acres is not sufficient land on which to carry on an experimental farm. You have to put buildings on the 160 acres which will, cost just about as much as buildings which would be suitable for an entire section, and to that extent the money is wasted. The minister shakes his head, but I want to tell him that the best way to utilize these experimental farms to advantage is to supply the farmers with the best quality of seed, and, in order to do that he would need a considerably larger area of land. If instead of 160 acres he had a section or two sections, he would find the buildings he has there quite ample. One of the best purposes served by the experimental farms established throughout the west is the production and distribution of the best quality of seed. The great difficulty in that western country is that the farms are becoming polluted with weeds, and if the experimental farms were devoted to the production of clean seed, it
would in my opinion be of more benefit to that country than anything else that it could do. You cannot produce much seed on 150 acres, therefore I claim that that is not sufficient land for an experimental farm.

It is not often that I differ with my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), but I certainly differ with him when he says that his constituency affords a most ideal site in Manitoba for an experimental farm. That is by. no means the case, but Dauphin affords the ideal location. It comprises onc-third of the whole province of Manitoba, and is situated more advantageously than any other constituency in the province. It is a delta between the lakes in the north, the Riding mountains in the south, and the-Porcupine and Duck mountains in the west, and its possibilities are very much greater than those of any other part of Manitoba. A few moments ago the hon. minister said that he was doing the best he could with the money at his disposal. That is the great complaint of the representatives of the agricultural communities, that he has so litttle money at his disposal. The farmers are the greatest wealth producers of this country. Last year they produced over $500,000,000 by the sweat of their brows and the labour of their hands, for the benefit of Canada, and the minister has a paltry sum of less than one million dollars with which to experiment with for their benefit, and he sits quietly by and allows the Minister of War to snatch from the treasury of this country, for his gold-bedizoned officials, about $7,000,000 a year. Of what use are the militia of this country to the farmers? They would starve if it were not for what the farmers produce, and the Minister of Agriculture forgets his duties to the people when he allows what I would almost call a steal from him by another minister. I take it that the Minister of Agriculture is conducting experiments in all the various branches of agriculture. I have looked somewhat carefully into some of the experiments under his charge. He is making one experiment which, if it is a success will be of the greatest benefit, not only to Canada, but to the world. I see that at the experimental farm he has 18 horses of which 13 are geldings. If he ever gets these geldings to breed, he will confer the greatest benefit not only on Canada, but on the world. The minister said, in answer to my hon. friend from Souris, that $50 an acre was a great deal too much to pay for land for experimental stations. That would amount, roughly speaking, to $8,000 per quarter section. I

want to point out to him that if he had the $112,000 that was spent for the purpose of building eight cottages for some pot boys and understrappers for the officers at Kingston, and diverted it to the use of hi3 department, he would have been able to establish 14 experimental stations even at that price. While we on this side of the House, perhaps, do not take exception to the little that the Minister of Agriculture does, we do take exception to the great deal that he does not do for the farmers of this country.

The minister mentioned the other day that a site had been selected for a new experimental farm in northern Saskatchewan. Will he tell us exactly where that site is, and any other particulars of interest to the public?
I had reference to a site near a station called Scott, on the Grand Trunk Pacific line between Saskatoon an I Edmonton.
Any relation to Walter Scott?

Not that I know of. Scott station is about 120 miles west of Saskatoon. There is a small cluster of houses around the station, but a great many settlers have gone into the district. I was able to secure 220 or 222 acres there at what appeared to be a low rate, $13 an acre. I have a report that the land is of very good average quality all over. There is not an obstruction or a tree upon it. It is bounded on the north by the railway fence, and the eastern boundary of it is within a quarter of a mile from the station.
Can you tell the section number?
I could not offhand.
How many acres are there in the experimental farms at Indian. Head and Brandon?
There are nearly 700 acres at Indian Head, and about the same at Brandon, somewhere between 600 and 700 acres.

I claim that the minister has again made a great mistake, and that he has not sufficient land there to establish the kind of farm that I, as a farmer, think should be established. He will have to equip that land with the necessary buildings to carry on a certain line of farming, and he might just as well have got two sections of land for the purpose that is most beneficial to the farmers of the west, the production and distribution of the best quality of seed.

Might I ask the minister as to the matter of an experimental farm down in what is known as the dry belt. There are a great many settlers going into what is known as the dry belt, and I understand that representations have been made to the government for some experimental station there. Some years ago, I think the minister said that if he were granted a certain piece of land, he would pay for it a reasonable price, in order to test what he called a system of dry farming, the same as they have it in the United States. Has the minister taken any steps to establish a farm such as that?
We established a farm at Lethbridge for that purpose.
Oh, that is different. That is in the fall wheat district.

It may be, but that district is dry. The hon. member knows that the southern part of Alberta is dry. We have at Lethbridge an establishment ofi about 400 acres, which the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company were good enough to present the government with.
Why not have one at Zealandia?
Where?

I am surprised that the minister does not know where Zealandia is. He knows where the Scott township is. Zealandia is a place southwest, of Saskatoon between Saskatoon and Calgary, in the triangle between Saskatoon, Calgary and Moosejaw.
No, we have not any farm there. We have had representations that a farm should be placed south of that, and I have also had representations from other places in the neighbourhood.

Has the minister made any provision for establishing an experimental station in the Macleod district? I am sure there is a splendid opportunity there to help the farmers, of that locality, between Macleod and Calgary.
Lethbridge is only 40 miles from Macleod.
Well, it is in a semi-arid belt, you might say. It is not truly an experimental farm in a dry belt; at least I would not consider it so.
Why not?
Because the water distributed through the locality has a tendency to moisten the whole country.
No, no.

Well, I think that is the experience of the men who are in the busi-

ness. It extends for a considerable distance from the irrigation ditches, so 1 would not claim that Lethbridge is really a dry station. There should be one between Calgary and Macleod, or even at Pincher creek, if you can go so far.

Speaking of experimental farms, I should just like to say that we have a large district lying along Lake Winnipeg. About 2,000 settlers, including Ruthenians, Polanders and Germans have been placed there by the present government, and they find it impossible to make a living on these lands. It has been suggested that the government should establish an experimental farm in that district to instruct those people how to utilize their lands, and I think an experimental station could be established without any great expense. My own opinion is that these people should never have been settled there at all. I do not believe the land is fit for settlement, as it is poor and covered by water half the time. The local government of Manitoba is doing their best to drain it, but even when it is drained, I do not believe it will be of much use. This government had a grand opportunity when they had the lands of the St. Peter's reserve that I was speakng of a few nights ago. There you had 48,000 acres of the best land in the province, a part of which the hon. Minister of Agriculture could have taken for the purposes of an experimental farm. Then the government could have removed the settlers I refer to, and brought them into the neighbourhood of Selkirk and placed them on good lands. It would not have been necessary to have given the lands away, for these men would be prepared to pay reasonable prices, probably three times as much as they were sold for. They are just as fine a class of settlers as are to be found in Manitoba, but the men are forced to leave their places and their families in the summer time go into the cities to seek employment. Something should be done by the government to give these people good homesteads, or they should be placed in a position which would make them independent of the government or of anybody else. Two years ago it was necessary for the government to send out some assistance in the shape of flour, bacon and so on to these people, but they do not want charity; they are too proud for that sort of thing. I would urge upon the government and upon the Minister of Agriculture the advisability of seeing whether they could do something to help these people to get good lands.

Last session when this same question was up, the attention of the minister was called to the needs of an experimental station in the southern part of
British Columbia, particularly in the district of Kootenay. We have there a semiarid or dry belt where irrigation would be of great advantage. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Pacific railway and some private corporations have put in irrigation works along the line towards Fort Steele. Last session the minister said he had the matter under consideration, and I merely want to ask him whether anything has been provided in the estimates for any experimental station in that portion of British Columbia?
I am very glad to find that experimental farm stations are so popular.
Hear, hear.

Everybody wants one in his, own immediate neighbourhood. It is the best possible tribute to the efliciency of that kind of work. I may say to my hon. friend from British Columbia (Mr. Goo'deve) that I had an oflicer of my department examining different places in the Kootenay and Okanagan countries last summer, and am trying to arrange for the establishment of, I hope, more than one station in what is called the semi-dry belt of British Columbia. I do not desire to say more on the subject at present.
The minister asks about $98,000 in this vote. Can he state _ to the House how many experimental stations he purposes establishing?

I could not say positively. I hope that every now and then I shall be able to decide upon a location, and as soon as I do I will take the necessary steps to establish a station. I have every hope that I shall be able to establish several within the coming fiscal year.
It is very nice for all of us to hear an answer from the minister to my hon. friend from Kootenay, but I have not heard any answer to my suggestion with regard to Dauphin.

My hon. friend (Mr, Campbell) and his hon. friend the member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) were so at variance that I hesitated to decide. I would like to have an opportunity to consider what was said by both of these hon. gentlemen.
Does the minister intend to make any improvements in the poultry department of the experimental farm at Ottawa?

The poultry establishment here has been doing good experimental work along various lines. I do not consider, for my part, that the old poultry house is of the kind that is the best for the keeping of poultry in this part

of Canada; I think the experiments have shown pretty clearly that it is not. I am not yet ready to make a start in building a new poultry establishment there. Some additional buildings have been put up, of a much cheaper character, but fully as successful as the more expensive buildings. Everything in the poultry experiments seems to prove that there is no need for expensive buildings. We are trying experiments also as to the performance of individual hens; which seems ridiculous, perhaps, but it is believed that by selecting the individual bird and their eggs and breeding from these, you may establish an improved breed-not a changed breed, but an improved breed. We wish to carry out these experiments and amplify them as much" as possible.
Does the minister consider that the results attained at these experimental farms warrant the amount of money spent on the farm each year?

I am in the judgment of those who are fit to judge in these matters, of course. The poultry industry is a very great one, and I would not like to curtail the work done. But I may say that what is done at the Central Experimental Farm is only a portion of the work of the officers in the poultry department. Both Mr.. Gilbert and Mr. Fortier have spent most of their time in attending poultry meetings and farm institutes and giving instructions with regard to poultry. It is very valuable work, and there is great demand for the presence of these gentlemen in all parts of the country.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

It has occurred to me that there would be a certain amount of overlapping in the work of the different experimental farms throughout the country. We have the farm at Guelph controlled by the government of Ontario, and the experimental farm at Macdonald College in Quebec. I would think that these farms would be able to cover the ground in such a way as to serve all the purposes of the farmers, for whose benefit experimental farms are conducted. They would assist them in raising the best farm products of all kinds. I cannot see that the experimental station in Ottawa is the success it should be. I am chiefly interested in the poultry department. I am a farmer and I think that to be of real service to the farmers of the country better work should be done in that department than is done. I do not think it is encouraging to say to a farmer that the yearly average of a pen of fowl would be from

[DOT]
80 to 100 eggs. That would hardly pay the board of a chicken for a year, and I think the experimental farm is capable of turning out better results than are apparent. As the buildings have been there for 25 years and are out of date, it might be wise to do away with the department here and allow the (provincial institutions to carry on this work. The professors from the other colleges lecture throughout the country and Professor Gilbert of the Central Experimental Farm also lectures. They often meet at gatherings of poultry men and I think that either could give the necessary information at these meetings. If you abolished the poultry department here there would be a saving of $6,000 or $7,000 a year which would be an item worth considering. My idea would be that the Dominion Experimental Farm here should be the principal farm, while the provincial farms should be what you would call substations. There is some work that could be done at the institution here that is not being done by any of these institutions. The poultry industry is very important, and if properly developed would take a foremost place in our agriculture. For the year 1908 the value of the poultry and eggs produced in the United States amounted to something over $625,000,000. Taking the population of the United States and of Canada as a 'basis, our poultry industry here should amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000 to $70,000,000 a year. I believe it has been estimated at $25,000,000, but I do not think we have any statistics in Canada to prove that. There is no doubt that the demand is much greater than the supply to-day, and our people look to the farmers to meet that demand. The farmers are not paying sufficient attention to the poultry industry, and I 'believe if the proper means were used to show them what there really is in the business they would take it up to a greater extent than they have done. We should have at the Ottawa station a scientific man who would study the diseases of poultry, making a thorough investigation into all the different diseases. Little is known of these diseases either in this country or in the United States. In the last few years men have been engaged in that work in the United States and they have found out a good deal, but still they seem to be to a certain extent groping in the dark. If the minister abandoned some of the work that is now being done in the poultry department and devoted the money thus saved to the employment of an expert of diseases of poultry, he would he doing more for the industry than is now being done.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman that the work of the Experimental Farm could be improved

in the way he suggests. His idea is that the branch experimental farms might be dispensed with. I would suggest that what is required is more distribution, decentralization rather than the establishment of central stations. The Experimental Farm here is doing an excellent work, but the farmers throughout the country generally are not in a position to reap the advantages that are accruing because of the fact that the information which is obtained at that farm cannot be sufficiently demonstrated. Whilst the farms are doing good work and the institute lecturers do a great deal in the way of education, the people do not receive the same practical results from the operations of experimental farms as they should. Branch farms should be established all over the country. To explain my position I might quote from the speech of the hon. Minister of Agriculture on Friday. He said:
To instruct and teach the people, object lessons are of the primest importance. If those who live in a particular district can go to an easily accessible central point and there see illustrated the result of good management of the crops and of scientific treatment of tho soil, they can Jearn more than they can by any amount of reading and oral instruction.
The idea I wish to convey is that whilst the Experimental Farm is doing very good work, yet there are other branches of farming besides the cultivation of the soil, and the raising of dairy cows and beef. It is not being done, I contend, in the best way:	My contention is that the
best method would be to have local farms throughout the country. The minister on Friday last referred to the disease known as the Pictou cattle disease. He explained that an experimental station had been established at Antigonish to ascertain the cause of that disease, and he said it had been demonstrated by these experiments that the cause of the disease was a weed called ragwort. The work that was done there was certainly of importance, and I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Agriculture on having in his department men who are capable of conducting such experiments as those at Antigonish in the satisfactory manner in which they were conducted. I refer particularly to the veterinary director, Dr. Rutherford, who had charge of these experiments. He displayed that intelligence and executive ability which would be expected from him by all who know him and his position and standing in his profession. It is not detracting from him if I say that too much credit cannot be also given to Dr. W. H. Pethick, who was immediately in charge and those associated with him. What they accomplished in demonstrating the cause -of that disease, which had baffled the best skill of the continent for many years, is a great tribute to the men in charge of that work. What they have accomplished is the best tribute that could be .paid to the work that was done there. It was shown that the Pictou cattle disease was caused by a weed known as the ragwort.
We will come to another vote in connection with that, and perhaps-it would be better for my hon. friend to defer his remarks until then.

I was just leading up to the question of experimental farms. I am going to ask that an experimental farm be established in my part of the country, and I am trying to lead up to the reason why I shall make that request. The Minister of Agriculture stated the other day that sheep would destroy that weed known as the ragwort, and he intimated that he had been encouraging the farmers by assisting them in the way of improving their breeds of sheep, pointing out that in that way a profitable industry might be established, and in addition to that this pest of the ragwort could be gotten rid of. There is no question that sheep will destroy the ragwort, and the farmers of the weed infected district should feel a sense of gratitude towards the minister and Department of Agriculture for what they have done in that respect. I am quite sure that-I am speaking for them in stating that they appreciate all the good work that has been done. They appreciate the fact that the minister has sent, as he stated in his speech, and as is stated in the report of the Department of Agriculture, a number of pure bred rams into that infected district which, after being pastured in the summer, were sold to the farmers. It is all very well to say that the sheep industry is a profitable industry, but the thing is to demonstrate to the farmer that it is a profitable industry. What I am going to put forward is the fact that one of the things that we require in Nova Scotia is a sheep farm. The government have done a great deal for agriculture generally. Beef and dairy cattle have been improved gradually. There has been a great deal of information disseminated with regard to other stock, but in so far as the poor little lamb is concerned he is obliged to bleat just as of yore. The contrast that exists between the condition of the farmers to-day, and that of twenty-five years ago is striking. You will find better cattle, the cattle better .looked after, and a greater degree of prosperity. That is due, to a large extent, to lectures at the farmers' institutes, it is due also, to a considerable extent, to the work of the agricultural societies, but more than all it is due to the fact that when one farmer starts out on a certain line his neighbours

are bound to copy him. The farmer goes to the experimental station, he sees how things are done, how the stock is looked after, how it is housed and fed, and he, unconsciously, if you like, copies to a certain extent and good results follow. The Department of Agriculture has done a great deal in a way to inform the people, through literature and speakers, as to how to raise sheep, but there has been no practical demonstration given. They are no farther advanced than they were twenty-five years ago as far as sheep are concerned. Nova Scotia and -the maritime provinces offer one of the best fields in Canada and perhaps in the world for the raising of sheep. I venture to say that the highlands of Scotland cannot surpass the maritime provinces. Nova Scotia is in a position to rise sheep with profit, and to make sheep' husbandry an industry that will be of immense advantage to the country as a whole. The climatic conditions are favourable. As the minister pointed out in his address, and as was pointed out by Mr. Spencer, who has written an article on sheep husbandry, to which the minister referred, there are a million acres of suitable pasture land there. It has a well adapted climate, and with its short nutritious native grass interspersed with, white clover, Nova Scotia is particularly adapted to sheep raising. There is a large proportion of this area of one million acres which is not suitable for the feeding of dairy or beef cattle. The bleak, exposed hills can be utilized for sheep raising. This is a type of land not suitable' for ordinary cattle, but the conditions in so far as climate and soil are concerned are particularly favourable to the sheep industry. A great deal has been done for fruit culture. I think there have been about thirty-two model orchards established for the purpose of showing fanners who go in for fruit the best manner of prosecuting that industry, and how the best fruit can be produced. We have an experimental farm at Nappan which is more devoted to beef and dairy cattle, and we - have also an experimental farm at Truro, but there has been no practical demonstration of what can be done with sheep. The report of Mr. Spencer, and the report of the Minister of Agriculture, both bear me out in saying that sheep raising should be a most profitable industry in Nova Scotia. What do we find? We find that instead of that industry being in a prosperous state it is retrograding. We find that there are fewer sheep to-day in Nova Scotia than there were twenty-five, thirty or forty years ago. I have the figures of the number of sheep in Nova Scotia for a number of years., taken from the year-book, and they are as follows:

You will observe a gradual decrease in the number of sheep where there should have been a large increase, because of the fact that Nova Scotia is particularly adapted to sheep raising, and because in the last few years the prices of lamb, mutton and wool have been favourable. As a matter of fact, there are only 5-86 sheep per farm in Nova Scotia at the present time. It may be said that Nova Scotia is not an agricultural ' province. Let me deny that fact. Let me say too that in Nova Scotia the value of farm products, in the last year, increased over the previous year by upwards of $3,000,000, which shows that farming is not retrograding. I had occasion, Mr. Chairman, to interview the Minister of Agriculture with Tespect to the establishment of a sheep farm in Nova Scotia, and I suggested that it should be established in the county of Antigonish or within the region of the ragwort infected district. It would only be natural to ask that, because of the fact, in the first place, that experiments were conducted there to show the cause of the Picto-u cattle disease for which the government have paid a lot of money in the years gone by, and because of the fact that it was demonstrated that sheep would destroy the ragwort. It is only natural to suppose that in that locality sheep farms might be established. I have no doubt that it would be a profitable business from that start, and that it would be of incalculable benefit to the people of Nova Scotia. In his address on Friday last, the Minister of Agriculture referred to what had been done with respect to the experiments in the county of Antigonish, and he was about to conclude a sentence with, as I had hoped, an assurance that this experimental farm would be established in our province. He went on to speak about what had been done witn respect to the ragwort. He said:
We immediately set to work to try experiments with sheep on a farm in the neighbourhood of Antigonish, and we showed clearly in the course of three seasons that the pasturing of sheep on a piece of land infested with that weed, would destroy it and absolutely clean the land of it within a few years. The result is that to-day we have been able

Unfortunately, he was interrupted. I was in hopes that he would have completed the sentence by saying that:	We will
follow up, and finish the work we have begun, and establish a sheep farm in Antigonish. I had hopes that he would carry out the resolution which was passed by the

farmers' convention of Nova Scotia, held on the 23rd February, at New Glasgow, and which was as follows:
We, the committee appointed to consider the promotion of the sheep-raising industry of Nova Scotia, beg to report and recommend as follows:-	_
With regard to the promotion of the sheep industry, we recommend that, whereas the ragwort and other noxious weeds are alarmingly spreading in the eastern part of Nova Scotia- and Cape Breton, and it has been demonstrated, by experiments, made by the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion of Canada, that the ragwort has been the cause of the cattle disease of Pictou county, and that sheep offer the most effective and practical means of eradicating this noxious weed, at the same time thriving thereon, and whereas we believe sheep to be among the most profitable stock on a farm, and regarding, with apprehension, the diminution of the sheep-raising industry. in this province, and believing that the eastern part of Nova Scotia, as a whole, to be best adapted to sheep-raising, and being the area, at present, as most infected with ragwort, therefore we, the Farmers' Association, in session at New Glasgow, recommend that the Dominion government, having already done considerable work along the line of investigating the noxious weed question, be memorialized through our federal representatives, requesting that board to establish an experimental sheep station somewhere in eastern Nova Scotia, with a view to stimulating the sheep-raising industry.
The Minister of Agriculture received the representations made by me to him and to the officers of his department on this subject, but pointed out some difficulties in the way of establishing a sheep farm. These difficulties to my mind were the reasons why I expected and hoped the farm would be established. One thing the Minister of Agriculture cannot be accused of cowardice, and I felt that he would grapple with the situation, because of the difficulties that confronted him and that he would be in a position to assure the House when he brought down his estimates, that an experimental system would be established for the purpose of demonstrating to the farmers of Nova Scotia how sheep should be looked after, that that province was specially adapted to sheep raising, and for the purpose of encouraging them to engage in that- branch of farming with profit to themselves and to the country at large.

I desire to add a word or two in corroboration of the views of my hon. friend from Antigonish. I might be permitted to point out that while we have an experimental farm on the border between the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, it is situated in the vicinity of the marshland country which surrounds the Bay of Fundy in those two provinces, the fertility and productiveness of which, as the minister well! knows, are possibly unequalled in the Dominion of Canada. Therefore in the conditions as they exist that farm is not of so much value to other portions of the maritime provinces which are not as favourably situated. In the eastern part of Nova Scotia, beginning with Pictou and extending to Cape North in the island of Cape Breton, there exists a condition somewhat similar to what is found in the old country, where upland farming has been carried on with a great degree of success. When we consider that for over a hundred years these upland farms have been compelled to furnish the products necessary to meet the industrial conditions of that portion of the province, we shall realize at once that their power of reproduction has to a great extent become impaired. The desire of the people to turn their attention in some other direction is but a natural consequence of the Conditions that exist, and I think the energy of the minister might be very well directed towards the encouragement of sheep culture in that portion of the province. I am aware that he has looked to some extent into this question, and I trust that it will be speedily dealt with by him. When we realize that on the hills and in the valleys of eastern Nova Scotia, the conditions are such as hardly exist anywhere else in the Dominion, and are especially suited to the sheep industry, we shall at once become impressed with the idea that it is a matter with which the government should deal. The proposition to inaugurate experimental farms for sheep raising in that portion of the province does not involve an expenditure on the part of the government from which there would be no return. On almost all the other experimental farms the government spends a great deal more money than it gets back. The returns from the crops do not at all compensate for the experiments made in the various branches of agriculture. But, I am assured by those who have looked into this question that there is no reason why two or three sheep farms established in the eastern part of Nova Scotia should not yield returns great enough to meet or almost meet the expenditure in establishing them and carrying them on. While I do not begrudge our friends in the West anything that will develop the agricultural possibilities of their great country, while they are asking for experimental farms in the dry belt, the grain belt and every other kind of belt, and while the minister has been generous in meeting these requests, I would ask him to lend an ear to the request which we from the province of Nova Scotia are making, which will result not only in great benefit to the people interested, but in a return to the department that will almost, if not altogether compensate it for the expenditure involved.

Might I suggest that the minister allow this item for experimental farms to stand over? The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has something to say on this question, and he is not here to-night. We shall have to ask that some one of these items stand over, and I think it will facilitate matters to let this item stand and take up the non-contentious ones.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I cannot forbear the pleasure of making a few remarks on the subject which is now before the House. The hon. gentleman from East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) complained a moment #go of the manner in' wdiich the piggery is kept at the experimental farm. I may state to the hon. gentleman that to a certain extent I agree with him on that point; not that I would blame the department of the Minister of Agriculture on that account, but merely to call the latter's attention to the state of things in that connection, and request him, after improving, as he has done, all other departments of the farm, to take up in the near future the improvement of the piggery and deal with it in the same way.
I generally visit the experimental farm at least twice a year, partly through curiosity, and largely on account of the profit to be derived therefrom. The horse stables are very well kept; the horses are very well housed, in quarters which are kept clean and are up-to-date, as they say in English. The cow stable is such as none better could be desired. The cows are kept exceptionally clean, the herd is made up of fine animals, of superb appearance. In short, nothing better than this stable could be desired.
Now, on the day before yesterday, I visited the piggery. I saw there Yorkshires, Berkshires, White Chesters and Tamworths, the latter with a hide red almost beyond imagination. These are very fine animals, of excellent breeds. The only thing to do, in my' humble opinion, and in this I agree with the hon. member for East Peterborough, is to improve the buildings, which are not quite such as they should be. As for the stock, nothing better could be desired. However, if I was correctly informed by the men as late as the day before yesterday, it is the intention to rebuild part of the piggery. That is necessary, indeed, and I hope that the minister will include in the estimates the required vote.
The wrny things are managed a,t the experimental farm cannot be praised too hivhly. Those who, like myself, take an interest in agriculture, have observed the great strides which have been made as regards horses, cattle, sheep, poultry, and in a general way the stock kept at the experimental farm. Everything is really

fine. It is a pleasure to go around with a view to following as best one can in the footsteps of these people.
Why do we find such prosperity throughout the country, and especially among the farming classes? It is because agricultural lecturers have taught throughout the province how farmers might succeed in increasing their profits and improving everything in connection with their industry. Formerly, we used to send as we now do our apples, our poultry, our eggs, and our cheese across the ocean, but those products reached the English market in bad condition. Owing, to the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture, who started refrigeration on a large scale on board ships, those products now reach their destination in as good and fresh a condition as on the day they were shipped. To whom, I ask once more, are we indebted for this: to the minister who has charge of that great department.
Why have we considerably increased the revenue from our farms? It is because we obtained from the experimental farm- thanks to the generosity of the exchequer- specially well selected samples of grain. We sow that grain. From a small initial quantity we gradually obtain larger quantities, and in that way we soon secure crops of first rate quality.
We obtain eggs-I have myself ordered three hatchings of Brahmas-to improve the breeds which we now have. There we find Plymouth Rocks, Wyandots-, Spanish, Minorcas, Leghorns and Brahmas. We reap great benefits through the assistance of that farm, and I hope we will be in a position to profit by it more and more from year to year.
Hon. members who preceded me have made certain statements in reference J.o sheep. In my opinion, a farm without sheep is incomplete. In the case of the province of Quebec-and I pray the minister to bear this in mind-sheep breeding has gone down to a large extent. And why? Because sheep are devoured by dogs. It is to my knowledge that many farmers have given up the sheep business on account of that. Recently I came across a statute of the province of Ontario whereby municipalities are required to constitute a special fund towards compensating farmers to the extent of two-thirds of the loss sustained, whenever the owner of the dog remains unknown. That is most excellent legislation. I have drawm the attention of the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec to that enactment and suggested that he should introduce a similar Act for our province. In a single year my neighbour had fifteen sheep devoured by dogs whose owners could not be found. Once the sheep are strangled it is too late to collar the dogs. If only we know who the

owners are, we might sue them for damages, but these people are never in a hurry to admit their responsibility.
Numbers of my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec have ceased altogether beeping sheep on that account. I suggest that the minister should introduce an Act similar to that in force in Ontario. A tax or license might be exacted in the case of dovs, and the revenue obtained therefrom applied to build up a fund which would enable the municipalities to compensate farmers whose sheep have been strangled. It is admitted by all that the breeding of sheep is highly profitable, insures substantial returns, but as I said, that branch of farming should be protected.
We have learned from the Department of Agriculture how to protect ourselves against insects which prey on orchards and crops. We have learned how to plant and prune trees, hope to shape the head and look after the roots. In a great many cases farmers plant trees which die two or three years after. Why? Because they do not know how to plant them, protect them, feed the root system, shelter them against the wind. A good many even dispensed with the use of props. Well, to-day, thanks to the instructions given by the Department of Agriculture, we know how to plant trees and keep them healthy, and we are no longer obliged to replace them every three or four years.
We have learned how to look after manure and home-made fertilizers, we know the difference between a cold, a warm and a medium manure. We know how to take care of them. Many farmers were in the habit of leaving the manure in a heap all winter long next to the stable door. The best part of it was carried away in the streams, lost along fences and among the stones. To-day farmers look more closely after their own interest and know how to get the most out of farm manures. They know besides where to apply them to the best advantage and are greatly benefited thereby. How have we come to learn these things? Through the Department of Agriculture, and through its staff of lecturers. Why is the county which I have the honour to represent so rich and prosperous? It is on account of its having been looked after as it had the right to expect.
We have learned how to prepare tobacco in a special way, and the county of Montcalm is in a position to compete henceforth with the best producers in the counties of Essex and Rouville. Owing to the establishment of a government experimental station, we are now able to prepare hot beds, to put in the seed, plant the seedlings, look after the young plants, and later on cure the tobacco properly. How is it that we have succeeded from that time on in producing a first-class product? It is because we have had on the spot a Mr. Chevalier, who has been sent from the experimental farm, to teach farmers how to grow tobacco, prepare and deliver it on the markets.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture is a practical man, well acquainted with the details of farming. I remember a time when that department was presided over by a medical man, a man of parts, whom I do not wish to run down, and regarding whom I would not utter an unpleasant word; but one day that he happened to enter a farm yard, he thought fit to congratulate the owner on the fine geese that were about them. ' I beg your pardon, sir, replied ' the farmer, but they are ducks.' That minister did not know the difference between a goose and a pekin duck. The present minister can tell the difference, having spent his life on the farm as a practical farmer.
I shall not speak any longer. I wished to make these few remarks as a matter of fairness to the hon. minister and to my constitutents. I wish to impress them with the fact that their representative takes some interest in agriculture, has learned something of it, and is in a position to discuss such questions without blushing.

I wish to thank my hon. friend from Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) for the kind references he has made to my administration of the department and for his appreciation of the success of the wotk of the experimental farms. I had hoped that we would get through the agriculture items this evening so that the officers might return to the farm, but in deference to the wish of my hon. friend (Mr. Geo Taylor) who wishes the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Soroule) to be present when we are considering this item, we will pass on to some other thing in the hope that progress- will be made.
For the development of the dairying and fruit industries, and the improvement and transportation of, the sale and trade in, food and other agricultural products, $75,000.

increase here?

Towards the encouragement of the establishment of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of perishable food products, $56,250.

No.

There has been no formal application yet.
