Have the fruit inspectors superintendence of the cold storages?
No.
I would like to ask if an inspector is allowed to be connected with a factory?
Do you mean a fruit inspector?
Yes.
Certainly not.
Complaints have been made to that effect.

If any such complaint is brought to my attention I will see to it at once. The whole time of the fruit inspectors, when they are employed by the government, is given to the work of the government, and if any fruit inspector is
himself engaged in packing, it is distinctly contrary to his contract with us.
Is he allowed to be a member of the firm.?

I would not like him to be even a stockholder in a joint stock concern, but he undoubtedly should not be a member of the firm. I would not like to say off-hand that he should not be a stockholder in a joint stock company, although I think even that would be objectionable.
He would not be allowed to go out and buy apples?

Certainly not. I might say, however, that some of my inspectors are employed temporarily, not for the whole year, and when they are not employed they are at liberty to do as they like. But during their term of employment with the government they certainly cannot deal in or buy fruit.
A case has been brought to my attention where an inspector was buying apples during the fall months, while he was acting as inspector.
If I could get such information I would certainly cease to employ that man.

I would like to inquire whether the minister has given any consideration of the representations made to him from the people of Alberta as to the establishment of a cold storage system throughout the west. Mr. Palmer, I think, led the deputation when it was down here a couple of years ago, and I have had communications from him and I presume other members too, asking us to urge upon the minister to take some action along the lines suggested. It is one of the most important questions that could be considered from an agricultural standpoint. We all know the importance of the cattle trade in western Canada, and if the minister would- only take hold of this thing seriously, the cattle trade in that part of the country would increase much more than it * has done during the past few years. The hon. member for Victoria, (Mr. White) I think, had a resolution on the order paper this year, dealing with this question. Unfortunately it was left to a late period in the session, and was not brought up. I looked forward to a keen debate on that resolution, but things have been jockeyed in such a manner-
Order, order.
If the minister rises to a point of order
I do not think the hon. gentleman has a right to talk about the business of the House being jockeyed.

That is a term I find very often introduced in this House. There is jockeying done practically every day as to who should get the floor, and as to how-matters shall come up in the House. If it is not a parliamentary term I shall certainly withdraw it, if the chairman asks me to do so.
I would like to have the ruling of the chairman.

speechtext:
I can hardly say I am sufficiently acquainted with the term to rule it out of order, but if the hon. gentleman can find another term that would convey his meaning, it would relieve me.
I would not be willing to infer that it meant anything disagreeable or wrong, so far as my knowledge goes, but if the hon. gentleman can modify it, it would relieve me.

At the moment I cannot think of a word that conveys the same idea. At the same time I urn willing to submit to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and if it is not a proper word to use then I shall withdraw it, but I understand the chairman has not said that it is an improper word, and I presume it will be allowed to stay on the pages of ' Hansard.' This question of cold storage is a very important one in western Canada. It is a system that should have been adopted in this House, and I think it would have been adopted in this House if the resolution of the member for Victoria (Mr. White) had not been placed in a position on the order paper that prevented it from being discussed. For that reason the matter has remained without getting the consideration I think it is entitled to from this House. But it does not excuse the minister by any means. The minister has been aware of the situation for many years, and yet he has been content to patter along behind and has not taken -up the position that, as Minister of Agriculture, I think he should. He is too dilatory, , he hangs back. He wants to get down to bigger issues, and he forgets not only local conditions, but the conditions of this whole Dominion. We have now almost come to the close of the session, And no Action has been taken, but I hope the minister, even at this late period, will take steps to institute such a system throughout the Dominion, and build up the cattle trade and the other important industries of this country. It is most important, because while we are cultivating fruit and other cereals in the west, owing to the fact that we have a very fertile soil, the day is not far distant,
in fact it has already arrived in western Canada, when the farmers have to introduce mixed farming. However, I suppose the minister is content to let it drag along without taking action. I simply rise to call the minister's attention to the state of affairs, and I would urge him to take some action and not make it necessary for us to bring the matter to the attention of the House during the next four or five years.
I would be very glad to have a discussion on the question, and to go into it. But when a motion is on the order paper, a discussion at this stage would be out of order.

I would like to say a word in explanation to the member for Macdonald (Mr Staples) as to why the resolution was not placed earlier on the order paper. It was a resoluton that was passed by the United Farmers and Stock Growers of Alberta. Some time in February they sent a resolution to me and asked me if i would take the matter up. I immediately placed it on the order paper, though it was a little late in the season. Since that time I have written to the minister asking him if he would put in the estimates a sum of money to enable the matter to be investigated and to see whether this project was practicable or not.
I had a letter from the minister indicating .that he did not have any confidence in it, or in the promoters of this scheme. I may say with regard to the promoters, Mr. Palmer and Mr. Greenstreet, that they are two gentlemen who have had a great deal of experience along that line, I understand, with the people who control the cold storage plant in New Zealand, as well as in Cape Colony. As most of the western members will remember when they visited Ottawa last year, to see the minister, they simply asked for a guarantee of two-thirds of the amount of their bonds . I understand they, have already subscribed $500,000 of their own money and they only ask the government to guarantee the bonds. We must ship our cattle five thousand miles to market, and any one who knows anything about cattle knows that at the end of so long a journey cattle do not land in .good shape. Therefore, we are getting practically nothing for our light cattle;. Last year, light cattle sold throughout the west for from two to three cents per pound. In the spring we got a little more-up to five cents. There is Only a small percentage of western cattle . that are fit for export, and therefore command a high price. In a letter from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) that hon. gentleman states that there is not enough cattle to keep up a continuous supply. I do not know what he means by a ' continuous supply ' or how large a plant he consi-

ders necessary in order to handle the cattle business. But, according to the report sen! out by the Agriculture Department in 1908, there was some 180,000 cattle shipped to Winnipeg, some for export, and some for local consumption. The condition in the west is simply this: In Alberta, there is a great deal of waste land, for that province is not all wheat land like Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We have a lot of hay land, and other land not fit for farming. Therefore, the cattle industry is important to the people of Alberta as is wheat or any other grain. But, unless we have something like this proposition of Mr. Palmer to handle our light beef, we must go out of the cattle businesss. Last year, some
4,000	cows-breeding stock-were shipped out of the Victoria district along. The farmers are going out of the business because they find it not profitable to carry it on.
Where were they sent to?

Some were sent here to the east, but many were disposed of in the west. A considerable quantity of this cow beef went to the railway camps of the Canadian Pacific, Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern. Ten or fifteen years ago, when there was more vacant land' and the cattle were allowed to roam, beef could be raised a great deal more cheaply than at present. At one time, we could grow beef profitably for three cents per pound. To-day, we have to pay as high as $10 to $20 an acre for land for grazing our cattle. Therefore, we must have a higher average price for our beef, and until we have some way of handling the lighter beef, shipping it out chilled" or something of that kind, it will be impossible to continue the business. Of course, the export business will go on as usual, but this project would give us a market for our small and light beef. I wish to be clear on this matter. Some hon. members may have thought, as the hon member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples,) did, that I was not very anxious to bring this matter forward.
I believe you were.

I have been in the cattle business for many years, and have been forced out of the business for the reasons I have stated here that there is no way to handle the smaller or lighter cattle. To show the importance of this matter, T may state that the resolution to which I have reference was passed by every branch of the united farmers of Alberta, as well as by the stock growers. This bodv has over 5,000 members, and in their letter to me they claim that they represent nearly half a million head of cattle. So, I think the matter is important enough for the minister to consider it seriously, and Mr. W. H. WHITE.
to spend a reasonable amount of money to try and get this business established.

The situation of the cattle business in the west has been well explained by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. W. H. White). The whole province of Alberta was a cattle country a few years ago, but it is falling off so rapidly that, if it continues, in a short time we should have to import beef for our own consumption. We believe there is no salvation for that western country from a state of depression in the live stock trade except through the suggestion that has been made-that the government should take up the establishment of cold storage for the purpose of chilling beef for the export trade. It has already been explained that because of the distance of the British market our beef will not land there in proper condition to kill. Still, we are in a more favourable position than the countries that supply the bulk of the meat, including pork, beef and mutton; to the British market. The meat that goes from New Zealand and Australia must be frozen, making it worth only half as much as fresh meat. On the other hand, I understand the chilled meat is worth practically as much as fresh. If we had means to chill our beef it would enable us to land it in England in a condition to command a good price. There is no way by which our farmers can continue much longer in the business in which they have been engaged except by affording them a substantial market. The ordinary farmer of our portion of the country-the same condition exists all over the province-brings his hogs to market generally in the fall of the year, and as soon as the full supply comes in, the market being onlv local, the price drops even below the cost of production. And almost the same is true of beef. We cannot ship it profitably in the live state, and we have no means of shipping it in any other form. There can be no profit in the business unless the _ country will advance the money to establish such a system as has been proposed. I think the idea is worthy of the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and the government. I admit that it will cost a good deal of jnoney-a great deal more, I think, than the minister is prepared to expend at the present time. I think it might go to several millions. If they were to guarantee the bonds as has been suggested to two-thirds of the amount required-and as, my hon. friend suggests it would be only for the time being as the business would pay for itself-it would undoubtedly be a great benefit to the western country, because we have there the conditions under which beef and pork can be produced cheaper than in any other part of Canada. We have the climate, and a great deal of open land where beef and hogs

can be produced cheaply. These things all go towards producing a meat product cheap. This is a very serious matter, and I think the .minister should undertake a large scheme of that kind, not go into it in the little pleasant way we are doing from year to year, contributing towards some private enterprise some few dollars after a plant has been constructed and in operation. The government should take that matter up, and I do not think the minister should wait until these conditions arise. He and his officers should ascertain what is needed for the agricultural industry of the country and he should have his share out of the treasury to advance the interests of agriculture. We .spend money on every other department and what is left is what the minister gets. The minister, with his officers, should make an esti-' mate of what is required, and as agriculture is the leading industry of the country, it should come first in the estimates. Instead of spending $400,000 or' $500,000 or $900,000 as we are doing to-day, we should not be afraid to spend as many millions if necessary to advance the general interests of this industry, because when agriculture is down in Canada every other industry is down. It is the first and leading industry, it is the backbone of the country, and no industry is prosperous when the farmers are not prosperous. It should come in for first consideration from the minister.

The problem as put forward in several representations that have been made to me was so large and so doubtful of success that I confess I could not see my way to take it up seriously. It is, however, a very big and important question, and I shall certainly take pains to make inquiry and what investigations we can through the officers of the department in regard to it.

It is true that a resolution is on the order paper dealing with the same topic, and that to some extent would rule out the present discussion, but in view of the fact that it is impossible to take that up this session, and that the undertaking contemplated in the question is so transcendently important, it seems to me the discussion should proceed further, at all events until we get some more explicit statement of policy from the Minister of Agriculture. I need not emphasize, nor could I if I wished, the importance of the proposed undertaking of establishing a chilled meat industry more than has been done by the speakers who have preceded me. I would only refer to this fact, that while the exportation of cattle and the facility of that exportation, are topics which it is supposed more directly concern cattlemen and rangers throughout western Canada, none the less they have to do in just as important a manner with the general 234
farming industry of the whole of Canada, In Manitoba the cattle industry is marching very rapidly to extinction. Where they had ten cattle ten years ago, they have one to-day. The cattle are going out of existence. Why? Simply because it has been impossible under existing transport conditions to make them pay. The result of that, as the Minister of Agriculture, being such a practical farmer, well knows, is that the land values and the land production are affected in much the same degree. It is impossible even in a grain country to keep up the average production of grain without having cattle on the land. As a result, even in our province which is practically a grain province, the amount of * land given to summer fallow has to be increased each year because there are no cattle there to keep up the fertility of the soil. The same thing will take place throughout the west. It becomes more and more important the farther west one goes. As the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) has well pointed out, the cattle industry in Alberta and Saskatchewan, Alberta particularly, is just as important as and should be more important than the grain industry. I understand that the proposal put to the government very fully and explicitly was along the lines of the formation of a chilled meat exportation company, operating on the same principle as the Pullman Company with a capitalization of $2,000,000, of which the promoters subscribe in cash $500,000, the balance to be guaranteed by the government in the form of four per cent debentures. I, of course, will not say that the proposal as put to the government should have been accepted, but I will say that it presents some very good features, features that should have prevented it from being stigmatized by the minister as unworthy of consideration. I may be wrong in my details, but from what I have read, the company put up $500,000, the remainder to be guaranteed by the government, and the guarantee to be secured by a first mortgage on all the assets of the company. That would give a margin of 25 per cent against loss on the guarantee, and at the same time, by a proper system of supervision, the government could see that all the money produced by the guarantee was expended on plant and works, and consequently that there would be assets to answer for every dollar of guarantee. Consequently it bears on its face the aspect of bona fides, there seems to be no juggling about it. The first loss would fall on the promoters. I know nothing as to Mr. Palmer; the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) appears to know something of his history and his success, but at all events if the government are not disposed to accept the proposition that has been put down, they should either r-8



undertake this work as a government undertaking or invite propositions of a different character. The minister, I understand, has taken the ground, although not in the House, that there is not sufficient production at the present time to warrant such an expenditure as would make adequate a system for the transportation of chilled meats. That may be true, but the minister must realize that it only requires the expenditure, and that the system would follow the guarantee and the business would follow in its wake. It is simply because cattle cannot be made to pay in that part of the country, where they should of all places pay, that there is not now the foundation for this industry. In eastern Canada, the market for the cattle is largely local. In western Canada that is not, and that cannot be the case. The market must be an export market and must be an adequate market if there is to he cattle industry. I think the minister should not be too much impressed by the present cattle situation in the west as not warranting the expenditure which would be necessary for this system. I do not purpose going further, but I would urge the minister, in justice to the House and in justice to the western members who are particularly interested in this question, that he do not dismiss it so briefly, as he seems disposed to do at the present time, but that he state to us-and it will be of use to use in future discussions-what specific objection he finds as a representative of the government to the proposals already made, what he considers defective or faulty in these proposals, and that he indicate to the House along what general lines he is prepared to go, because I may say once and for all, that certain, at all events, of the western members are determined to see that action, not too remote, is taken along this line.

All I can say to my hon. friend is that without having my notes and without having the proposition before me,
I could not undertake to discuss it. If the motion had been reached I would have been prepared to go into the matter. I have not all the information here, and I could not possibly answer the question that my hon. friend has put to me.

cerned he did not expect that ho would be looked upon as deputy Minister of Agriculture. I wish to read the minister's own words to show that such was the case. In reply to my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) he made use of this language, as will be found on page 4356, ' Hansard,' 1903:
My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson), of course,' must be constitutionally blind to the appearance of anybody having a seat on the floor who is not a member of this House. I can tell the hon. member that the deputy Minister of Agriculture now is Mr. George F. O'Halloran, and that he was appointed within the last year to succeed the late deputy, Mr. W. B. Scarth. There is another point, and I will tell the hon. minister my own practice. bespeak hon. gentlemen's assistance in that direction.

perience, and whether Canadian tobacco was being received more favourably by the people, and whether it was being cured better.

[DOT] w'sh to point out to the minister that instead of knocking at his doors, instead of asking him to aid them every year, as is done by the counties, it might 'be better for him to put a small vote in the estimates which would be a great benefit to those four
counties, it might result in great improvement.

. ^r* FISHER. While I object to smok-mg chewing, or anything of that kind, while I do not do any of those things myself, and think it would be much better if nobody else did, still, if tobacco is to be used, I think the better the (tobaocto that is used the better.

Where were the experiments carried on?

A considerable number of boxes were put into cold storage at London in the Cold Storage Company's warehouse there, some in Montreal, some in St. John, New Brunswick, and some in a frost proof but not cold storage building at Ottawa to compare the results when kept in good cold but not refrigerator storage.

No, we paid the usual rates for storage to these companies, just as any one else would.

sincere and most sympathetic consideration. I have no doubt that when it is organized and arranged Canada would present such a magnificent display as would charm, enchant and attract everybody that came to see it, and that instead of a modest estimate of 500,000 people there would be over a million people who would come to see it. (Translation.) measures to educate the people in preventative means, and with that object in view, I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that the Dominion government should institute a tobacco exhibit at each of the Dominion exhibitions. The suggestion has been made that we should have a fishery exhibit, an agriculture exhibit, a railway exhibit and so on at these exhibitions, but the government has never undertaken to do so. To encourage the production and use of superior seeds of farm crops and for the enforcement of the Seed Control Act, $50,000.

So long as you allow noxious seeds to be scattered broadcast through the Dominion by means of the screenings which are sold for foodstuffs there is very little use in your spending money to combat the spread of weeds. These screenings from the western provinces are sent to Fort William, and are then shipped to the eastern provinces. When I mentioned this matter a short time ago the minister said it was a provincial affair, but I certainly think it is a matter which the Dominion Department of Agriculture should attend to. Many of the most dangerous weed seeds come in these screenings. It is poor policy to expend
$50,0)10 to try and get pure seed when we allow these foul seeds to be distributed in that way at a loss of hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars to our farmers in the course of a year. Last year in the province of Ontario it was estimated that there was a shortage of $l,uo0,000 in the crop because of the sow thistle alone. If these people are determined to put these screenings on the market they should be compelled to try and get rid of the impure seeds in some way.

I sympathize very much with the views expressed by the hon. member. The information in the department shows that many weed seeds are contained in feedstuffs. I do not know what remedy can be applied, but I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Sexsmith) that the department will investigate the matter with a view to seeing what can be done.
I am glad the minister has promised to look into the matter, but I would remind him that six months' delay means a great loss to the farmers.
We do not think we can deal with it under the law as it stands to-day.

Then an amendment should have been introduced in the Bill passed this session, giving the government authority to take preventative measures. I would not advocate the destruction of these feedstuffs if any other means can be found to purify them, but I think that if they^ were kiln dried the germinating quality of these seeds would be destroyed. Our expenditure to procure pure seeds will be nullified if we do not put a stop to this, practice.

Last year notice was given that if applications were made to the department for seeds up to a certain date in February, the seeds would be supplied.
I informed a number of people in my county, and they sent me their applications Most of those applications were honoured, and a great deal of satisfaction was given to the people by the seed they obtained. I would like to know if similar applications will be honoured if sent in each year. Some of the farmers who sent in applications this year have informed me that they have not received any seed.

We send the seed for the year in which the application comes, but do not repeat it, and we make it a condition of sending the seed that the recipient report to us at the end of the season the result of his sowing the seed. We do that as a precaution against the seed being neglected or not used. One of the advantages which the country derives from the distribution of seed is that the small quantity of seed with which the farmer is sup-

plied mutiplies year after year. ^ Another advantage is that we get a great deal cf information as to the adaptability of the seed to different localities, which is useful to our experts. If we send a sample to a farmer, we expect him in return to' send us a report.
Do you send a form with the seed?

Yes, always, and when a farmer neglects to send that report we are a little chary about sending him another sample. I do not say we do not send him one, but we reprimand him, and perhaps say that if he does not make a report on the second sample we will not send him another. We do not allow lists of farmers to be-sent in for these purpose. We found when that was done that much seed was wasted. We have to get the personal application of the farmer as a guarantee of good faith.

Probably the department, in sending out the seed this year has not taken into account the fact that this season is exceptionally early, which perhaps accounts for the farmers calling attention to the fact that they have not received the seed.
We send out the samples as rapidly as we can.

The increase of $1,000 is in consequence of an increased allotment to the nuns who take charge of the cases at Traeadie.
Is this disease increasing or decreasing?
